#5502. Exclusive: Menlo IRIS extension gives security teams control over AI use without a new browser

Browser security company Menlo Security Inc. today launched the Menlo IRIS Browser Extension, a new offering that adds its enterprise browser security controls to the browsers employees already use with no need to switch them to separate secure ones.

Delivered as a centrally managed extension, Menlo IRIS is said to give security teams visibility into and control over generative artificial intelligence use, data movement, files and third-party extensions. Installation is claimed to take only hours, as no additional hardware is needed.

Chief Executive Bill Robbins, who took over the top job from co-founder Amir Ben-Efraim in February, said security teams have known for some time that the browser is a blind spot. Many have nonetheless held off on fixing it to avoid replacing an existing security stack, which typically means a big migration project, he added.

“Menlo IRIS removes those obstacles,” Robbins said. “Even a small team can get essential security running quickly on the browsers employees already use.”

To make its case, Menlo pointed to Verizon Communications Inc.’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, released in May, which found regular AI use on corporate devices tripled from 15% to 45% of employees in a single year. Some 67% of people accessing AI services on corporate devices were found to be using noncorporate accounts, with more than 15% of users at the average company also running unauthorized AI browser extensions.

Among the headline capabilities is an audit of third-party browser extensions. Menlo says the audit covers every extension installed across a company, with an enterprise-wide inventory, real-time risk profiling and management controls all included. Few security teams have a count of the extensions their users have installed, according to Menlo. The company also warned that an extension’s risk profile can change at any time without notice.

Data-loss controls cover the clipboard, printing, uploads and downloads, with watermarking, read-only pages, restrictions on developer tools and screenshot deterrence also included. Web filtering steers users toward sanctioned tools, including generative AI services, with limits on what data can be entered into them offered as an alternative to banning the tools outright.

File security is part of the package as well, with inline inspection for data loss prevention violations, viruses and malware. For customers that want it, content disarm and reconstruction can be switched on to strip malicious content from files so they remain usable. Also available as an add-on is HEAT Shield AI for protection against zero-day phishing, social engineering and malvertising at the time of the click.

Deployment is through the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Intune, Jamf or other device management tools, with support for Chrome, Edge, Safari, Firefox and Chromium-based AI browsers. Since nobody has to switch browsers, security patches from each browser’s vendor are said to keep reaching users as normal.

Most controls are enforced inside the browser session itself, which the company says removes the need for a proxy to route traffic. Menlo IRIS is intended to sit alongside existing network and endpoint tools.

The Menlo IRIS Browser Extension is available now.

Menlo Security has raised $250 million in funding, including a $100 million round in November 2020. Investors in the company include Vista Equity Partners Management, JPMorgan Chase & Co., American Express Ventures and General Catalyst Group Management.

#5501. Rolls-Royce is announcing a $2 billion stock buyback as demand grows

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The £1.5 billion interim repurchase is due to finish by Feb. 25, 2027 and is part of a £7 billion-£9 billion plan through 2028

Rolls-Royce announced an interim stock buyback of £1.5 billion ($1.99 billion) on Thursday, according to The Wall Street Journal. The company said the buyback will be completed by its full-year results on Feb. 25, 2027.

The interim buyback is part of an existing £7 billion to £9 billion buyback program across 2026 to 2028, the company said. It added that it has completed most of its previously announced £2.5 billion buyback for 2026. Rolls-Royce said the move signals its belief that its cash generation will keep expanding on a durable basis.

The company said its backlog of orders for large engines has swelled to roughly 2,500 units. Orders in the second half include 70 Trent 7000 engines for Avolon and 22 Trent 7000 engines for the Cathay Group. Air China selected 15 Trent XWB-84 engines, and Philippine Airlines selected 18 Trent XWB-97 engines.

The company said large engine flying hours were up 4% from a year earlier over the first 10 months of 2026, at 114% of the 2019 level.

In Power Systems, order intake in the first nine months of the year rose 62% from a year earlier. The order backlog stood at a record £8.6 billion at the end of September, up from £8.0 billion at the half-year mark. Rolls-Royce said it is finalizing a multi-year deal to provide a hyperscaler with backup engines, together with a framework agreement that runs through 2031.

Rolls-Royce also held to its full-year targets, forecasting free cash flow of £3.8 billion to £4.0 billion and underlying operating profit of £4.7 billion to £4.9 billion. It plans to reassess its medium-term goals alongside its annual results due in February, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Rolls-Royce stock rose about 2.5% in early trading in London. The stock has gained 20% so far this year.

The company raised its full-year guidance in July as demand grew across its civil aerospace, defense and power systems divisions. First-half underlying operating profit was £2.5 billion, up 46% from a year earlier.

#5500. SupplyHouse Announces Plan to Open Atlanta Facility, Expanding Fulfillment Network to Deliver Faster Shipping Across Southeast

Location strengthens one-day footprint to Georgia, Florida and Carolinas

MELVILLE, N.Y., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SupplyHouse, a leading online supplier of plumbing, HVAC and electrical supplies, today announced plans to open a new fulfillment center in Atlanta, Georgia, further expanding the company's national distribution network to reduce shipping times, improve product availability and make it easier for customers throughout the Southeast to get the supplies they need.

The 715,000-square-foot fulfillment center will include 35,000 square feet of office space and represents another strategic investment in SupplyHouse's growing infrastructure, positioning inventory closer to customers while increasing the company's ability to provide fast, dependable delivery. The facility strengthens SupplyHouse's nationwide fulfillment network to five locations â Atlanta, Nevada, New Jersey, Ohio and Texas -- and supports the company's long-term commitment to serving contractors, trade professionals and DIYers where they live and work.

"Every investment we make in our fulfillment network is driven by one goal: making it faster and easier for our customers to get the products they need," said SupplyHouse Chief Operating Officer Nando Cunha. "By expanding our presence in the southeast, we're bringing inventory closer to our customers, reducing transit times and continuing to deliver the reliable service our customers count on every day."

SupplyHouse's planned facility will grow the company's one-day footprint for deliveries, with customers in Georgia, Florida and the Carolinas getting supplies in-hand faster. With optimized receiving, storage, picking and packing operations, the fulfillment center will be built to improve efficiency and shorten delivery times for customers who depend on SupplyHouse to keep jobs and projects moving. SupplyHouse offers customers 350,000 products from more than 500 of the industry's top brands.

Opening in 2027, the new SupplyHouse facility will be located at 3090 Highway 42 near Atlanta's Locus Grove area. The company will add more than 300 people in management, administrative support, technical positions, operators, maintenance and quality control in Atlanta.

#5499. Cosmos Hub Approves Gaia v29 With 99.41% Support Ahead of October 28th Upgrade

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Proposal #1059 passed with 49.59% turnout as the chain counts down now to block 33,618,500 on October 28th, where validators are told to run the security-patched v29.0.1 binary, not the version named in the proposal.

The Cosmos Hub's latest upgrade drew almost no opposition. About 168.5 million ATOM voted on Proposal #1059, and only 2,335 ATOM voted No. Under that one-sided result is an unusual change: the Hub's stakers voted to remove the governance route that earlier generations of Cosmos proposals used to change the chain's own settings.

Proposal #1059 schedules the upgrade of the Cosmos Hub to Gaia v29.0.0. It finished voting on October 27 at 12:00 UTC with a PASSED result. The vote approves the upgrade, but the software has not run yet. The chain still has to reach the upgrade height, halt, and restart on the new binary. Until that happens, Gaia v29 is approved but not yet live.

On-chain records show 49.59% of staked ATOM voted, against a 40% quorum requirement. Yes took 99.41% of the vote, or 167,514,965 ATOM. No With Veto took 0.58% (982,855 ATOM), Abstain took 0.01% (14,360 ATOM), and No rounds to 0.00% (2,335 ATOM).

The veto share is the main number to watch in a Cosmos governance vote, because a large enough veto rejects a proposal even if Yes wins. At 0.58%, the veto bloc was far too small to matter. That fits the proposal's nature. It is a maintenance release that removes deprecated code and updates dependencies, and it has no economic or political stakes.

The forum discussion covered one governance point: a delegator's own vote overrides their validator's vote. A few large validators did not decide the result on their own. Delegators could have overridden them, and very few chose to vote differently.

The proposal names v29.0.0, but operators are not supposed to run that build at the upgrade height. On October 23, three days into voting, the Gaia team tagged v29.0.1 and updated the official forum post to recommend it.

The patch changes only one thing: it rebuilds Gaia with Go 1.26.10 instead of Go 1.26.7. That picks up the Go security fix tracked as CVE-2026-111943 (GO-2026-6809). The project's upgrade notes call v29.0.1 a non-state-breaking patch release, so it computes the same chain state as v29.0.0. Nodes that already installed v29.0.0 can switch at any time by replacing the binary and restarting.

Operators using Cosmovisor need to know one detail. The on-chain upgrade name stays v29.0.0, so the v29.0.1 binary still goes into the upgrades/v29.0.0/bin/ directory. If a validator names the folder after the patch version, Cosmovisor will not find the binary when the chain halts. The project's sample service configuration has automatic binary download turned off, which means each operator has to put the correct binary in place before the halt.

Gaia v29 removes the x/params module from the Cosmos Hub. That module is the original, centralized store for parameters, and it backed the legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route. The release changelog lists the change under API-breaking changes: "The legacy ParameterChangeProposal governance route and cosmos.params.v1beta1.Query service are no longer available."

In practice, governance has already moved on. Each module now owns its parameters, and changes go through that module's own governance message. The legacy route remained as a fallback, and v29 removes it. The rate-limiting module was the last part of the Hub still wired to the old params subspace. In v29 it no longer depends on it.

The forum Q&A states who is affected. RPC providers, wallets, explorers, and governance dashboards should check whether they still call the params v1beta1 query service or create legacy parameter-change proposals. After the upgrade, those calls will fail on the Hub. For most users nothing changes. The proposal requires no token migration, and balances, delegations, and IBC assets are unaffected.

The second API-breaking item affects multisig accounts specifically. Gaia v29 moves the Hub from Cosmos SDK v0.53.4 to v0.53.8, and the changelog warns: "As of cosmos-sdk v0.53.8, --gas auto gas simulation is broken for multisig senders. Multisig transactions must specify a fixed --gas value until this is fixed upstream."

This matters in practice. The Hub's weekly update of October 22 said the problem applies to the Community Pool migration multisig. That multisig is handling a USDC.n migration spend that was moving toward an on-chain proposal during the same week. Treasury signers, custody desks, and DAO operators who build transactions with --gas auto will need to set gas by hand until the upstream SDK is fixed.

The same release also brings CometBFT from 0.38.23 to 0.38.25, the IBC rate-limiting middleware from 10.1.0 to 10.7.0, and runc from 1.2.8 to 1.3.6. It also moves the build toolchain from Go 1.25 to Go 1.26.

The upgrade handler, the code that runs once at the upgrade height, does more cleanup than the proposal summary describes. It first deletes everything in the deprecated provider store, the state left over from the Hub's time as an Interchain Security provider. Next it wipes the legacy x/params store. Last, it removes a receipt left behind by the earlier v28.3.1 balance migration.

The code also shows how cautious the Gaia team is about the upgrade. The stores stay mounted, and their contents are cleared as ordinary state changes. Unmounting them entirely could cause version-mismatch errors when nodes load the chain from disk. Gaia v29 has also run on the Hub's provider testnet since October 13, about two weeks before mainnet.

At 15:32 UTC on October 27, Mintscan showed block 33,618,500 as "not yet created". The chain was at block 33,604,199, with 14,301 blocks to go. At the recent average block time of 5.722 seconds, the Mintscan countdown for block 33,618,500 estimated the height for about 14:16 UTC on October 28. The forum's original estimate was 13:50 UTC. The real time depends on how fast blocks are produced over the next day.

When the chain reaches that height, block production stops. It restarts only after validators holding more than two-thirds of voting power are back online on the new binary. That makes the vote result only half the story. The other half is whether validators show up on v29.0.1 promptly, so that the halt lasts minutes rather than hours.

#5498. U.S. charges Canadian drug importer CanaRx's treasurer in yearslong smuggling scheme

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Company president Bob Howard is wanted in the federal case, and CANARX's general counsel says both Howards deny the charges

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of Canadian prescription drug company CanaRx, faces smuggling and conspiracy charges after his arrest on Nov. 8, according to CNBC.

The arrest warrant adds two further counts: putting misbranded medications into interstate commerce and importing drugs unlawfully, according to CNBC. No plea is on file.

His brother, Bob Howard, is CanaRx's president and a director. He is sought as part of the federal probe and remains at large, according to CNBC.

FDA special agent Dustin Dobbs wrote in an affidavit that "there is probable cause to believe that (CanaRx) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States," according to CNBC. The affidavit does not name the medications the agency believes were imported illegally. The criminal complaint covers Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

CanaRx general counsel Joseph Morris responded in a statement. "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court," Morris told CNBC.

CanaRx is based in Windsor, Ontario. On its website, the company says it sources medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand, according to CNBC.

The FDA has scrutinized the company for several years, according to CNBC. The agency sent CanaRx a warning letter in 2019 saying the company was replacing medicines that U.S. clinicians had prescribed and the FDA had approved with unapproved ones. Morris countered that CanaRx was not deceiving patients, though the company consented to end imports of medications requiring administration by a physician. In 2023, the FDA confiscated a CanaRx shipment of medication that, according to the agency, might have been mislabeled and fake, based on an email a patient received, which CNBC obtained.

CanaRx is one of a group of businesses known as alternative funding programs, which offer high-cost specialty drugs to employers at lower prices. These programs frequently buy drugs abroad and deliver them straight to patients, which federal authorities have called unlawful and a safety hazard, according to CNBC. The FDA permits Americans to bring in drugs for their own use under certain circumstances, provided no domestic supply exists.

Gilead $GILD Sciences has a pending civil lawsuit that names CanaRx among several firms it alleges unlawfully brought Biktarvy, its HIV drug, into the country, according to CNBC. CanaRx has not responded to that suit. A Gilead spokesperson told CNBC on Wednesday that the company welcomes "the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk."

#5496. Nvidia's board is preparing to oust Jensen Huang over two affairs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Huang has said he is opposed to succession planning, and it remained uncertain who would take over if he is ultimately removed

Nvidia $NVDA's board is getting ready to push out CEO Jensen Huang following two extramarital affairs, according to The Wall Street Journal. The board convened Wednesday to consider Huang's future, and Nvidia had yet to disclose any decision on Thursday morning.

Nvidia stock fell 8% in after-hours trading Wednesday to $159.95, after closing at $173.73. The stock was still off almost 8% ahead of Thursday's open.

Huang told employees in a Sunday letter that he had cheated on his wife. That affair was with Alice Huang, a former executive at Megaspeed, a data company based in Singapore. U.S. intelligence officials think she is employed by Chinese spy agencies.

The second affair was with Kimberly Powell, who runs Nvidia’s healthcare business, according to The Journal and other outlets. Powell did not respond to the Journal’s requests for comment.

Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, has spent months under scrutiny from U.S. investigators over suspected chip smuggling, according to Bloomberg. Megaspeed and Nvidia have denied wrongdoing. The Justice Department is heading several probes that touch on Alice Huang, according to The Journal.

Huang, 63, has said he is opposed to succession planning, and it remained uncertain who would take over. He is Nvidia's biggest shareholder, holding roughly 3.6% of its stock.

Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation on Sunday, overseen by a committee of independent directors. The independent directors retained former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct it, the company said Tuesday. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised and that it had confidence in Huang.

China’s Foreign Ministry has called the espionage allegation unsubstantiated. Nvidia is scheduled to report fiscal third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

#5495. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns following affairs scandal

Nvidia Corp.’s board of directors today announced the resignation of Jensen Huang, now former chief executive and president, amid a scandal, naming Colette Kress, current executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The news arrives following numerous industry reports that the board intended to replace Huang as CEO after revelations of a second extramarital relationship with an executive at Nvidia, coming mere days after he admitted to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

News initially broke over the weekend that Huang had an affair with Alice Huang, no relation, an executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed International Pte. Ltd. and an alleged Chinese spy. The Information reported on Tuesday that Alice Huang facilitated $7.5 billion in chip sales to China. According to another report, Huang also had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who serves as vice president of healthcare.

The New York Times reported last month that United Sates authorities concluded Alice Huang acted as a Chinese intelligence asset. Upon revelations of the affair, the AP reported that U.S. President Trump announced that the Federal Bureau of Investigation was looking into the allegations, while adding, “I think that he’ll be in good shape.”

Late Wednesday, the Nvidia board met to decide whether to oust Huang or not and discussed a potential replacement as CEO. Huang has no obvious successor and owns around 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. Reportedly, the board sought counsel from an outside firm to find someone to fill the role.

With the announcement, Nvidia stock fell more than 10% to 152.71 in premarket trading. Yahoo Finance calculated that Nvidia has lost more than $600 billion in market value since the previous Thursday, likely with more shocks to come.

“Nvidia’s strength has always come from its people, and together with our leadership team, I am committed to building on the extraordinary foundation Jensen created over the last 33 years,” said Kress, now interim CEO and current CFO. “We will continue advancing the work that has made Nvidia a leader in accelerated computing and AI, and execute on the opportunities ahead.”

Kress has served as executive vice president and CFO since joining in September 2013. Her accolades include leading the company’s finance organization and working to build the company’s dominance in the AI chip industry. Before joining Nvidia, she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at leading technology companies, including Cisco Systems Inc. and Microsoft Corp.

Huang is best known for cofounding Nvidia in 1993 and has served as its CEO since. His departure will likely send further ripples through the AI silicon and software industry. He has been deeply involved in Nvidia’s product strategy and built longstanding customer relationships, helming the company as it became the colossal behemoth it is today.

Nvidia commands roughly 80% of the data-center AI chip market, although industry estimates vary by methodology. Epoch Artificial Intelligence Inc. puts its share of AI computing power shipped at 63% in the second quarter of 2026. Other market carve-outs include custom chips built by cloud companies within the broader supply, including Google LLC’s TPU at 25%, Amazon Inc.’s custom silicon at 5% and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s AI hardware accelerators at 4%.

Nvidia is expected to report its third-quarter fiscal 2027 finances on November 17.

The crypto market is showing another worrying sign for altcoin investors. Ethereum and Solana price are struggling to recover as Bitcoin dominance climbs toward 61%. Ethereum trades at the $2,050 level, while Solana changes hands below $85. Both coins remain under pressure as market sentiment deteriorates.

Bitcoin dominance has reached 60.5%, gaining one percentage point over the past 30 days. The shift shows investors are favoring Bitcoin over altcoins during the market downturn.

Bitcoin dominance measures BTC’s share of the total crypto market cap. When the metric rises, Bitcoin is outperforming the rest of the market. The reading puts Bitcoin’s market share at 60.4%, compared with 59.4% one month earlier. Ethereum dominance, meanwhile, has fallen to 10.3%, losing 0.65 percentage points over the same period.

One metric to understand is that Bitcoin dominance can rise even when BTC itself loses value. Investors do not necessarily need to buy Bitcoin aggressively. Altcoin valuations simply need to fall faster.

This appears consistent with Wednesday’s market conditions. The total crypto market cap has dropped around 4.1% over 24 hours. Only 27 of the top 100 cryptocurrencies were trading higher.

Ethereum has also struggled to maintain its position. Its market share has declined while Bitcoin continues commanding a larger portion of the market. The latest dominance figures offer little encouragement for altcoins.

Ethereum price weakness is particularly important because ETH traditionally plays a major role in altcoin market recoveries. Its declining dominance suggests investors remain cautious about moving beyond Bitcoin.

Solana’s performance tells a similar story. Despite its established position among major altcoins, SOL has struggled to outperform during the latest downturn. Neither asset currently provides convincing evidence of an aggressive return to altcoin risk.

Bitcoin dominance has gained one percentage point in 30 days while Ethereum’s market share has declined, and sentiment remains firmly negative. This creates an uncomfortable combination for altcoin holders.

#5493. Identity Theft Prompts Industry Veteran to Launch American Institute for Identity Safety

New institute will advance nonpartisan reforms for victim restoration, stronger identity security, and protection from scams and AI-enabled deception.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eric Haller spent more than 30 years working in identity and fraud prevention. Then his own identity was stolen, giving him a firsthand view of how difficult it can be for victims to clear their names and restore their lives.

That experience led Haller to establish the American Institute for Identity Safety (AIIS) and to focus on identity safety through his fellowship at Harvard University's Advanced Leadership Initiative.

About 18 million Americans are affected by identity fraud each year, according to Javelin Strategy & Research's 2026 Identity Fraud Study, so the need extends far beyond his own experience.

AIIS launches with a central question: What should happen after someone says, "That's NOT me!"?

"I had spent decades working on systems designed to detect fraud and protect identity. Becoming a victim gave me a different perspective," said Haller, founder of AIIS. "We have invested heavily in detecting fraud, but people still face a fragmented process for resolving the damage. Victims need a clear path to getting their lives back."

The institute's initial focus is on proposed state and federal reforms to give identity-theft victims faster relief and a coordinated path to restoration. Under the proposed approach, victims could securely verify their identity, submit evidence through a national hub, receive provisional protection while claims are reviewed, and get timely decisions that participating institutions can act on. Strong identity verification, human oversight, and safeguards against fraudulent claims would be central to the process.

"Victims need a process that works, and banks need a process they can trust," Haller said. "A coordinated approach can help both, reducing the burden on innocent people while giving institutions greater confidence in how claims are resolved."

AIIS's broader mission spans national identity security and scam protection, with particular attention to children, older adults, and other vulnerable populations. Its work will connect better recovery with stronger prevention, including ways to make stolen personal information less useful to criminals.

Artificial intelligence adds urgency to that agenda. Deepfake voices and video create new opportunities for impersonation, while emerging technologies also offer ways to strengthen identity verification and fraud prevention.

"Identity safety means preventing harm where we can and helping people recover when prevention fails," Haller said.

Haller brings senior leadership experience from his time with Experian and TransUnion. He created and led Experian DataLabs and served as TransUnion's Chief Data & Analytics Officer. His work combines industry experience in identity, fraud, and artificial intelligence with the perspective of someone who has navigated identity theft personally.

AIIS is inviting policymakers, researchers, consumer advocates, and industry leaders to help develop practical, nonpartisan solutions.

Learn more at www.americaninstituteforidentitysafety.com.

About AIIS: The American Institute for Identity Safety, Inc. is a California nonprofit corporation advancing nonpartisan public-policy solutions focused on identity-theft victim restoration, national identity security, and protection from scams and AI-enabled deception.

Media Contact: Eric Haller, American Institute for Identity Safety[email protected] (949) 648-3406

#5492. Nebius stock falls after cutting its 2026 revenue forecast on delays

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Nebius reported third-quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571%, while guiding for $12 billion to $13 billion in 2027 revenue

Nebius Group cut its 2026 revenue forecast on Thursday, guiding to the bottom of its earlier $3 billion to $3.4 billion range because some third-party capacity has been delayed, the company said. Nebius stock fell between 10% and 12% in premarket trading.

The AI cloud company reported third-quarter revenue of $980.8 million, up 571% from a year earlier. That beat analyst estimates of $907.5 million, according to CNBC. Net loss was $37.5 million, or 13 cents per share, versus $119.6 million, or 50 cents per share, in the prior-year period. Adjusted EBITDA was $465.8 million, compared with a loss of $5.2 million a year earlier.

Some third-party capacity that Nebius planned to have running by the end of this year will now arrive in the first six months of 2027, the company said. It said the agreements covering that capacity are still in force, so a portion of 2026 revenue will shift into 2027. Analysts polled by FactSet expected full-year revenue of $3.35 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Nebius issued an initial 2027 outlook of $12 billion to $13 billion in revenue, "reflecting a conservative approach to the pace of our build-out," the company said. It expects to bring over a gigawatt of additional capacity online every year.

The company expects capital expenditures of $27 billion in 2026, up from its previous guidance of $20 billion to $25 billion. It expects $40 billion to $45 billion in 2027.

CEO Arkady Volozh said customer prepayments, along with financing secured by current contracts with investment-grade clients, should pay for 75% to 85% of 2027 capital expenditures.

"Our focus remains on building a healthy, profitable business for the long term," Volozh said in a letter to shareholders, according to The Wall Street Journal.

During the third quarter, the company received proceeds of $5.75 billion from issuing convertible notes, according to its financial statements. Nebius stock climbed 15% on Wednesday.

Ballmer Group awards Genesys Works $4M to expand paid high school internships as AI reshapes entry-level work.

The investment will fund Genesys Works' growth through 2030, including testing new approaches to program delivery and updating its curriculum to meet employers' changing needs. It also helps kick off Genesys Works' fundraising campaign tied to its 25th anniversary in 2027, supporting its vision for the next 25 years of career opportunity and economic mobility.

Through paid, yearlong internships with employers such as Accenture, Kirkland & Ellis, Mayo Clinic and Target, Genesys Works students take on real responsibilities, build professional relationships and learn how their education connects to career opportunitiesâall before graduating from high school. A September 2026 report from the National Association of State Boards of Education notes that as many as three in four Gen Z high school students feel unprepared for life after graduation, and about a third of teachers think their students are not ready for what comes next.

Many are the first in their families to attend college.

"Genesys Works shows that when high school students get real professional experience, it changes their trajectory," said Emma Uman, Director, Career Success at Ballmer Group. "They carry that experience into college and careers, earning degrees, building strong professional lives, and often outearning their parents. We're investing so that more students have that opportunity."

The value of that opportunity in high school lasts well beyond graduation. According to Genesys Works' 2025 Impact Report, alumni seven or more years out of the program earn an average annual income of $67,000. Of those alumni, 73% report earning more than at least one parent and 20% own their home. Alumni also earn bachelor's degrees at 2.4 times the rate of their peers within six years.

Since its founding in 2002, Genesys Works has served more than 14,000 students in Chicago, Houston, Jacksonville, Minneapolis/St. Paul, Nashville, New York City, the San Francisco Bay Area, Tulsa and Washington's National Capital Region.

#5490. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

#5489. Foxconn posted profit up 34%, beating expectations on AI server demand

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Foxconn expects AI rack shipments to grow by a high double-digit rate in 2027, while the chairman flagged tight chip and component supply

Foxconn, the world’s largest contract electronics maker, reported a 34% rise in third-quarter net profit to NT$77.52 billion ($2.36 billion) on Thursday as demand for AI servers stayed strong.

The result beat an LSEG consensus estimate of NT$69.6 billion, according to Reuters. Revenue for the quarter reached NT$3.016 trillion, and cloud and networking products made up more than half of it.

Foxconn kept its forecast of strong revenue growth for this year. The company projected that shipments of its AI server racks would climb by a high double-digit percentage in 2027, helped by a growing roster of server clients and a wider global production network.

"We remain very confident about our operations next year and expect continued growth," Chairman Young Liu said at an earnings conference, according to Reuters. Liu said he expects capital spending on AI by cloud service providers around the world to keep climbing next year. He said cloud and networking products should account for more than 60% of revenue within three to five years.

Liu also pointed to risks. Semiconductors, memory and certain critical parts are in short supply throughout AI and consumer-electronics sectors, he said. He said new production capacity should progressively relieve the crunch, though he expects demand to outpace available supply next year. Liu said he takes a guarded view of prospects for the PC segment.

Liu described the geopolitical and economic backdrop worldwide as highly uncertain, adding that movements in inflation and currency rates could weigh on operating costs. He said the U.S. midterm elections are unlikely to move the industry much in the near term, though their longer-run consequences deserve watching.

Foxconn stock slipped 0.8% at Thursday's close, before the results were published, while Taiwan's benchmark stock index dropped 2.6%. According to The Wall Street Journal, the shares are down roughly 20% from their June high.

Foxconn builds AI servers for Nvidia $NVDA and is erecting plants in Mexico and Texas to produce them, according to Reuters.

#5488. HelloNation Features Banking Expert Trent Nelson on Common Checking Account Mistakes

The article highlights simple habits that help customers avoid unnecessary fees and better manage their everyday banking.

GLUCKSTADT, Miss., Nov. 12, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- What are the most common checking account mistakes to avoid?

HelloNation answers that question in an article featuring insights from Banking Expert Trent Nelson of PriorityOne Bank. The article explains how understanding a checking account and making use of available banking tools can help customers avoid common mistakes while improving everyday financial management.

The HelloNation article explains that even small oversights can create unnecessary fees, missed payments, or financial frustration. Whether someone recently opened a checking account or has been banking for years, developing consistent habits can help maximize the value of a checking account while avoiding preventable issues.

One of the first areas highlighted in the article is understanding account requirements. Some checking account options include minimum balance requirements, monthly maintenance fees, or transaction limits that customers may overlook when opening an account. Reviewing account requirements carefully helps ensure the selected account matches individual banking habits and reduces the likelihood of unnecessary charges.

The article also emphasizes the importance of monitoring account balances regularly. Checking a checking account on a routine basis helps customers stay aware of available funds, identify unexpected transactions, and reduce the risk of accidental overdrafts. Spending just a few minutes each week reviewing account activity can prevent avoidable financial surprises.

Another valuable tool discussed in the article is account alerts. Many financial institutions allow customers to customize account alerts for low balances, large purchases, direct deposits, and unusual activity. Enabling account alerts helps customers stay informed without constantly logging into their accounts while also providing added awareness if unauthorized transactions occur.

Regularly reviewing transactions through online banking is another habit encouraged in the article. Online banking allows customers to verify purchases, confirm deposits, and identify possible errors before they become larger concerns. Frequent use of online banking also helps customers better understand their spending patterns and maintain greater control over their finances.

The article also explains how mobile banking simplifies account management. Mobile banking applications allow customers to review balances, transfer funds, deposit checks, manage debit cards, and receive notifications from virtually anywhere. By taking advantage of mobile banking, customers can stay connected to their finances throughout the month instead of waiting for monthly statements.

Another recommendation is to review account features periodically. As financial needs change through new jobs, growing families, or retirement, the article notes that a community bank can help customers determine whether another checking account better fits their current lifestyle. A community bank can also explain available services, review account requirements, and answer questions as banking needs evolve.

The article further advises customers to keep contact information current so important account alerts, security notifications, and other account communications arrive without delay. Maintaining accurate information helps financial institutions communicate quickly when necessary.

The article concludes that managing a checking account successfully relies on simple, consistent habits rather than complicated financial strategies. By understanding account requirements, using account alerts, regularly reviewing activity through online banking, taking advantage of mobile banking, and working with a trusted community bank, customers can avoid common mistakes while making everyday banking more efficient and convenient.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Brent crude climbed as much as 1.8% to top $94 a barrel after falling on signs of higher Saudi exports

President Donald Trump said Thursday that Washington has no need to strike a bargain with Tehran, and crude prices recovered their earlier declines.

Trump made the comment in a Truth Social post. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" he wrote.

In London, Brent crude futures rose by as much as 1.8%, briefly moving above $94 per barrel. The January Brent contract was 1.1% higher at $93.78 as of 8:28 a.m. ET. West Texas Intermediate futures advanced 1.3%, changing hands at $87.62 a barrel.

The post fed concern that the U.S.-Iran war may continue with no resolution on the horizon, according to CNBC.

Iran has taken a firm position as well. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said the country will not send “a single atom” of its enriched nuclear stockpile abroad, according to Bloomberg.

Prices had fallen before Trump's post on signs that exports from the Persian Gulf were holding up. Saudi Arabia told OPEC that its output climbed 26% in October, reaching one of its highest monthly totals in years, according to Bloomberg. Iraq said its output hit a wartime peak, Bloomberg said.

Trump's remarks follow a week of swings in crude. On Sunday, he said additional U.S. strikes on Iran were improbable while negotiations to wind down the war advanced. Brent fell below $100 a barrel on Monday.

Oil also moved sharply in October. Brent rose 4% to around $104 a barrel on Oct. 8 after Trump said he did not want a deal with Iran to end the war. A tanker attack in the Persian Gulf coincided with that jump.

#5486. Resigned vs. fired: 6 differences that decide a CEO's exit pay

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CEO severance often hinges on whether a chief executive resigned or was fired, and these six differences shape cash pay, unvested equity, option deadlines and exit terms

A company's announcement of a CEO departure often uses neutral wording such as "stepping down." Behind that phrase sits a legal classification that can decide how much money changes hands. The same departure can be worth very different amounts. The result depends on whether the paperwork records a resignation, a termination without cause or a termination for cause.

The rules behind that classification are usually set long before anyone clears out an office. Boards and executives typically negotiate the terms when the CEO is hired or promoted. The employment agreement defines what counts as cause and what counts as good reason. The equity plan and individual grant agreements spell out what happens to stock awards at each kind of exit. By the time a departure arrives, much of the outcome is already written down.

That is why the definitions in a contract matter as much as the dollar figures when CEO severance is calculated. A resignation usually leaves an executive with less than a firing without cause. A firing for cause can leave even less. A resignation for good reason, as the contract defines it, is often treated much like a no-cause termination. Each label points to a different set of contract provisions.

The six differences below are a selection, not a complete list, and they reflect common U.S. practice. Every outcome depends on the specific employment agreement, plan documents and grant terms. A provision that appears in one executive's contract may be missing from another's.

The list starts with cash severance and the role of termination without cause. Next come good reason clauses, which can let an executive quit and still collect a package. A third difference is what a for-cause finding can erase. The list then turns to unvested stock options and restricted stock units, which often carry the most value. It covers the short windows for exercising options after a departure. It closes with the conditions attached to an exit. Those include the release of legal claims and restrictive covenants such as non-competes. They also include the Form 8-K disclosure a public company must file and the clawback rules that apply however a CEO leaves.

Together, these provisions explain how two departures that read alike in a headline can end on very different financial terms.

A CEO's employment agreement usually promises cash severance only if the board ends the job without cause. A chief executive who resigns voluntarily usually walks away with no severance payment at all.

That one distinction often decides whether a departing CEO leaves with a cash package or with only the pay already earned. Severance is a contractual benefit. U.S. federal law does not require employers to provide it. A CEO's right to severance comes from the employment agreement or from a company severance plan.

A termination without cause is a firing in which the board does not allege the kind of misconduct the contract defines as cause. A board might remove a CEO over results, strategy or a wish for new leadership. Under a typical agreement, that kind of exit triggers the severance promise.

The payment is often calculated as a multiple of the CEO's base salary and annual bonus. The multiple is negotiated, and it differs from one agreement to the next. Two CEOs with identical salaries can be owed very different sums when they are let go.

A voluntary resignation sits on the other side of the line. A CEO may leave to take another job, to retire or for personal reasons. The agreement typically treats that decision as the executive's own. The company usually owes salary through the final day of work and any benefits already earned, but no severance.

The structure gives the board room to act. It can replace a CEO without building a case for misconduct. The severance terms, set out in advance, establish what that decision will cost the company. For the executive, the same terms offer financial protection against being pushed out of the job.

Generous exit packages of this kind are often described with the informal label golden parachute. The amount a CEO dismissed without cause is actually owed depends on the wording of that executive's agreement, including how it defines cause and which payments it lists.

A CEO who resigns for good reason, as the employment agreement defines it, typically receives the same exit package as a chief executive the board terminated without cause. The clause turns a departure that looks voluntary into one that is paid like a firing.

The clause addresses a question of leverage. A board might want a CEO gone without paying severance. Without a good reason clause, it could make the job worse rather than end it. The executive would then have to choose between staying in a diminished role and quitting without severance. Good reason language closes that route by treating certain company actions as the equivalent of a dismissal.

Many agreements spell out what qualifies. Common examples include a material cut in pay, a material reduction in duties or a forced relocation. The word "material" carries weight in these clauses. The contract's terms, not the executive's view of the change, set where that line sits.

The triggers are negotiated one agreement at a time. No single list applies across companies. Two CEOs running similar businesses can hold very different protections. Some contracts define good reason broadly. Others limit it to a short set of specific events.

The clause usually comes with a procedure as well as a trigger. A CEO typically must give the company notice that identifies the condition said to amount to good reason. The company then gets a cure period — a window to reverse the pay cut, restore the duties or drop the relocation. Only if the company fails to fix the problem can the CEO resign and claim good reason treatment.

The cure period gives the board a chance to undo a change before it becomes a severance obligation. It also means a CEO who skips the notice step, or leaves before the window closes, risks being treated as having resigned voluntarily.

A single resignation letter can lead to a full severance package or to none. The result typically depends on whether a good reason condition in the contract was met. It also turns on whether the executive followed the notice and cure steps.

A CEO fired for cause typically leaves without severance, and the finding can also cost the executive other awards. Cause is a defined term in the employment agreement. Whether a firing qualifies depends on the contract's wording, not on how the board or the press describes the exit.

Cause definitions commonly cover fraud, a felony conviction, willful misconduct and a material breach of the agreement. The exact list is negotiated with each executive. The final version can be broader or narrower than that core set.

Small drafting choices matter. A clause that requires misconduct to be "willful" sets a higher bar than one that covers any misconduct. A clause tied to a felony conviction does not reach an indictment or an investigation that has not ended in a conviction. A company that wants more room to act typically pushes for broader language. A CEO candidate with bargaining power typically pushes for narrower language.

Weak performance is often left out of the definition. A board can still remove a CEO over poor results. That exit usually counts as a termination without cause. The executive then typically receives the severance the contract promises.

The label decides the money. A termination without cause typically triggers the package the agreement promises. A cause finding typically shuts that package off. Depending on the plan and award terms, it can also mean the loss of other compensation the executive would otherwise have kept.

The board's finding is not the last word. A CEO can dispute whether the conduct meets the contract's definition. Some executive agreements send such disputes to arbitration rather than court. The forum depends on the contract.

A dispute does not reopen every fact of the departure. It turns on a narrower question: whether the specific events fit the specific words the two sides agreed to. Because each definition is negotiated, the same conduct can count as cause under one CEO's contract and fall outside it under another's.

A CEO who resigns typically forfeits unvested stock options and restricted stock units, known as RSUs. A termination without cause often brings accelerated or continued vesting instead, depending on the award terms.

The gap comes from how equity grants are built. Boards usually award options or RSUs that vest over several years. Until an award vests, the executive does not own it outright. The grant works as a promise that depends on the executive staying with the company.

A stock option gives the holder the right to buy shares at a fixed price, called the exercise or strike price. An RSU is a promise to deliver shares, or sometimes their cash value, once vesting conditions are met. Both tie an executive's reward to staying with the company. Both can also disappear if the executive leaves before the vesting date.

Equity forfeiture on resignation follows from that design. When a CEO walks away voluntarily, the plan typically treats the unvested portion as unearned. Those awards go back to the company. Vested awards are a separate matter. They generally belong to the executive, subject to the plan's rules on exercising options.

A termination without cause often produces a different result. Grant agreements frequently soften the loss when the board, rather than the executive, ends the relationship. Accelerated vesting means some or all of the unvested awards vest at the moment of departure. Continued vesting means the awards keep vesting on their original schedule, as if the executive were still employed. Some agreements use one approach, some use the other and some combine them.

Performance-based awards add another layer. Many CEO grants vest only if the company hits set targets over a multi-year period. Agreements often spell out separately how those awards are handled after a no-cause exit.

The controlling terms usually sit in more than one document. The equity plan sets the general rules. Each grant agreement can set terms for that specific award. An employment agreement may also address what happens to equity on departure.

Grants made in different years can carry different terms. A single CEO can therefore face several outcomes at once, with some awards accelerating, others continuing and others lapsing. For a CEO whose pay leans heavily on stock, those award-by-award terms can determine how much unvested value survives a departure.

A departing CEO typically has a short, fixed period to exercise vested stock options before they lapse. Under U.S. tax law, an incentive stock option must be exercised within three months after employment ends to keep its incentive stock option treatment.

That three-month limit comes from the Internal Revenue Code's rules for incentive stock options, often called ISOs. Missing it does not by itself cancel the option. The option instead loses its favored status. If the plan still allows a later exercise, the option is taxed as a nonqualified stock option.

That change affects how the gain is taxed. With a nonqualified option, the spread between the exercise price and the stock's market value at exercise is taxed as ordinary income. With an ISO, exercise does not create ordinary income at that point. The spread can still count toward the alternative minimum tax.

Many company plans set a post-termination exercise window of similar length, whatever the tax label on the option. Once that window closes, unexercised vested options are typically forfeited. The clock usually starts on the date employment ends, not the date the departure is announced.

How the CEO left can change the length of that window. A for-cause termination can cut it to nothing. In that case, vested options can lapse when employment ends. Some employment or grant agreements allow a longer exercise period after a termination without cause. That extension is contract-specific, and there is no standard length across companies.

A longer window cannot normally run past the option's original expiration date. ISOs generally carry a maximum term of 10 years under the tax code. Plans typically state that a post-departure window ends on the earlier of its own deadline or the option's expiration.

The window also raises a cash question. Exercising an option means paying the exercise price, plus any tax due. Public companies often let executives use a broker-assisted cashless exercise, selling some of the shares to cover those costs. Whether that route is available depends on the plan.

Disability is handled differently. The tax code extends the ISO deadline to one year when employment ends because of permanent and total disability.

A departing CEO's severance is typically paid only after the executive signs a release of legal claims against the company. Several other obligations outlast the job however it ends, including restrictive covenants, a public disclosure filing and federal clawback rules.

The release is the condition attached to the money. By signing it, the CEO usually gives up the right to sue the company over the departure and the events leading up to it. In return, the company gets assurance that the payout settles the matter. A CEO who declines to sign typically forfeits the severance the agreement would otherwise provide.

Restrictive covenants work differently. Non-compete, non-solicit and confidentiality obligations are often written into the employment agreement or the equity award documents. They can continue to bind a CEO who resigned in the same way they bind one who was fired. A non-compete restricts where the former executive can work. A non-solicit limits recruiting former colleagues or approaching the company's customers. Confidentiality terms protect internal information after the CEO has left.

The Federal Trade Commission issued a rule in 2024 that targeted non-compete agreements. A federal court in Texas set that rule aside in August 2024. The covenant language in a CEO's own contract remains the document that defines what the executive can and cannot do after leaving.

Public companies also have to tell investors. A public company must report its CEO's departure on Form 8-K under Item 5.02, generally within four business days. That filing becomes part of the public record. The text of the announcement is often negotiated as part of the exit. One common point of negotiation is whether the company says the CEO is stepping down or was terminated.

Clawbacks are one area where the resigned-or-fired label makes no difference. SEC Rule 10D-1 and the matching NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards took effect on October 2, 2023. They require listed companies to recover incentive pay that was erroneously awarded, as shown by an accounting restatement. The rules reach both current and former executive officers. They apply regardless of fault. A CEO who left voluntarily and one who was dismissed face the same recovery obligation.
