#5485. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO: what happens next

Free daily briefing on global business news.

What happens when a CEO resigns, explained through Nvidia's Nov. 12 announcement: interim leadership, board statements, SEC disclosure rules, the successor search and the earnings call

A chief executive's resignation sets off a chain of board decisions, and many of them land within hours. The board has to put someone in charge of daily operations. It has to tell investors, employees and customers what changed. It has to start looking for a permanent leader. It also has to show that contracts, products and financial reporting will carry on as planned.

Nvidia $NVDA is now moving through that sequence. On Nov. 12, 2026, the company's board of directors said Jensen Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately. The board named Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO. She keeps the CFO role while she fills the top job. She will hold the interim post until the board names a permanent successor. The board said its search will consider both internal and external candidates.

The announcement left several questions open. Nvidia gave no reason for Huang's departure. It set no timeline for the search, named no candidates and disclosed no terms for Huang's exit, such as severance or equity. Other outlets have published reports about the circumstances, but those reports are unconfirmed. Nvidia did say it will release third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, Nov. 17, as scheduled, with its earnings call starting at 2 p.m. PT.

What Nvidia did disclose follows the standard steps of a leadership transition at a public company. That makes the case a practical way to understand what happens when a CEO resigns, from the first board statement to the first earnings report after the exit. The seven slides that follow cover the announcement itself, the choice of a sitting CFO as interim leader and the board's role. They also explain how a CEO search runs, what Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure rules require and how companies keep customers and product plans steady. Each slide separates what Nvidia has said from the general process that applies to U.S. public companies.

Nvidia $NVDA's board of directors announced on Nov. 12, 2026, that Jensen Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive officer and board member, effective immediately. The board delivered the news in a written press release.

The release quoted Harvey C. Jones and Colette Kress. It included no statement from Huang himself.

The announcement went out as a paid press release distributed by GLOBE NEWSWIRE and carried on Yahoo Finance. That makes it Nvidia's own account of the change. It contains what the company chose to disclose on that date and nothing more.

The board's wording set out how far the exit reaches. Some departing chief executives give up the CEO title but keep a board seat. Others move into an executive chair or adviser position. Nvidia's board said Huang left the board as well as the top executive job. The release does not say whether he will hold any advisory role. It also does not say whether he remains connected to the company in another way.

The timing differs from a planned handover. Many CEO transitions are announced weeks or months ahead. A set departure date leaves time for the outgoing and incoming leaders to overlap. An immediate effective date removes that overlap. A board in that position generally names interim leadership in the same announcement. Nvidia's release did so, naming Colette Kress, the company's executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO.

The release gave no reason for Huang's departure. It does not say whether the decision was his, the board's or a mutual one.

A written, public announcement also fits U.S. securities rules on fair disclosure. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Regulation Fair Disclosure in 2000. The rule bars public companies from sharing material nonpublic information with select analysts or investors without disclosing it publicly at the same time. A press release distributed over a newswire is one of the standard ways companies meet that requirement. A wire release reaches newsrooms, trading terminals and financial websites at about the same time. That limits the chance that one group of investors learns of a leadership change before everyone else.

Nvidia $NVDA's board named Colette Kress, the company's executive vice president and chief financial officer, as interim CEO after Jensen Huang's departure. Nvidia said she keeps the CFO job and will hold both roles until the board names a permanent successor.

The choice puts the company under an executive who already knows its finances in detail. Kress joined Nvidia in September 2013 and has served as CFO since then, according to the company. That is a run of more than 13 years in the same finance seat.

Her career before Nvidia was also in technology finance. Nvidia said she spent nearly 25 years in finance roles at technology companies before joining. Cisco $CSCO and Microsoft $MSFT were among those employers.

Harvey C. Jones, quoted in Nvidia's announcement, pointed to that familiarity. He said Kress has a deep understanding of the company's business, customers, operations and financial position.

An interim CEO fills a gap rather than setting a long-term direction. The role lets a board keep decisions moving while it runs a search. It also removes pressure to name a permanent leader overnight.

Picking an insider for the temporary post has a practical logic. An outside executive would first need time to learn the company's products, people and commitments. An existing officer can act from the first day.

A finance chief brings specific strengths to that job. The CFO works with every division on budgets and forecasts. The CFO also deals directly with investors, auditors and lenders. Those relationships matter when a company has to explain a sudden change at the top.

Holding both posts combines two sets of duties. A CFO oversees financial reporting, cash management and the close of each quarter. A CEO sets priorities, represents the company in public and manages the senior team. Those responsibilities are normally split between two executives.

The arrangement also concentrates accountability for disclosure. Under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, a public company's principal executive officer and principal financial officer each certify its quarterly and annual reports. If Kress holds both posts when a report is filed, the same executive signs both certifications.

Keeping the CFO title also avoids a second vacancy. Had Kress left the finance office entirely, the board would have needed another temporary appointment there at the same moment.

Some questions remain open. Nvidia did not say whether Kress is a candidate for the permanent job. It said only that the board will consider internal and external candidates, and it gave no end date for the interim arrangement.

After a CEO leaves, the board of directors takes direct control of the transition. It names who runs the company in the meantime, decides how to find a permanent leader and tells investors that oversight is intact. Nvidia $NVDA's board took all three steps on Nov. 12, 2026.

The authority sits with the board for a structural reason. Under Delaware corporate law, which governs many large U.S. companies, a corporation's business is managed by or under the direction of its board of directors. Executives run daily operations. Directors hire the chief executive, set that person's pay and can remove them. When the top job opens, no one inside management has the power to fill it alone.

Nvidia's announcement came from the board rather than from management. The board said Jensen Huang had left his roles as president, CEO and board member, with immediate effect. Because he also held a director's seat, his exit changed the makeup of the board as well as the executive suite.

The board's first decision was who would lead in the interim. It chose Colette Kress, Nvidia's executive vice president and chief financial officer. She keeps the CFO role while she serves as interim CEO. The board's second decision was to open a search for a permanent chief executive.

The third task is less formal but carries weight with investors and employees: a public statement of confidence. Nvidia's release included remarks from Harvey C. Jones. Jones said Kress has a deep understanding of Nvidia's business, customers, operations and financial position. He said the leadership team has been instrumental in executing the company's strategy. He also said the board has full confidence in Kress and the team.

A statement like this has a specific function in a sudden exit. It shows shareholders that the directors have endorsed the interim leader by name. It also places the board's own credibility behind the executives who remain. It does not lay out what happens next in detail. It records the board's position at the moment of the change.

An open board seat is a separate matter from the open CEO job. Under Delaware law, the remaining directors can generally fill a board vacancy unless the company's charter or bylaws provide otherwise. Nvidia's announcement did not say whether or when the board would fill the seat Huang left. That detail would have to come from a later company statement or filing.

The board of directors runs a CEO search. It decides what the company needs in its next leader, then measures insiders and outside executives against that profile. Nvidia $NVDA's board said on Nov. 12, 2026, that it is starting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider both internal and external candidates.

The first step is usually about structure. Boards often hand the daily work to a small search committee of independent directors. That committee reports back to the full board, which still holds the final vote on who gets the job.

Next comes the job specification. Directors set out what the role will demand over the next several years. That includes the company's strategy, the markets it sells into, the scale of its operations and any skills missing from the current leadership team. The specification becomes the yardstick for every candidate, inside or outside the company.

Internal candidates bring existing knowledge of the products, customers and culture. Boards typically judge them on their track records and on direct conversations with directors. Some boards also use formal leadership assessments. A company with a written succession plan may already have a short list of executives it has been preparing for the top job.

External candidates widen the field. Boards often hire an executive search firm to build that list. Spencer Stuart, Heidrick & Struggles, Russell Reynolds Associates, Egon Zehnder and Korn Ferry are among the large firms that specialize in this work. A search firm approaches executives at other companies, screens them confidentially and presents a slate to the committee.

Finalists then meet directors over several rounds of interviews. The board checks references and runs background checks. It also negotiates pay, a task that usually involves the compensation committee. An outside hire may expect to be compensated for equity left behind at a previous employer.

An interim CEO can also be considered for the permanent role. The interim appointment does not make that person a candidate automatically. Nvidia has not said whether Colette Kress, its interim CEO and CFO, is under consideration.

The board has given no timeline for its search. It has also named no candidates and no search firm. Once directors settle on a choice, they vote, the company announces the appointment and the interim arrangement ends.

A U.S. public company whose chief executive resigns must report the departure to the Securities and Exchange Commission on Form 8-K, under Item 5.02, within four business days. The filing is posted to the SEC's EDGAR database, where anyone can read it.

Item 5.02 is the section of Form 8-K that covers changes among directors and top officers. It reaches beyond the CEO. The same duty applies when a president, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer, principal operating officer or any named executive officer retires, resigns or is terminated.

Director departures fall under the same item. The rules ask for more when a director leaves over a disagreement with the company about its operations, policies or practices. The same applies when a director is removed for cause. In either case, the company must describe the circumstances. If the director sent a letter describing the disagreement, the company must file it as an exhibit. The company must also give the director a copy of its disclosure and a chance to reply by letter. Any reply is filed as well.

New appointments carry their own disclosure. When a board names a new principal executive officer, including an interim one, the 8-K must state the person's name, position and start date. It must also summarize the appointee's business experience. Any family relationships with directors or officers must be disclosed, along with certain transactions between the appointee and the company.

Pay is a separate trigger. Material new or amended compensation arrangements for named executive officers generally must be reported under Item 5.02(e). Separation agreements can fall into this category. That makes an 8-K one place where severance or equity terms for a departing executive can first become public, if the company has agreed to any.

Regulation FD adds another layer. It bars a public company from sharing material nonpublic information with selected analysts or investors before telling the market at large. A chief executive's exit is generally treated as material information. That is one reason boards announce it broadly, through a press release and a regulatory filing, rather than through private calls.

Nvidia $NVDA's Nov. 12, 2026, press release does not mention a Form 8-K. Jensen Huang's exit as president, CEO and board member, and Colette Kress's appointment as interim CEO, are the kinds of events Item 5.02 is written to cover. Any related filing would appear on EDGAR under Nvidia's company listing.

A company keeps customers and product plans steady after a CEO exit by doing three things quickly. It says that operations will continue, names who is in charge and contacts key partners directly.

Nvidia $NVDA's Nov. 12, 2026, announcement of Jensen Huang's departure carried that kind of continuity message. In the statement, Harvey C. Jones said Nvidia expects its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. He said interim CEO Colette Kress has a deep understanding of the business, customers, operations and financial position. He also said the board has full confidence in Kress and the leadership team.

Kress, who also remains Nvidia's chief financial officer, addressed the company's outside audiences in her own remarks. She said she is committed to building on the foundation Huang created over the last 33 years. She said Nvidia's focus remains on customers, partners, developers and shareholders.

Each of those four groups has a different stake in a leadership change. Customers want to know that orders, delivery schedules and support agreements will hold. Partners want assurance that joint projects keep moving. Developers who build on a company's platforms look for signs that tools and software will keep getting support. Shareholders want to know who is accountable for results.

The legal structure of a corporation does much of the work. Supply agreements, customer contracts and licensing deals are made in the company's name, not the chief executive's. A CEO's departure does not, on its own, end those obligations.

Product work at a large technology company is spread across many people. Chip designs, software releases and manufacturing plans are run by engineering and operations teams, often on schedules set well in advance. An interim or permanent successor inherits those plans and can decide later whether to change them.

The outreach steps often run at the same time. Senior sales and account executives call major customers to repeat the company's message. Internal memos tell employees who they report to and what stays the same. Investor relations teams take questions from analysts and large shareholders.

Keeping the rest of the executive team in place is part of the same effort. Jones credited Nvidia's leadership team with being instrumental in executing the company's strategy. Public backing of the remaining executives signals support for the people who run daily operations.

The test comes in the months after the change. Customers and investors then see whether shipments, product launches and public commitments arrive as the company said they would.

Nvidia $NVDA said it will still release its third-quarter fiscal 2027 results on Tuesday, Nov. 17, as scheduled, despite Jensen Huang's departure. The call puts the company's leadership in front of analysts five days after the board announced the change.

The company said the results are due at about 1:20 p.m. PT. Its earnings call is set to begin at 2 p.m. PT. Keeping the original date means Nvidia's reporting calendar has not shifted along with its management.

Earnings calls at U.S. public companies follow a familiar pattern. Executives walk through revenue, profit and margins for the quarter. They then take questions from Wall Street analysts. Many companies also give a forecast for the quarter ahead.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation FD bars a public company from giving material information to select investors before releasing it to everyone. A webcast earnings call open to the public is one common way companies meet that rule. Any new detail executives share about the transition on such a call reaches all investors at once.

Colette Kress's dual role changes who answers which questions on this call. Nvidia named her interim CEO while she keeps her job as executive vice president and chief financial officer. CFOs typically present the financial detail on earnings calls. At Nvidia, the person who holds the finance job is now also the company's top executive. Analysts can direct questions about the quarter's numbers and about the leadership change to the same person.

Nvidia's fiscal year does not line up with the calendar year. That is why results released in November 2026 carry a fiscal 2027 label. The figures cover a quarter that closed before the board announced Huang's exit.

The forward-looking parts of the call are the ones most closely tied to the transition. Those include any outlook for the next quarter, any comment on the product roadmap and any update on the board's search for a permanent CEO. Nvidia has not said whether the call will address the search.

The stock had already moved before the call. A Yahoo Finance market widget showed Nvidia shares at 152.96, down 20.77, or 11.96%, when the page was captured. That reading was an intraday snapshot, not a closing price or a final measure of the market's response.

#5484. Most Founders Look Successful. These 4 Questions Reveal Who’s Actually Built to Last.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

After years of interviewing founders with polished media kits and unknown ones, I’ve learned the two look nothing alike up close.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

After years of interviewing business owners, developers, and the like, I’ve paid attention to their audience growth and polished media kits, which have been substantial. I’ve also interviewed and discussed business with founders who are still commonly unknown.

What I noticed after talking with them is that the most well-known, strongest founders were not the loudest people in the room. It’s the details, the specific information they know about their audience, finances, marketing, operations, etc. What I enjoyed most about this experience was that they admitted they were still learning.

Most people get this wrong. Building a successful business and appearing successful are two different animals. An online business can appear polished and grand but could be running on fumes and by the skin of its teeth. To help founders evaluate authenticity, I’ve identified four key questions that reveal whether they are building a truly sustainable and genuine business.

Founders who are serious about business know who pays them and why, which builds confidence in their strategy. They don’t rely on vague terms like “disruption” or “community” without specifics. A clear, detailed answer shows they understand their revenue sources and their purpose.

Business founders need to understand the difference between an audience member and a customer. Audience members support the business from the outside without buying anything. Customers turn their trust in your product into action. In today’s world, likes seem to be the most relevant and surefire way to support a business. However, likes without an offer or a clear path will not translate into revenue, which is what business is all about.

When I interview someone and they can identify their audience’s needs, wants, and objections to making an offer, I know I’m talking to a serious business individual. Someone who gets it. It’s evidence that the person has spent time beyond the mirror and out in the market.

Viral posts are thrilling. Media appearances can be riveting for business, but neither one is a customer-acquisition system.

Founders who impress me know their channels. They understand where their business comes from, whether it’s email, live events, podcast appearances, search traffic, or direct outreach. These people understand which channel(s) work and which ones convert into customers.

As a business owner, if you said, “I post on social media,” it wouldn’t fly. Where do you post? When do you post? Who responds? Where do you invite these people next? Do you send out an email list, book a call, etc.?

The best businesses use multiple channels to build trust and interest while providing backup options. This approach reassures founders that diversifying channels reduces risk and builds resilience.

There’s a common trap many entrepreneurs fall into. If every decision requires the founder’s approval, every customer needs the founder’s attention, and every task lives rent-free in the founder’s head, it can become increasingly difficult to manage it all. Being “everywhere” can feel freeing but can also be a headache.

I once spoke with an innovation strategist about basic delegation to real operational management. Implementing tools like Loom recordings, detailed written processes, and clear decision ownership can create reliable building blocks that ensure the business runs smoothly even when the founder is unavailable.

It can feel risky for a founder to hand over responsibility to someone else. You may want to keep business “close to the chest.” However, in my experience, it creates a sense of dependency on the founder, and the business could go under just like that.

Business owners and entrepreneurs need to be sustainable. They need to ask these questions:

Delegation of tasks should be deliberate and strategic, not a risk hazard.

Revenue matters, but it’s a large piece in a larger puzzle. A company can continually lose money while making sales, struggle with cash flow, or spend more to keep customers from leaving.

Every business has a different set of priorities, but understanding which numbers-like profit margin, retention, and customer acquisition cost-drive decisions is crucial. Business owners should learn to interpret these metrics to assess their business health and guide strategic choices effectively.

I pay attention to when the conversation becomes financial. Entrepreneurs can be specific in their approach or fall back on followers, press mentions, awards, and gross revenue. Those achievements may be healthy, but they don’t determine whether a business is “successful.”

Numbers and creativity are not enemies. Numbers protect creativity. They can determine which channels and actions deserve more attention and which ones are wasting money. This data can also determine which customers are staying and whether the company can afford its next move. Business people can be creative and good with numbers. Numbers give a chance for a vision to survive.

Real entrepreneurs do not necessarily have perfect answers. What matters is whether they understand their customers, acquisition strategy, operations, and financial reality and whether they are willing to learn.

I no longer judge a business by the confidence of its founder or the size of its online audience. I listen for specificity. Real entrepreneurs know what is working, what is not, and what they still need to figure out.

After years of interviewing business owners, developers, and the like, I’ve paid attention to their audience growth and polished media kits, which have been substantial. I’ve also interviewed and discussed business with founders who are still commonly unknown.

What I noticed after talking with them is that the most well-known, strongest founders were not the loudest people in the room. It’s the details, the specific information they know about their audience, finances, marketing, operations, etc. What I enjoyed most about this experience was that they admitted they were still learning.

Most people get this wrong. Building a successful business and appearing successful are two different animals. An online business can appear polished and grand but could be running on fumes and by the skin of its teeth. To help founders evaluate authenticity, I’ve identified four key questions that reveal whether they are building a truly sustainable and genuine business.

#5483. How boards handle a CEO scandal: 7 moves they make first

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How boards handle a CEO scandal often starts with seven early moves, from independent investigations and evidence holds to disclosure filings, pay clawbacks and succession plans

When a CEO is accused of misconduct, the board faces a structural problem. It has to investigate the person who normally runs the company and often helps set the board's own agenda. That tension shapes almost every decision directors make in the first days of a scandal.

Those early days carry outsized weight. Employees want to know who is in charge. Investors want to know whether the problem touches the financials. Regulators, lenders and customers watch for signs that the company is hiding something or moving too slowly. A board that stumbles at the start can turn one executive's conduct into a governance crisis for the whole organization.

Understanding how boards handle a CEO scandal means looking past the headlines about resignations and firings. Much of the work happens out of public view. Directors decide who will oversee the inquiry and who will conduct it. They lock down records before anything disappears. They check their insurance policies, review their disclosure obligations and pull out the CEO's employment contract. That contract shows what the company owes and what it might recover.

This slideshow covers seven moves boards commonly make early in a CEO scandal. It is a selection, not a complete checklist, and the moves do not follow a fixed order. In practice, several run at the same time. A special committee may hire investigators on the same day lawyers issue a legal hold. A board may weigh an interim leader while counsel drafts a securities filing.

The specifics vary by company, jurisdiction and the nature of the allegation. A financial fraud raises different questions from a workplace relationship that broke company policy. A U.S.-listed company faces filing deadlines that a private firm does not. The same broad concerns recur, though: independence, credibility, evidence, leadership, disclosure, pay and communication.

Each slide below takes one of those moves and explains what it involves, why boards use it and where its limits lie. Each one can be read on its own.

Boards facing allegations against a CEO usually move oversight to a special committee of independent directors — members with no personal, financial or business ties to the executive. This keeps the accused leader, and anyone close to them, out of decisions about their own conduct.

Without that step, the executive under scrutiny could steer the inquiry. A CEO usually controls the flow of information from management to directors. Many CEOs also hold a seat on the board. Either position could influence an investigation into the CEO's own behavior. Handing the matter to a separate group of directors removes that influence before the first interview takes place.

Independence in this setting goes beyond the formal label. NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards generally require listed companies to have a majority of independent directors. A director who qualifies on paper can still be conflicted in a specific case. Examples include a longtime friendship with the CEO, a business deal with a company the CEO controls or a seat the CEO personally recruited them to fill. Directors with ties like these typically step back from the committee.

The committee then takes charge of the CEO misconduct investigation. It decides the scope of the inquiry, controls who receives updates and sets how often it reports to the full board. Management stays out of those reporting lines. The committee also decides which documents and witnesses matter. It holds the authority to recommend outcomes ranging from no action to dismissal.

Courts pay attention to this structure. In Delaware, where many U.S. public companies are incorporated, judges examine whether committee members were independent when weighing their decisions in shareholder litigation. The Delaware Supreme Court set out that kind of review for special litigation committees in Zapata Corp. v. Maldonado in 1981. A committee seen as conflicted gives plaintiffs an opening to challenge its conclusions.

Nestlé offers a recent case. In September 2025, the Swiss food company dismissed CEO Laurent Freixe over an undisclosed romantic relationship with a direct subordinate. Chair Paul Bulcke and lead independent director Pablo Isla oversaw the investigation that preceded his exit.

The Nestlé case also points to the role of a lead independent director. Many boards create that position to give independent members a leader of their own, separate from management. In a CEO scandal, the lead independent director can serve as a point of contact for the committee's work and for questions from investors.

Boards typically retain an outside law firm to investigate a CEO scandal, and that firm reports to the independent directors rather than to management. The goal is findings that regulators, investors and courts will treat as credible.

The reporting line is central to that credibility. If investigators answer to the CEO, the general counsel or anyone else under scrutiny, their conclusions can be dismissed as compromised. When the firm takes direction from a committee of independent directors, those directors control the scope, the budget and the final report.

Many boards also pass over the company's regular outside counsel. A firm that has advised management for years may have close working relationships with the executives involved. It may also have signed off on decisions that are now being questioned. Hiring a firm with no prior ties removes that objection at the start.

The work usually combines document review with interviews. Lawyers collect emails, text messages, expense records and calendars, often with help from e-discovery vendors. When the allegations involve money, forensic accountants may trace payments and reimbursements. Interviews generally move from peripheral witnesses toward the executive at the center of the inquiry.

Privilege shapes much of how the investigation is run. Communications between a company's lawyers and its employees can be protected by attorney-client privilege. The U.S. Supreme Court addressed that protection in Upjohn Co. v. United States in 1981. Investigators typically open interviews with what is known as an Upjohn warning. It tells the employee that the lawyer represents the company, not the individual. It also explains that the company may later decide to share what was said.

Those protections have limits. Handing findings to regulators or prosecutors can waive privilege, and that can open the material to plaintiffs in later lawsuits. Boards therefore weigh whether to receive a full written report or an oral briefing. They also decide whether to publish a summary of the conclusions.

Cooperation with regulators is part of the calculation. The SEC's 2001 Seaboard Report sets out the factors the agency considers when deciding how much credit to give a company for cooperating. Those factors include whether the company investigated the conduct itself and shared what it learned. They also include who conducted the review and how independent that reviewer was from management.

Counsel normally issues a legal hold early in a CEO scandal, ordering that emails, messages and financial records tied to the matter be kept rather than deleted. The board also checks whether its directors-and-officers liability insurance requires prompt notice of a potential claim.

A legal hold, also called a litigation hold, suspends a company's routine deletion practices for anyone whose records may be relevant. Those people are known as custodians. In a CEO case, the list usually starts with the chief executive. It then extends to assistants, direct reports and anyone named in the allegations.

The hold has to reach the places where records actually live. That includes corporate email, chat platforms such as Slack $WORK and Microsoft $MSFT Teams, text messages, calendars, expense systems and shared drives. It can also cover personal phones and messaging apps like WhatsApp or Signal if they were used for company business. Automatic deletion settings on those tools are typically switched off for the custodians involved.

The duty to preserve generally begins once litigation or an investigation is reasonably anticipated, not when a lawsuit is filed. In U.S. federal courts, Rule 37(e) of the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure covers lost electronically stored information. It lets judges impose remedies when a party loses that data by failing to take reasonable steps to keep it. The harshest sanctions require a finding that the party intended to deprive the other side of the information. One such sanction is an instruction that the jury may presume the lost evidence was unfavorable.

Destroying records to obstruct a federal inquiry can also be a crime. The Sarbanes-Oxley Act created a federal offense covering the destruction or falsification of records with intent to impede an investigation. Boards often have forensic specialists collect and copy devices rather than relying on the executive under scrutiny to hand material over.

Insurance notice runs on a separate track. Most D&O policies are written on a claims-made basis. They respond to claims made during the policy period, and they set conditions on how and when the insurer must be told. Many also allow a notice of circumstances. That lets a company report facts that could lead to a claim. A lawsuit filed later can then attach to the current policy.

Late or incomplete notice can give an insurer grounds to contest coverage. Policies may also require the insurer's consent before the company settles or commits to certain defense costs. Public-company D&O programs usually have three parts. Side A covers individual directors and officers when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B reimburses the company when it does indemnify them. Side C covers the company itself, typically for securities claims.

Many policies also contain conduct exclusions for fraud or intentional wrongdoing. These often apply only after a final, nonappealable adjudication. Until then, an accused executive may still have defense costs covered. Where allegations involve harassment or other workplace conduct, the company may also need to notify the carrier of its employment practices liability policy.

One of the first calls a board makes is whether the CEO keeps running the company while the facts are gathered. The choices are to leave the executive in place, put them on leave or suspend them. If the CEO steps aside, the board often names an interim leader to run the business in the meantime.

Keeping the CEO in the role signals that the board sees no immediate reason to act. It also leaves the person under scrutiny in charge of the staff, records and budgets an investigation may need to examine. That tension is why boards often look for a step short of removal.

Leave is the lighter of those steps. It takes the executive out of daily operations without a finding of wrongdoing. That keeps the board from prejudging the outcome. It also preserves the option of a return if the allegations are not substantiated.

Suspension carries more weight. It usually signals that the board considers the conduct serious enough to bar the CEO from acting on the company's behalf. The executive's employment contract shapes what the board can do here. Some agreements spell out when a suspension is permitted and whether pay continues during it.

When the CEO steps aside in either form, someone has to run the company. An interim CEO may come from inside, such as a chief operating officer, a chief financial officer or another senior executive. A board may instead ask a director, sometimes the chair, to take on the role temporarily. The mandate is usually narrow. The interim leader keeps operations stable, reassures staff and avoids major strategic shifts until the board settles the CEO's status.

The data software company Astronomer faced this decision in 2025. A video of CEO Andy Byron with a colleague at a Coldplay concert spread online. The company placed Byron on leave. He later resigned.

That sequence shows what leave can offer a board. It buys time to review the facts before committing to an outcome. It also lets a company show it has responded without announcing a conclusion it has not yet reached.

The choice also has consequences beyond the executive suite. Employees, customers and investors read the board's decision as an early signal of how seriously it is treating the matter. A CEO who stays at work during an inquiry may make staff less willing to come forward with information.

For a U.S.-listed company, a CEO's departure triggers a Form 8-K filing under Item 5.02. That report is due within four business days of the event. The board also has to decide whether the conduct behind the departure is material enough to disclose sooner.

Form 8-K is the Securities and Exchange Commission's current report. It exists so investors learn about significant corporate events between quarterly and annual filings. Item 5.02 covers the departure and appointment of certain senior officers and directors, a group that includes the principal executive officer. If the board names a replacement, including an interim chief, that appointment is also reported under the same item.

The four-business-day clock starts from the triggering event, not from the date a press release goes out. That timing forces boards to settle basic questions quickly. They need to know whether the CEO resigned, was terminated or remains in place on leave. Each answer affects whether a filing is required and what it must say.

The harder call concerns the misconduct itself. A scandal can become a disclosure issue well before anyone leaves. The test for materiality in U.S. securities law traces to the Supreme Court's 1976 decision in TSC Industries v. Northway. Under that standard, information is material if there is a substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important. Allegations involving financial reporting, related-party dealings or misuse of company funds tend to raise that question more directly than purely personal conduct.

Outside counsel and the audit committee usually guide this judgment. The audit committee oversees financial reporting and the company's relationship with its outside auditor. If the conduct touches the books, the auditor may need to be told. The company's internal controls may also come under review.

Disclosure rules also constrain what executives say elsewhere. The SEC's Regulation FD bars public companies from sharing material nonpublic information selectively with analysts or large investors before telling the wider market. A private call to a major shareholder about the investigation can create a separate compliance problem.

Companies listed outside the U.S. face their own regimes. In the European Union, the Market Abuse Regulation requires issuers to disclose inside information as soon as possible. The U.K. applies its own retained version of that regulation. Under both, delay is permitted only on limited grounds.

Whether a CEO leaves "for cause" or on negotiated terms largely decides what the executive takes on the way out, including severance and unvested equity. Clawback rights can let a company go further and recover pay it has already awarded.

Most CEO employment agreements define what counts as cause. Typical definitions include serious misconduct, a breach of company policy or a violation of law. A for-cause termination usually cuts off severance. It can also mean forfeiting stock awards that have not yet vested. A departure without cause, or a negotiated resignation, often triggers the payouts written into the contract.

That makes the label a financial decision as well as a disciplinary one. The board's compensation committee typically handles it alongside counsel. The investigation's findings carry weight here. A for-cause call has to rest on what the facts show. A CEO who disputes it can challenge it in court.

Clawbacks deal with pay that has already been handed over. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 10D-1 under the Dodd-Frank Act. It requires companies listed on U.S. exchanges to adopt written clawback policies covering their executive officers. The exchange listing standards that carry out the rule became effective on Oct. 2, 2023.

The rule has a narrow trigger. It covers incentive-based pay awarded on the basis of financial results that were later corrected through an accounting restatement. It reaches back over the three completed fiscal years before the restatement. It applies whether or not the executive was at fault. A scandal about personal conduct, with no restatement, does not bring the mandatory policy into play.

Some companies write broader clawback provisions into their own policies or employment contracts. Those can reach misconduct that the federal rule does not cover. Whether a board can use them depends on the language it adopted before the scandal began.

McDonald's $MCD offers a case in point. The company fired CEO Steve Easterbrook in November 2019 over a relationship with an employee. It later sued to recover pay after finding further misconduct. The two sides settled the dispute.

A separation agreement signed early sets terms based on what the board knows at that moment. If more misconduct surfaces afterward, getting money back can require a lawsuit, as it did at McDonald's.

A board facing a CEO scandal speaks through one consistent message, telling employees, shareholders, customers and regulators what it knows and what happens next. At the same stage, it starts or speeds up the search for a permanent chief executive.

Message discipline sits at the center of this step. The board typically designates one spokesperson, often the chair or lead independent director. Counsel usually reviews every statement before release. Mixed signals from different executives can suggest the board has lost control of the situation. Conflicting versions of events can also create legal exposure.

The message itself tends to follow a narrow pattern. It states the facts the board has confirmed and describes the process under way. It explains who is running the business day to day. It avoids speculating about findings that are not yet complete. A statement that later proves wrong may need a public correction. That correction can reopen the story.

Employees usually hear from the company first or at the same moment as the public. Staff who learn about a leadership crisis from news coverage or social media may fill the gap with rumor. Internal memos and town-hall meetings let senior leaders explain what changes for teams and what stays the same. Managers often receive talking points so they can answer questions in the same terms.

External audiences have different concerns. Large shareholders want to know whether strategy and financial guidance still hold. Customers and suppliers want assurance that contracts, deliveries and service will continue. In heavily regulated industries such as banking or health care, regulators may expect direct contact beyond any public statement.

The permanent CEO search runs alongside this outreach. Boards with a standing succession plan can draw on internal candidates who have already been assessed. Boards without one often retain an executive search firm and weigh outside candidates against internal ones. The nominating or governance committee usually leads that work and reports to the full board.

The choice of successor also carries a message. An internal pick can signal continuity in strategy and operations. An outside hire can signal a break from the previous leadership and its culture. In either case, the board's explanation of why it chose that person becomes part of the public record of how it handled the scandal.

#5482. This $14 Billion Tech Company Is Giving All of Its 7,000 Employees a Day Off to Play Video Games

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The entire workforce is getting a flexible day off, and the occasion isn’t a holiday.

Forget about the meetings and the deadlines. Pick up a gaming controller instead.

A day spent playing video games usually means taking time away from work. Now at Logitech, that time away is company-approved.

The $14 billion tech company is giving its entire workforce a flexible day off to play video games, including the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, which comes out on November 19.

Logitech’s new initiative is called “Logi Game Day,” and it gives every employee, including interns, the chance to take one paid day off to play a game. Workers can choose a day that works best for them, from now until this time next year.

The initiative marks the first gaming day in the company’s history, per a company press release. It saves employees the hassle of using a sick day for gaming.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” Hanneke Faber, Logitech’s CEO, said in the release. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other. ”

Employees can even play video games in the office. Logitech’s gaming brand, Logitech G, revealed this week that it will launch a streaming event to celebrate Game Day. The event will take place at the company’s Americas headquarters in San Jose on November 19. Robin Piispanen, Logitech G’s general manager and a former competitive gamer, will act as the event host.

“Whether diving into a game like GTA VI or Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4, shaving seconds off lap times in Forza, or teaming up in an online battle, Game Day gives our team a shared purpose,” Piispanen said in a press release statement. “We see firsthand how Logitech employees who sharpen their skills in-game translate directly back to work and problem-solving.”

Faber herself plans to play Grand Theft Auto VI when it comes out. She will head into Logitech headquarters, which will transform into a fully equipped gaming lounge that day.

“I’m ready for some fun and (friendly) competition,” she said in an interview with Fortune.

Other executives celebrated the decision to offer a day off for gaming.

“Play is not the opposite of work,” Elaine Laird, Logitech’s chief people officer, said in a press release. “When people have dedicated time to log off, decompress and immerse themselves in play, they return with clearer focus, renewed energy and fresh approaches to complex challenges.”

Research conducted by the company backs up these claims. In Logitech’s recent Ctrl Tomorrow study, 81% of gamers said playing helps build real-world confidence and improve work performance. A separate study conducted by the company in August found that 98.8% of respondents said gaming skills had a direct connection to workplace abilities like problem-solving.

Forget about the meetings and the deadlines. Pick up a gaming controller instead.

A day spent playing video games usually means taking time away from work. Now at Logitech, that time away is company-approved.

The $14 billion tech company is giving its entire workforce a flexible day off to play video games, including the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI, which comes out on November 19.

#5481. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5480. From Gates to Gelsinger: 9 CEO exits and how investors read each one

Free daily briefing on global business news.

A look at what happens to a stock when the CEO quits, through nine exits from Bill Gates at Microsoft to Pat Gelsinger at Intel

A CEO exit is a message, and investors have to decode it before they can price it. The same news can signal a planned handoff to a longtime deputy, a founder moving into a new role or a board that has run out of patience. What happens to a stock when the CEO quits depends on which of those stories the market believes it is reading.

Several variables shape that reading. The first is where the successor comes from. Tim Cook at Apple $AAPL, Steve Ballmer at Microsoft $MSFT, Andy Jassy at Amazon $AMZN and Parag Agrawal at Twitter $TWTR were all insiders. Cook had been chief operating officer, Jassy ran Amazon Web Services and Agrawal was chief technology officer. Brian Niccol, who left Chipotle $CMG to run Starbucks $SBUX, was an outside hire.

The second variable is whether the departing leader really leaves. Bill Gates stayed at Microsoft as chairman and took the title chief software architect. Steve Jobs became Apple's chairman. Jeff Bezos moved to executive chairman at Amazon. Each arrangement kept a founder close to the company while someone else held the CEO title.

The third is the circumstance of the exit. Dave Calhoun announced in March 2024 that he would leave Boeing $BA at the end of the year. That announcement followed the January 2024 door-plug blowout on an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9. Pat Gelsinger left Intel $INTC in December 2024 following pressure from the board. Intel named Lip-Bu Tan CEO in March 2025. Disney $DIS's board removed Bob Chapek in November 2022 and brought back Bob Iger, who had handed him the job in February 2020.

Outside events can cloud the picture. Jeff Immelt took over General Electric $GE from Jack Welch days before the September 11, 2001 attacks. That timing makes it hard to separate investors' view of the handover from the shock that hit the entire market.

A leadership change can also touch more than one company. On August 13, 2024, Starbucks said Laxman Narasimhan was out and Niccol would take the top job. Starbucks shares rose sharply that day. Chipotle shares fell.

This is a selection of nine exits from 2000 to 2025, not a complete or ranked list. The slides run in chronological order, starting with Microsoft and ending with Intel. Each one looks at the conditions investors faced when the news broke and what came next for the company's leadership.

Microsoft $MSFT announced on January 13, 2000, that Bill Gates would hand the chief executive job to Steve Ballmer. Gates did not leave the company. He stayed on as chairman and took a new title, chief software architect.

That arrangement shaped how investors could read the news. A founder who gives up the CEO seat but keeps the chairman's role still holds a formal position at the top of the company. The chief software architect title pointed to where Gates would focus: technology and product direction rather than day-to-day management.

The choice of successor carried its own message. Ballmer came from inside Microsoft rather than from another company. An internal pick gives shareholders a leader the board already knows. An outside hire, by contrast, arrives without a track record inside the business.

The new structure divided responsibilities that had sat with one person. Ballmer took on the duties of running the company. Gates kept a hand in governance through the board and in technology through his new title. For shareholders, the change was less a founder walking away than a redrawing of who handled what.

The split also raised a question the announcement itself could not settle. Investors had to weigh how much authority Ballmer would hold while the founder still chaired the board and set technical direction.

Timing complicates any reading of the market's response. The announcement came as the dot-com boom was nearing its peak. Technology shares at that point were driven by forces much larger than one company's leadership plans. That backdrop makes it hard to isolate how investors judged the handover itself.

The Microsoft case shows one form of CEO succession: a change in title as much as a change in people. The founder stepped back from running the company without stepping out of it. That is a different event from a founder's full departure.

Jack Welch's retirement from General Electric $GE in September 2001 shows why a stock's reaction to a CEO handover cannot always be measured. Jeff Immelt took over days before the September 11, 2001 attacks. The market shock that followed makes the response to the leadership change impossible to separate from everything else.

Welch left after about two decades as GE's chief executive. A tenure that long changes what a succession means to shareholders. They are not just trading one executive for another. They are weighing how the company will run without the leader who led it for that long.

Welch's departure was a retirement, not a firing or a sudden resignation. A retirement is a planned event. That gives it a different character from a board-driven removal or an exit forced by a crisis.

The calendar is what sets this handover apart. Immelt had been in the job only days when the attacks took place. Whatever investors made of the new CEO, their view was quickly overtaken by a much larger event.

That creates a measurement problem. A clean read on a CEO change needs a quiet window around the transition. In that window, the leadership news is the main new information reaching investors. GE had no such window in September 2001.

Any move in GE shares in the weeks after Immelt took over carried the weight of the attacks and the wider market shock. A chart of the stock from that period cannot show how much of the movement belonged to the succession itself.

The GE case illustrates a broader point about reading CEO departures. A share price responds to all of the news at once, not to one headline at a time. When a leadership change lands alongside a market-wide event, the effect of the new CEO cannot be pulled apart from the rest.

Steve Jobs resigned as Apple $AAPL's chief executive on August 24, 2011, and Tim Cook, then the company's chief operating officer, took over the role. Jobs stayed on as chairman, a structure that kept his name attached to the company's leadership after the handover.

In the Apple case, the successor's résumé was part of the news. Cook was not an outside hire. He came from inside the company, from the job that oversees Apple's day-to-day operations.

That background shapes how shareholders can interpret a leadership change. An internal pick from the operating side can signal that a board favors continuity over a new strategy. A chief operating officer usually already works closely with a company's suppliers, product schedules and senior staff.

An outside hire can send a different message. It can suggest the board wants something to change. Apple's choice pointed the other way.

The chairman role added a second layer. Jobs giving up the CEO title did not mean he left the boardroom. As chairman, he led the board that oversees the chief executive. Shareholders could read that as a gradual transfer rather than a clean break.

That arrangement did not last long. Jobs died on October 5, 2011, about six weeks after his resignation. His death ended the chairman arrangement. Cook was left to lead without his predecessor on the board.

The short gap between the two events complicates any attempt to read the market's view of Cook on its own. The resignation and the death were separate pieces of news. Investors had to weigh each one as they judged Apple's future without Jobs.

What the episode shows is a sequence of conditions investors had to weigh. The successor was an insider. The departing leader stayed on as chairman. Then a second piece of news arrived before the new arrangement could settle.

Disney $DIS's board removed Bob Chapek as CEO on November 20, 2022, and brought back Bob Iger, the executive Chapek had succeeded. The reversal came less than three years after Iger handed Chapek the top job on February 25, 2020.

The two changes reached investors in very different forms. The first was a planned handoff, with the outgoing CEO passing the role to his chosen successor. A scheduled transfer like that frames the news around continuity rather than disruption.

The second came from the board, not from a CEO deciding to step aside. A board-driven removal is a separate category of exit from a planned succession. It tells shareholders that directors took the leadership question into their own hands.

The choice of replacement also shaped how the news could be read. The board did not search for an outside hire or promote a new executive. It reinstated Iger, whose record as Disney's CEO investors had already watched.

A returning CEO arrives with an existing reputation inside the company and on Wall Street. Shareholders weighing the 2022 decision were assessing a leader they had seen in the role before, not a newcomer.

A return leaves one question unanswered. Reinstating a former chief executive fills the top job, but it does not settle who will lead the company next. The search for a long-term successor, which the 2020 handoff had appeared to resolve, was open again.

The two dates bracket Chapek's entire run as Disney's chief executive. Within this selection of nine exits, Disney is the only case in which a former CEO came back to replace his own successor.

The sequence also shows that one succession can produce two separate moments for investors. The 2020 handoff and the 2022 reversal each presented a new leadership arrangement to assess, under different circumstances and for different reasons.

Jeff Bezos announced on February 2, 2021 that he would step down as Amazon $AMZN's CEO and become executive chairman. Andy Jassy, who ran Amazon Web Services, took over as chief executive on July 5, 2021.

The timing of the announcement shaped how investors could read it. Amazon released the leadership news alongside its fourth-quarter 2020 results. The succession plan and a full set of quarterly numbers reached the market at the same moment.

That pairing makes any stock reaction to the CEO departure hard to isolate. Quarterly figures and a change at the top are separate pieces of news. Investors weigh both during the same trading session. The share price then reflects one combined response rather than a separate verdict on each.

The role Bezos took on was the second signal. An executive chairman leads the board of directors and keeps an active hand in the company. Bezos founded Amazon in 1994. The new title meant the founder was stepping back from daily management without leaving. For shareholders, the person most closely tied to the company stayed inside its governance structure.

The choice of successor was the third signal. Jassy was an internal pick rather than an outside hire. He had led Amazon Web Services, the company's cloud computing business. That made the new CEO someone who had already run one of Amazon's major operations.

The length of the handover was the fourth signal. About five months separated the February announcement from Jassy's first day as CEO on July 5. That gap gave the board, employees and investors a defined transition period with a fixed end date.

Taken together, the early announcement, the founder's continuing board role and the internal promotion pointed to a planned succession rather than a forced exit. None of those features decides on its own how a stock trades. They shape the information investors have when they make that decision.

Jack Dorsey stepped down as Twitter $TWTR's CEO on November 29, 2021, and Parag Agrawal, the company's chief technology officer, took his place. The clearest price shareholders later received came from a takeover agreement, not from the leadership change itself.

The handover kept the top job inside the company. Agrawal was already a senior Twitter executive when he was promoted. With an internal pick, investors are judging someone who already knows the company's products and engineering. The open question is how that person will run the whole business.

A CTO in the top seat also says something about priorities. The chief technology officer oversees the systems a product is built on. Picking that executive puts a technical leader in charge of a consumer platform. It does not, on its own, tell investors what strategy will follow. That answer would come from his first decisions as chief executive.

The larger price event came later. Elon Musk agreed to buy Twitter for $54.20 per share. The deal was valued at roughly $44 billion. It closed in October 2022, less than a year after Dorsey left the CEO role.

That timing shortened the window for judging Agrawal on his own record. Once a sale price was on the table, the stock's moves were tied more to the deal's prospects than to the new CEO's choices.

A takeover works differently from an ordinary trading day. Buyer and seller agree on a fixed price for each share. When the deal closes, shareholders receive that price, whatever the stock had been doing before.

The two events are separate. Dorsey's resignation did not set the $54.20 figure, and the order of events does not show that one caused the other. Twitter's case shows a limit of judging a CEO exit by later share prices. A takeover can set the final number shareholders receive, whether or not it has anything to do with the succession.

Dave Calhoun announced on March 25, 2024 that he would leave Boeing $BA at the end of 2024. The decision came after the January 2024 door-plug blowout on an Alaska Airlines 737 MAX 9. That sequence made it a crisis-linked departure rather than a routine retirement.

The distinction matters for anyone trying to read the market's response. A planned handover asks investors one question: is the successor ready? A crisis exit asks two. Shareholders have to weigh the damage from the incident itself. They also have to judge whether a change at the top can repair it.

The order of events in Boeing's case shows how tangled those questions become. The blowout came first, in January. Calhoun's announcement followed in March. Any move in Boeing shares over those months would have reflected both the incident and the leadership news. Separating one from the other is not straightforward.

Calhoun also chose not to leave at once. He set his exit for the end of the year, months after the announcement. A long runway of that kind can signal an orderly transition. It also means the outgoing chief keeps running the company while investors wait.

That waiting period carries its own uncertainty. Until a successor takes over, shareholders cannot size up the person who will lead the recovery. They are pricing a departure without yet knowing what replaces it.

Kelly Ortberg started as Boeing's CEO in August 2024. That was months ahead of the end-of-year date Calhoun had given in March. Ortberg took charge about five months after Calhoun's announcement.

For investors, the Boeing case is a reminder that a CEO's stated exit date is a plan, not a guarantee. A successor can arrive well before the outgoing chief's announced departure. The stock's reaction to the original news is only part of the story.

On August 13, 2024, Starbucks $SBUX announced that Laxman Narasimhan was out as CEO and that Brian Niccol, then the chief executive of Chipotle $CMG, would take the top job. Starbucks shares rose sharply that day, and Chipotle shares fell.

That split makes this leadership change unusual. A single announcement involved two publicly traded companies. Their stocks moved in opposite directions on the same trading day.

A second company was involved because of where the successor came from. Many CEO changes stay inside one business. A board promotes an executive from within or names an interim leader while it searches. In this case, the incoming chief executive was already running another listed company.

The hire and the departure were therefore one event. Starbucks gained a new CEO, and Chipotle lost its sitting one in the same announcement.

For Starbucks shareholders, the news carried two pieces of information at once. Narasimhan was leaving, and his replacement was already named. There was no interim arrangement and no open-ended search.

For Chipotle shareholders, the same news arrived as a CEO departure. Their company's chief executive was moving to another restaurant chain. Chipotle's board now had its own succession question to settle.

Starbucks did not promote an insider to fill the role. Its board went outside the company and chose a leader who held the top job elsewhere in the restaurant industry. That choice is what tied a second stock to the news.

The case shows that the stock reaction to a CEO departure is not always confined to the company making the change. When the successor comes from another public company, investors in both businesses face a leadership change on the same day.

Pat Gelsinger left Intel $INTC on December 1, 2024, after pressure from the company's board. Intel did not name a permanent successor at the time. David Zinsner and Michelle Johnston Holthaus took over as interim co-CEOs.

A board-driven exit sends a different signal from a planned retirement. A planned retirement typically arrives with a successor chosen and a handover date set. A departure under board pressure tells investors that directors wanted a change at the top. It also shows they moved before a replacement was ready.

Other boards in recent years paired a removal with a named successor. When Starbucks $SBUX pushed out Laxman Narasimhan, it named Brian Niccol in the same announcement. When Disney $DIS's board removed Bob Chapek, it brought back Bob Iger at the same time. Intel's board announced Gelsinger's exit with no permanent replacement attached.

The interim structure reflects that gap. An interim title means the job is held temporarily while a search runs. Splitting the role between two executives adds a second question. Shareholders had to judge who was setting direction and for how long.

The interim arrangement ran from December 2024 into March 2025. That month, Intel named Lip-Bu Tan as CEO. The appointment returned the company from a temporary setup to a single permanent leader.

For anyone tracking a stock's reaction to a CEO departure, the Intel case contains three separate moments rather than one. The first is the exit itself. The second is the stretch under co-CEOs. The third is the naming of Tan as permanent CEO. Each step gave investors new information about who would run the company.

The sequence also shows how the cause of an exit shapes the way it is read. Intel's path ran from board pressure to shared interim leadership to a permanent appointment. That order points to a rethink of the company's leadership, not a planned handoff.
