#5479. Washington voters keep millionaires tax, splitting tech leaders over the state’s competitive edge

by Todd Bishop, Lisa Stiffler & Kurt Schlosser on Nov 4, 2026 at 10:10 amNovember 4, 2026 at 10:18 am

Washington voters appear to have upheld the state’s new tax on high earners, putting the state on track to lose its place among the nine states without an income tax — a status that tech leaders have long touted as an edge in recruiting companies and talent.

Initiative 645, which would repeal the 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, was trailing 58% to 42% in election-night returns. King County voters rejected the repeal by an even wider margin, with 66.5% voting no. The repeal would need about 62% of the remaining ballots to pass, according to a Seattle Times estimate.

The tax has divided the Seattle tech community since lawmakers unveiled the proposal in February. Some founders and investors warned it would drive talent and capital out of the state, while others called those fears overblown.

Madrona, the Seattle venture capital firm, gave $250,000 to the repeal campaign, making it one of the biggest donors.

“The outcome on the income tax should be disappointing for all Washingtonians as having no income tax was a major source of competitive advantage for the state,” said Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director, responding to questions from GeekWire.

McIlwain, who urged voters to repeal the tax in a GeekWire op-ed in October, said the state saw record economic growth and job creation after voters rejected an income tax in 2010. “I am concerned for the future ability of Washington state to be competitive,” he wrote.

Ben Golden, an attorney and advisor to Pacific Northwest startups and investors, countered that the election outcome demonstrates “that Washingtonians are ready to invest in ourselves.”

“There’s lots of hard work to follow to ensure that revenue is spent wisely, but at least (Washington) will be ready for the wave of Medicaid cuts and AI job disruption on the horizon,” added Golden, who in February penned an op-ed in support of the tax.

And while some residents will leave for tax havens, Golden said, “the opportunity remains ripe for the investor community and startups to build and grow in this healthy and talent-packed region.”

Brian Fioca, a Seattle-based serial entrepreneur and investor, hopes the additional tax dollars will improve the quality of life in the state overall.

“Washington is a wonderful place to live and build a company, full of extraordinary people and talent,” said Fioca, who also offered an earlier op-ed on the issue. “If someone decides not to start a business here, or chooses to leave because of this tax, that’s not someone I’d be particularly excited to work with or invest in anyway.”

Asked whether the outcome changes how Madrona thinks about investing in Washington, McIlwain didn’t address the state specifically. “Our goal remains to find and partner with amazing founders and their teams to build enduring companies that create innovative products, jobs and economic returns,” he said.

State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was an original architect of the tax and the prime sponsor of the bill that created it. As Senate majority leader, he kept reworking the measure to win votes until the final days of this year’s legislative session. Pedersen, who has been in the Legislature since 2007, is also executive vice president and general counsel at Seattle construction and engineering firm McKinstry.

At the No on 645 campaign’s election-night event in Seattle on Tuesday, Pedersen celebrated the outcome.

“We have been saddled with an anchor around our neck, with a tax system that is bad for working people, that’s bad for small businesses, that’s bad for just about everybody except for the one percent,” he said, as seen in a video posted on Instagram.

The No on 645 campaign touted a coalition of working families, labor unions, teachers, small business owners and others — and attracted endorsements from state celebrities like Rick Steves, the Edmonds-based travel writer, and “Jeopardy!” host Ken Jennings.

The tax applies only to income above the $1 million threshold, so a household earning $1.5 million would owe $49,500. It takes effect on 2028 income, with the first payments due in April 2029.

Jeff Bezos, Howard Schultz and Rich Barton have all moved out of state in recent years, though each described the move in personal terms.

McIlwain, who moved with his family from Georgia to Seattle 26 years ago, became a Georgia resident again two years ago. That was before lawmakers unveiled the millionaires tax in February.

In 2010, Steve Ballmer and Microsoft helped fund the campaign that defeated a statewide income tax, but the region’s biggest tech companies stayed out of this fight. The state projects the tax will raise $3 billion to $4 billion a year from roughly 25,000 households. Gov. Bob Ferguson signed it into law in March, along with tax breaks for small businesses and lower-income families.

A lawsuit filed in April by former Attorney General Rob McKenna and former state Supreme Court Justice Phil Talmadge argues the tax is unconstitutional, citing a 1933 ruling that classified income as property, which the state constitution says must be taxed at a uniform rate.

The case will likely go to the state Supreme Court, where Democrat-backed candidates led four of five races on Tuesday’s ballot as of election-night returns, according to the Washington State Standard.

#5478. The Next Digital Gold Mine Isn’t Content. It’s Paid Participation.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As consumers shift from paying for access to paying for participation, businesses have an opportunity to capitalize.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A virtual gift flashes across a livestream. A creator reacts, the audience joins in, and seconds later the animation is gone. Nothing physical changes hands. Yet the purchase has changed the experience for everyone watching.

The interesting business question is not why someone would pay for something intangible. We already pay for concerts, games and experiences that end. It is what happens when a purchase becomes part of the experience itself, and when customers can influence what others see in real time. That shift creates a business model worth examining: monetizing participation, not just access.

Traditional entertainment largely separates the audience from the performance. A ticket buys entry; the show goes on whether or not any particular attendee contributes. Interactive digital environments make that boundary less rigid.

In a livestream, viewers can comment, join challenges, celebrate milestones and send virtual gifts. Some actions are free; others involve spending. Both can affect the atmosphere. A digital purchase may trigger a visible moment that the entire audience experiences, even though only one person paid for it.

At Tango, where I work, this is an everyday feature of live entertainment. A gift can punctuate a performance or become part of a group celebration. The product is not simply an animation. It is the opportunity to contribute to a shared event as it unfolds.

That distinction matters beyond livestreaming. Companies accustomed to selling content or access should ask whether customers also value the ability to shape the experience.

Gaming offers a useful parallel, although its economics differ from live gifting. Players buy optional digital items to customize how they participate. On Roblox, creators earned approximately $1.5 billion in 2025, up from about $923 million in 2024, according to the company’s Form 10-K for fiscal year 2025 (Business section). Roblox’s economy centers on in-game items rather than live gifting, but the scale illustrates the economic potential of virtual engagement.

The broader lesson is not that every virtual object deserves a price tag. It is that ownership is only one way to create value. Customization, contribution and shared experiences can matter too. A company evaluating digital products should distinguish what the customer receives from what the customer gets to do.

For business leaders, this changes the fundamental question: instead of asking what else they can sell customers, they should ask what customers would value being part of, and whether that participation creates a compelling reason to spend.

Participation-based commerce changes product design priorities. A purchase embedded in a live experience has at least two audiences: the person spending and the people witnessing its effect. That creates opportunities, but also responsibilities.

First, make the contribution legible. If a paid action affects an experience, participants should understand what it does. An unclear effect weakens the connection between spending and value.

Second, design meaningful ways to participate without paying. Comments, community activities and other free interactions help ensure that spending is a choice rather than the price of belonging.

Third, measure more than transaction volume. Conversion and average spend matter, but leaders should also examine whether people return, continue participating and feel in control of their experience. A monetization feature that generates a short-term spike while eroding trust is not a durable success.

This also means looking at the experience from both sides of the transaction. The paying customer should receive clear value, while the wider community should benefit from the interaction without feeling excluded from it.

Visible feedback is part of what makes digital gifting distinctive. A creator may acknowledge a gift immediately; other viewers may respond; the moment becomes communal. But it would be simplistic to conclude that people are merely purchasing attention.

Someone might give to appreciate a performance, celebrate an achievement, or seek direct recognition and attention from the creator. While gaining a creator’s attention is often a primary driver for viewers, businesses should resist reducing diverse motivations to a single psychological explanation. The design challenge is to make the interaction rewarding without manufacturing pressure to spend.

Transparent pricing, clear purchase mechanics and user control are not separate from the experience. They help make participation sustainable.

For companies exploring virtual goods, the useful question is not, “What digital object can we sell?” It is, “Where does customer participation genuinely improve the experience, and would someone willingly pay to contribute in that way?”

The answer will differ across entertainment, gaming and online communities. Not every interaction should be monetized. But businesses that understand the difference between selling access and enabling participation may discover value that conventional product thinking overlooks.

The future of digital commerce will not be defined only by what people can own. It will also depend on what they can help create together.

A virtual gift flashes across a livestream. A creator reacts, the audience joins in, and seconds later the animation is gone. Nothing physical changes hands. Yet the purchase has changed the experience for everyone watching.

The interesting business question is not why someone would pay for something intangible. We already pay for concerts, games and experiences that end. It is what happens when a purchase becomes part of the experience itself, and when customers can influence what others see in real time. That shift creates a business model worth examining: monetizing participation, not just access.

Traditional entertainment largely separates the audience from the performance. A ticket buys entry; the show goes on whether or not any particular attendee contributes. Interactive digital environments make that boundary less rigid.

#5476. A rare second exit: AI startup Suplari acquired by Docusign nearly 3 years after Microsoft spinout

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 12:43 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 12:44 pm

Some startups dream of getting acquired by a big tech company. Suplari has now done it twice.

Docusign on Tuesday announced its acquisition of the AI-powered spending analysis company, five years after Microsoft bought the Seattle-based startup and nearly three years after the Redmond tech giant spun the company back out to its founders.

Financial terms of the latest deal weren’t disclosed. Docusign said it plans to fold Suplari’s technology into its contract management platform, pairing the startup’s analysis of corporate spending and supplier data with Docusign’s Iris AI engine.

The idea is to find savings, track what suppliers agreed to deliver, and flag purchases that fall outside contract terms.

“Joining Docusign allows us to connect that intelligence more closely to the agreements that shape a company’s spending,” Suplari CEO Jeff Gerber said in a statement.

It’s a remarkable double-dip in startup M&A for a company that was applying AI to corporate spending years before the current agentic boom.

Suplari was co-founded in 2016 by Nikesh “Niki” Parekh, a Seattle tech veteran who previously held leadership roles at Trulia and Market Leader, along with Gerber, a longtime engineering leader, and product leader Brian White. Gerber and White had worked together at iConclude, an earlier startup that Gerber co-founded.

The startup, in its first incarnation, pulled together procurement and spending data scattered across corporate systems such as SAP, Workday and Oracle, and used machine learning to flag savings opportunities, supplier risks and other inefficiencies. The pitch was an alternative to having teams of analysts comb through the data in Excel or Tableau.

Gerber has traced the idea to his time at Apptio, the IT cost management company, where he helped lead machine learning work. That opened his eyes to the ways that connecting financial data with IT activity could turn up problems such as auto-renewing contracts and services still running for employees who had left.

By 2021, Suplari had raised about $18 million from investors including Madrona, Amplify Partners, Shasta Ventures, Two Sigma Ventures and Workday Ventures.

Microsoft acquired Suplari in July 2021, saying it would pair the technology with its Dynamics 365 business software. The startup had about 40 employees at the time.

Then ChatGPT arrived in November 2022. Microsoft redirected all of its new-product investment to Copilot, Parekh recalled in a blog post earlier this year.

Succeeding inside Microsoft would have meant rebuilding Suplari from scratch to deploy across 400 to 500 data centers, “exactly the kind of investment Microsoft was now reserving for Copilot,” he wrote. By then, Suplari had become core to the finance and procurement operations of 40 to 50 of Microsoft’s most strategic customers.

“Microsoft concluded, and we agreed, that customers would be better served if Suplari operated as an independent company again,” Parekh wrote.

Suplari’s founding team bought the company back in late 2023, with Microsoft retaining a minority stake. Gerber, Suplari’s original CTO, led the spinout and became CEO. He had been chief AI strategy officer for Microsoft’s Dynamics finance and operations products after the acquisition.

Parekh stayed at Microsoft, working on Copilot Studio and the Power Platform, before leaving in June 2025 to start the AI recruiting startup Provn.

Since the spinout, Suplari has added an AI agent that helps procurement teams act on what its software finds, Gerber said on an Art of Procurement podcast in June. Its customers include BT Group, Nordstrom and MediaNews Group, according to Docusign. The company has about two dozen employees, according to LinkedIn.

Gerber declined an interview with GeekWire after the acquisition announcement, citing a quiet period. In a statement, Docusign CEO Allan Thygesen said Suplari’s “technology and talent” will help Docusign connect what companies’ supplier agreements say with their actual spending.

Parekh has remained a Suplari shareholder and advisor. Asked about the deal, he said via email that generative AI is “enabling a renaissance in many ‘traditional’ systems of record” like enterprise resource planning and contract lifecycle management.

Connecting contracts with their outcomes, he said, “will be the future.”

As for Suplari’s own outcome, Parekh said he’s “ecstatic” about the startup’s second exit.

#5475. How companies pick a new CEO: 10 stages of a board's search

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The CEO search process runs from succession planning and a board committee to interviews, pay talks and an SEC filing — these 10 stages shape how boards decide

Few decisions belong to a board of directors as squarely as the choice of who runs the company. Directors leave budgets and daily operations to management. Hiring, evaluating and replacing the chief executive is a different matter. It is one of the board's core responsibilities, and directors do not hand it to the people the CEO will lead.

The work often begins well before anyone leaves. Many boards keep succession plans ready ahead of any vacancy. One plan covers a sudden departure, when the company needs a leader on short notice. Another covers a planned retirement, when the board has time to prepare an orderly handover.

When a vacancy arrives, a small group of directors usually does most of the work. This can be a special search committee or the existing nominating and governance committee. The committee reports to the full board. The full board makes the final decision. Along the way, many boards bring in an executive search firm to build a list of candidates, approach them quietly and keep the process confidential.

The CEO search process that follows usually moves through a broad sequence. A board settles on what kind of leader the company needs, drawing on its strategy and the challenges ahead. It then weighs internal executives against outside candidates using the same criteria. If the seat is empty, it may name an interim CEO to keep the business running. Finalists typically face several rounds of interviews, followed by assessments and checks. The board then negotiates pay and employment terms. For U.S. public companies, the appointment must be disclosed in a regulatory filing within four business days.

This walkthrough breaks that sequence into 10 stages. The first six follow the core steps of a board's search, from succession planning to the interim leadership question. The last four cover what happens once finalists emerge: interviews, reference and background checks, pay negotiation and the public announcement. Each stage stands on its own. Together they show how a boardroom decision becomes a new name at the top of the company.

CEO succession planning is work a board does before any vacancy exists, and it usually takes two forms. An emergency plan covers a sudden departure. A longer-term plan prepares for a scheduled retirement.

Planning ahead follows from the board's own duty to hire, evaluate and replace the chief executive. Without a plan, directors face that duty under time pressure, with no agreed view of who could step in.

The emergency plan answers a narrow question: who runs the company tomorrow if the CEO cannot? A chief executive can leave without warning through death, serious illness, an abrupt resignation or a dismissal. The emergency plan sets out who would take charge in the short term. Its purpose is continuity rather than a permanent choice.

The long-term plan works on a much longer horizon. It looks ahead to a retirement or a planned handover that the board can see coming. Here the board considers which senior executives could one day be ready for the top role. It also considers what experience they still lack. Boards often use this period to give promising executives wider responsibilities, such as running a larger division or a new region.

Stock exchange rules put the topic on the formal agenda for many listed companies. The New York Stock Exchange's listing standards require listed companies to adopt corporate governance guidelines. Section 303A.09 of the NYSE Listed Company Manual says those guidelines must address management succession. Its commentary says succession planning should include policies for selecting the CEO and for succession in an emergency or on retirement.

Shareholders can raise the issue too. In Staff Legal Bulletin No. 14E, issued in 2009, SEC staff said companies generally could no longer exclude shareholder proposals on CEO succession planning as ordinary business.

The preparation shapes what follows. A board with a current plan already holds a view of its internal bench and of what the company needs from its next leader. That gives any later search a starting point instead of a blank page.

A small committee of directors usually runs the day-to-day work of a CEO search, and the full board keeps the final decision. That committee is often a special search committee formed for the job, or the board's standing nominating and governance committee.

A committee gives the search a working group that can meet on short notice. It also keeps sensitive discussions among a handful of directors.

The choice between the two committee types shapes who does the work. A special search committee is put together for one assignment and exists only for that search. The board can pick its members for relevant experience, such as directors who have run companies themselves.

A nominating and governance committee already exists. It already handles questions about board membership and leadership. Using it means the search begins with a group that has a set mandate and a regular meeting schedule.

For companies listed on the New York Stock Exchange, that standing committee comes with rules attached. Section 303A.04 of the NYSE Listed Company Manual requires listed companies to have a nominating and corporate governance committee. Every member of that committee must be an independent director.

The legal basis for handing work to a committee is also well established. Many U.S. public companies are incorporated in Delaware. Section 141(c) of the Delaware General Corporation Law lets a board designate committees of directors and assign them powers.

In a CEO search, that delegation has limits. The committee reports back to the full board as the process moves along. It narrows the field and brings forward a recommendation. The full board then votes on the appointment.

That split keeps accountability with the whole board. Every director shares responsibility for the choice, not only the directors who sat on the committee. Directors outside the committee can also question the reasoning behind a recommendation before the vote.

The committee also serves as the main point of contact for others involved in the search, from outside advisers to the candidates themselves. Deciding who sits on it is an early step in any search.

Before any candidate names come up, a board typically agrees on a written profile of the CEO role. That profile draws on the company's strategy, its current challenges and the skills and experience the next chief executive will need.

In executive search, this document is often called a position specification. It describes the job as the company needs it done in the years ahead. It does not simply describe how the departing CEO happened to do it.

Strategy is the starting point. A company planning to expand into new international markets may want a leader who has run operations across several countries. A business dealing with falling sales or heavy debt may look for turnaround or restructuring experience. A company shifting toward software or digital products may give technology expertise more weight than before.

Current challenges narrow the picture further. Directors weigh pressures such as regulatory scrutiny, a pending merger, labor relations or demands from investors. Each of these points toward a different kind of background.

The skills section usually covers both track record and leadership qualities. Track record can include responsibility for a profit-and-loss statement, leadership of a large workforce or experience at a public company. Leadership qualities can include how a person builds a team, communicates under pressure and works with a board.

A profile often separates essential requirements from desirable ones. That split matters when no candidate matches every line. It tells directors which gaps they can accept and which would rule a person out.

The document also gives directors a shared yardstick. Board members often arrive with different views of what the company needs. Writing those views down and agreeing on them moves the debate to the start of the process. That happens before personal preferences attach to specific people.

Every later stage of the search measures candidates against this profile. It shapes who is approached, what interviewers ask and how finalists are compared.

A profile is not fixed. If the company's plans change while the search is under way, the board can revise it. When it does, the revised criteria apply to every candidate still in contention.

Many boards bring in an executive search firm to handle the mechanics of a CEO search. The firm helps build the candidate list, keeps the process confidential and makes the first approach to potential candidates.

Four firms are well-known names in board-level searches: Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds Associates, Heidrick & Struggles and Korn Ferry. Korn Ferry and Heidrick & Struggles are publicly traded companies. Spencer Stuart and Russell Reynolds Associates are privately held. Some boards use smaller boutique firms instead. Others run the search entirely on their own.

In a CEO search, the client is the board rather than the management team. The search firm takes direction from the directors leading the process and reports back to them. This keeps the work independent of a departing chief executive or senior managers who may hold views about who should come next. Some of those managers may also be candidates themselves.

List building is the first of the firm's core jobs. A search firm can map executives at competitors, at companies in adjacent industries and in roles that fit the board's profile. Many strong prospects are not looking for a new job. Part of the firm's value lies in surfacing people a board might not identify on its own.

Confidentiality is the second job. Sitting executives at other companies often cannot be seen exploring a move. Internal contenders face a similar problem inside their own company. Using an intermediary lets a board gauge interest without exposing names until both sides are ready to go further.

Outreach is the third. The firm makes the initial calls and describes the opportunity in general terms. It then screens for interest before any director gets involved. This saves the board's time. It also lowers the risk for candidates who decide not to proceed.

Search firms at this level typically work on a retained basis. The firm is hired exclusively for the assignment and paid whether or not the eventual hire comes from its list. Contingency recruiting works differently. There, a recruiter is paid only when a placement is made.

Boards also ask about conflicts before signing on. Large search firms often observe off-limits arrangements that stop them from recruiting executives away from their current clients. Those arrangements can narrow the pool a given firm is able to approach. Directors check which companies are excluded before choosing a firm.

A CEO candidate slate is the shortlist of people a board will seriously consider for the top job. It can mix internal executives from the company's own leadership team with outside candidates, and boards often measure both groups against the same set of criteria.

Internal candidates usually come from the senior ranks below the CEO. Typical names include a chief operating officer, a chief financial officer or the head of a major business unit. Directors may have watched these executives work for years. They may have seen their board presentations, their quarterly results and the way each person handles a setback.

That history gives the board a body of direct evidence about an insider. It also shapes how an insider is judged. Directors know the candidate's weaknesses as well as strengths. An outsider arrives with a record the board has mostly read about.

External candidates come from beyond the company. They can include sitting chief executives at other businesses, senior leaders at competitors or executives from other industries whose experience matches what the board wants. An outside search can surface skills the internal bench lacks, such as experience with a turnaround, an acquisition or a new market.

One set of criteria for both groups keeps the comparison even. The yardstick is normally the role profile the board agreed on earlier. That profile is built from the company's strategy and the skills the next CEO needs. Each name on the slate is weighed against it, not simply against the other names.

The slate usually narrows as the search moves forward. A long list of possible names is cut to a smaller group the committee wants to meet. That smaller group becomes the finalists who go through formal interviews.

Some boards use an executive search firm to build the outside portion of the slate. The firm handles outreach to external names. Insiders, by contrast, are already known to directors and can be approached directly.

A board can appoint an interim CEO to run the company while the search for a permanent leader continues. The interim is usually either an existing senior executive or a member of the board itself.

The role exists because a company cannot pause while directors work through candidates. Someone still has to sign off on budgets, run the leadership team and speak for the business to employees, customers and lenders. An interim appointment fills the gap with a named person and a clear line of authority.

The title varies. Some companies use "interim CEO," while others use "acting CEO." Either way, the person holds the authority of the office for as long as the appointment lasts. The temporary label tells staff and investors that the board has not yet made its permanent choice.

Choosing an existing executive keeps day-to-day knowledge in place. A chief financial officer or chief operating officer already knows the company's finances, managers and pending decisions. The trade-off is that the executive's own job may need covering. Colleagues may also read the appointment as a hint about the final outcome.

Choosing a director brings a different kind of knowledge to the role. A board member knows the company's strategy and the reasons for the search. Some boards hand the job to the chair, who then holds both roles for the duration. A director who becomes an employee typically stops counting as independent. That person then usually steps off committees that require independent members, such as the audit committee.

Boards also decide whether the interim is a candidate for the permanent post. Some interims rule themselves out from the start. Others enter the search and compete against the rest of the field. Internal and outside candidates alike often ask whether the interim is a rival.

The interim's brief tends to be narrow. It usually centers on keeping operations steady and avoiding major commitments that would bind the next CEO. Large strategic moves are often left for the permanent leader to make once the board completes its choice.

Finalists for a CEO job usually sit for several rounds of interviews. These start with the directors who run the search and widen to the full board. Formal assessments of the strongest candidates typically follow those conversations.

The early rounds belong to the search committee. Directors test each finalist against the role profile the board agreed on before the search began. They ask about past results, leadership record and how the candidate would approach the company's specific challenges.

Later rounds bring in the wider board. That step matters because the full board, not the committee, casts the final vote. Directors who sat outside the search get their own chance to judge each finalist before they are asked to approve one.

Board-level meetings can take several forms. Some are one-on-one conversations. Others are small-group sessions or informal meals, where directors see how a candidate handles less scripted discussion.

Interviews run in both directions. A finalist is also deciding whether to take the job. The sessions give a candidate a view of how the board operates, what it expects from management and how directors relate to one another. What a candidate sees in these meetings feeds into the decision to accept an offer.

Internal and external finalists face different conditions. Directors often already know inside executives from board presentations and committee work. Their interviews focus on whether they can handle the top job rather than the one they hold now. Outside finalists often hold senior roles elsewhere. Their meetings are usually scheduled discreetly to protect their current positions.

Assessments give the board a second source of evidence beyond the interviews. Boards may commission structured evaluations of leadership style, decision-making and judgment. Outside specialists, such as industrial-organizational psychologists, sometimes conduct them. Some boards also ask finalists to present their view of the company's strategy and priorities.

The combined record from interviews and assessments lets the board narrow the field to a leading candidate. That person then moves on to verification before any offer is made.

Reference and background checks begin once a board has a leading CEO candidate. They test whether the person's record matches what the interviews and assessments suggested, and they come before the board makes a final offer.

The two checks do different jobs. A reference check gathers judgment from people who have worked with the candidate. A background check verifies facts on paper, such as degrees, past job titles and any legal or regulatory history.

Reference calls for a CEO role usually reach well beyond the names a candidate supplies. Directors or the search firm may speak with former bosses, fellow executives, board members who oversaw the candidate and people who reported to the candidate. Each group sees a different side of a leader. A former board chair can speak to how the candidate worked with directors. A former direct report can describe how the candidate ran a team day to day.

Searches also often use what recruiters call backdoor references. These are conversations with people the candidate did not list. They can confirm a pattern or raise a question that the supplied references left out.

A CEO search is usually confidential. That means the board has to weigh whom to call and when. An early call to the wrong person can let the candidate's current employer learn of the search.

The background check is more mechanical. It typically confirms education and employment dates. It also searches court records for litigation or criminal history. For a candidate who has served as an officer or director, the review may extend to regulatory actions. It may also look for possible conflicts of interest, such as outside board seats or business ties.

In the U.S., a company that uses an outside screening firm for this work falls under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. That federal law requires the employer to tell the candidate in writing and get written permission before ordering the report.

Boards generally run these checks late, on one finalist or a very short list. That limits how many people learn of the search. It also keeps sensitive inquiries focused on the person most likely to get the job.

The results go back to the committee leading the search and then to the full board. A clean result clears the way for pay negotiations. An unresolved issue can send the board back to its other finalists.

Once the board settles on its preferred candidate, the compensation committee usually negotiates the new CEO's pay package and employment terms. Depending on the company, the committee approves the final terms on its own or together with the board's other independent directors.

The committee's task is to turn an agreement in principle into a binding contract. That contract covers how much the CEO earns and how the pay is structured. It also covers what happens if the relationship ends.

A typical package at a large public company has several layers. Base salary is the fixed cash component. An annual bonus ties cash to goals set for the year. Long-term incentives, such as stock options, restricted stock or performance shares, link pay to the company's results and share price over several years.

Outside candidates add a complication. An executive who leaves another company can forfeit unvested equity from that employer. Boards often answer with a make-whole award. This is a grant meant to replace some or all of what the candidate gives up by moving.

The employment agreement reaches beyond money. It can set severance terms and define what counts as termination for cause. It can also spell out change-in-control protections that apply if the company is sold.

Many agreements include non-compete and non-solicitation clauses. Their enforceability varies by jurisdiction. California, for example, generally does not enforce non-compete agreements.

At U.S. public companies, the committee works within specific rules. NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards require compensation committee members to be independent directors. Committees often retain outside compensation consultants. Before selecting one, a committee must consider that adviser's independence.

Recovery provisions are part of the package as well. SEC Rule 10D-1, adopted in 2022, requires listed companies to maintain clawback policies. Those policies recover incentive pay that was awarded on the basis of financial results later restated.

Shareholders review the outcome after the fact. A public company describes executive pay in its annual proxy statement, including a section called the Compensation Discussion and Analysis. Under the Dodd-Frank Act, shareholders also cast a nonbinding say-on-pay vote on executive compensation at least once every three years.

The committee negotiates with those disclosures in view. Much of what it agrees to, from salary to severance terms, will later be set out in public filings for investors to read.

For a U.S. public company, naming a new CEO creates a disclosure duty. Item 5.02 of Form 8-K, a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, requires the company to report the appointment of a principal executive officer. The filing is due within four business days.

Form 8-K is the current report that public companies file when certain significant events occur. The SEC's rules list the specific events that trigger it, and Item 5.02 is one of them. The annual 10-K and quarterly 10-Q follow a fixed calendar. An 8-K is filed when an event happens.

Item 5.02 covers changes among directors and certain officers. The same item also applies when a principal executive officer retires, resigns or is terminated. A single CEO handover can therefore produce disclosure about both the departing leader and the arriving one.

The appointment section of the item asks for more than a name. The filing states the new officer's position and the date of the appointment. It also covers the person's age and business experience. Any family relationships with directors or executive officers must be disclosed. Certain transactions between the new officer and the company are reported too. A brief description of any material plan, contract or arrangement tied to the appointment is required as well.

The timing rule has some flexibility. A company that announces the appointment through another public channel, such as a press release, may hold the 8-K until the day of that announcement. Filings become public on the SEC's EDGAR database. Investors, analysts and reporters can read them there.

The press release is the version most people see first. Companies usually issue one to name the new chief executive and give a start date. The release describes the leadership change in plain language for employees, customers and the media.

The announcement opens a transition period rather than ending the work. The incoming CEO typically meets with the outgoing CEO to hand over open issues and key relationships. Meetings with senior executives and employees follow. The new leader also meets with investors, who hold a direct stake in how the company is run.

#5474. The Hidden Reason Leaders Often Get Sick After Their Busiest Season — and How to Stop It

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Many leaders push through their hardest seasons and then get sick the minute things calm down. Here’s why it happens and what to do about it, so your body doesn’t force the break for you.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

When my oldest brother died suddenly, I kept working. I run my own business, so there’s no paid time off and nobody to cover for me. My clients still needed me, and there, of course, were bills to pay, so I kept showing up. When things started to settle down, I got sick, and then sick again. I don’t think it came out of nowhere. My body had been running on stress for months, and once I slowed down, it gave out. The same thing happened during my divorce. I worked straight through it, and it was only after everything was done that I got really sick.

I’ve spent 15 years studying how people change, and it still took me a while to see the pattern in myself. The same thing happens to leaders all the time, just on a smaller scale. A funding round closes, or a big launch wraps up, and a week later they’re sick. When you’re the one running the company, that is going to affect the business as well.

UCLA psychologist Marc Schoen calls it the let-down effect: getting sick after a stressful stretch ends, not during it. Dutch psychologist Ad Vingerhoets studied a version he called leisure sickness, symptoms that show up on weekends and vacations. In his 2002 study of nearly 1,900 people, about 3% recognized the pattern. They tended to be high achievers with a strong sense of responsibility and real trouble adjusting to not being busy.

Not every sniffle means something, and if you’re getting sick a lot, your doctor should be your first call. What I’d pay attention to is the repeated pattern. You crash every time a big deal closes, or you lose the same weeks every year.

A client I’ve coached for two years, I’ll call her Michelle, runs a business that gets really demanding toward the end of the year. From fall through December, she’s all gas. And for years, she spent the first couple of weeks of January sick on the couch.

It was so predictable that she’d bring it up in our sessions in November. She’d tell me she was already dreading it — that it was just her pattern.

This past January was the first time it didn’t happen.

When you’re under pressure, your nervous system stays on, and stress hormones help you push through. Your body is still sending signals the whole time, like tight shoulders, shallow breathing or a stomach that’s off before every big meeting. When you’re busy, it’s easy to override them. Once things get quiet, they’re a lot harder to ignore.

I always say we don’t have problems — we have patterns. For a lot of driven people, staying busy is how they avoid feeling the hard stuff. After my brother died, it was easier to keep working than to sit still and feel it. So rest didn’t always feel relaxing. It felt uncomfortable.

And success doesn’t make that pattern better. It makes it bigger. The more you build, the more people depend on you and the more reasons you have to keep going. Just knowing about it doesn’t fix it, either. Michelle knew January was coming every year, and it came anyway.

More vacations won’t fix this on their own. What helps is learning to listen to your body sooner.

Check in with your nervous system a few times a day, not just when you’re falling apart. Pause and notice your jaw, your shoulders, your breathing. Most leaders are surprised how often they’re running hot while telling themselves they’re fine.

One of the quickest ways I know to calm your body down is bilateral stimulation. That’s any steady left-right rhythm, like walking, tapping your knees one side at a time or crossing your arms and tapping your shoulders. It’s the same rhythm used in EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing), and it helps the nervous system settle quickly. A few minutes between meetings is often enough to take the edge off.

Spend more time with people who make you feel calmer. Pay attention to who you feel most like yourself around, the people you don’t feel like you have to be on for. It might not be who you’d expect. For a lot of people, it isn’t family, and that’s okay. It could be an old friend, a neighbor or a coworker who doesn’t need anything from you. Our nervous systems take cues from the people around us. Psychologists call it co-regulation. Being near someone who’s calm helps your body calm down too, without you having to do anything.

Take time off before you need it, and plan around your hardest season. Schoen’s advice is not to go from 100 to zero overnight, and the easiest way to avoid that is to never hit 100 for months at a time. Spread your time off through the year, and lighten the week after a big push instead of booking the next big thing.

What helped Michelle wasn’t one big change. She started putting time off on her calendar, a few days here and there, instead of waiting for the holidays. She got better at noticing when she was pushing too hard and pulling back before her body did it for her.

Looking back, I wish I’d listened to myself after my brother died. I knew I needed to slow down, but I was so worried about money that I didn’t let myself. If I had, I might have avoided a lot of what came after.

Your body gives you signals all the time. Most of us ignore them until we can’t. If you don’t stop, your body will make you. I’d rather you choose when that happens.

When my oldest brother died suddenly, I kept working. I run my own business, so there’s no paid time off and nobody to cover for me. My clients still needed me, and there, of course, were bills to pay, so I kept showing up. When things started to settle down, I got sick, and then sick again. I don’t think it came out of nowhere. My body had been running on stress for months, and once I slowed down, it gave out. The same thing happened during my divorce. I worked straight through it, and it was only after everything was done that I got really sick.

I’ve spent 15 years studying how people change, and it still took me a while to see the pattern in myself. The same thing happens to leaders all the time, just on a smaller scale. A funding round closes, or a big launch wraps up, and a week later they’re sick. When you’re the one running the company, that is going to affect the business as well.

Dutch psychologist Ad Vingerhoets studied a version he called leisure sickness, symptoms that show up on weekends and vacations. In his 2002 study of nearly 1,900 people, about 3% recognized the pattern. They tended to be high achievers with a strong sense of responsibility and real trouble adjusting to not being busy.

#5473. A year in, Smartsheet CEO Raj Singh bets on a new vision beyond the company’s flagship product

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 3:31 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:53 pm

Smartsheet’s biggest new product in years doesn’t require Smartsheet.

The Bellevue, Wash.-based company on Wednesday unveiled vsActual, as in “plan versus actual,” an AI product that reads a company’s strategy and budgets, tracks the work across tools such as Jira, Workday and Slack, and flags when projects drift off course.

It’s the first standalone product under CEO Raj Singh, the Concur co-founder who took over Smartsheet a year ago, and it’s aimed at CEOs, CFOs and COOs rather than the project managers who have long been Smartsheet’s core users.

At the company’s Engage conference in Seattle, Singh showed a slide from a year ago labeling Smartsheet “a product company,” with the company and its software in a single box.

“Smartsheet, the company, and Smartsheet, the product, were exactly the same thing — same box, same ceiling — an attractive ceiling, but still a ceiling,” he said. Now, he explained, Smartsheet is a multi-product company, with vsActual as a key milestone.

Singh was relaxed and at home on the stage, engaging warmly with the crowd and his fellow presenters like someone who’d been running Smartsheet for years. He went off script often enough that he paused at one point to reassure the teleprompter operator everything was OK, and his talk ultimately ran so long that it threw off the morning’s schedule.

In an interview with GeekWire after the keynote, Singh said the company has more room to grow by working with the software that customers already use than by trying to move everything into its flagship product.

“Most of the competition is saying, ‘Well, if you move all your stuff onto my platform, you’ll be totally in control,’” he said. “I think every CIO is thinking, I’m never going to do that.”

Founded two decades ago, Smartsheet is best known for spreadsheet-style software that teams use to plan projects, track tasks and automate routine work.

It went public in 2018 and was taken private in January 2025 by Vista Equity Partners and Blackstone in an $8.4 billion deal, when it had more than $1 billion in annual revenue. Its rivals include Microsoft, Google and Salesforce, as well as Asana, Monday.com, Airtable and ClickUp.

Singh described vsActual as part of a broader product lineup that also includes Smartsheet’s flagship software and Brandfolder, the digital asset management service the company acquired in 2020.

All three draw on the same underlying data, built from 20 years of tracking how work gets planned, approved and done in Smartsheet, which the company calls its Execution Graph. Future products will be built the same way, Singh said.

“The Execution Graph is the long-term differentiated value of our company,” he said.

A change in pricing: Smartsheet is also moving away from charging by the user. Under a new consumption-based model, customers pay a base fee plus credits that are drawn down as people use the software, including its AI features, automations and API connections. Seat-based plans remain available.

Singh said customers balked at paying full price for people who use Smartsheet only occasionally. As an example, he said creating a dashboard might cost 50 cents, rather than a license that runs hundreds of dollars. Customers who switch won’t be charged for going over their credits, though he didn’t say for how long.

He said the net effect on revenue should be “nothing but positive,” describing the shift as a way to unlock demand from customers who held back under per-seat pricing.

“Agents are clearly going to be users moving forward,” he added.

Competition and risks: The new product enters a crowded field. Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday and others are adding AI agents that plan and track work inside their own products, and AI-native startups are going after the same status-report busywork.

The software also depends on data from systems run by other companies, including rivals such as Asana. Singh said Smartsheet connects to them through APIs and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for linking AI models to outside software, depending on how deep the integration goes.

The approach carries some risk: if companies can track their work through vsActual without moving it into Smartsheet, they have less reason to expand their use of the core software, the company’s main business.

Asked about that, Singh pointed to new AI features in Smartsheet itself, including its Smart Assist agent and an MCP server that lets customers use Smartsheet from AI assistants such as Claude and Copilot. “The core keeps growing,” he said.

Keith Kirkpatrick, a Futurum Group analyst, wrote Wednesday that vsActual is “the company’s clearest move yet from managing tasks to governing strategy,” but said the strategy requires Smartsheet to sell to a different kind of buyer.

“Its sellers are also not used to finance-led deals with long evaluation cycles,” he wrote, adding that many executives still see Smartsheet as a “glorified Excel” project management tool.

Singh said Smartsheet’s sales force already knows how to sell to large enterprises, but acknowledged that the company will need people who understand corporate planning. It will build a team of vsActual specialists, as it has for Brandfolder.

Kirkpatrick also noted that vsActual requires a company to work from one official plan, unlike Smartsheet’s more flexible core software, and said the company will need to show that its Execution Graph offers the same depth for customers whose work lives mostly in other systems.

“Decoupling widens the market but strains the main differentiator,” he wrote.

Smartsheet hasn’t said when vsActual will be generally available or how it will be priced. It’s building the product with 12 enterprise design partners, including some of the world’s largest food service, financial services and health systems, Singh said.

From Concur to Smartsheet: Singh started Concur in the early 1990s with his brother, Steve Singh, and Mike Hilton, and the company grew into a top provider of corporate travel and expense software before SAP acquired it for $8.3 billion in 2014.

Raj Singh later led health benefits company Accolade through its IPO and sale, and took over as Smartsheet CEO in October 2025, after longtime CEO Mark Mader retired and Apptio co-founder Sunny Gupta served as acting CEO.

Smartsheet cut jobs that month and again in February. Singh has since rebuilt the leadership team, including several executives he worked with at Concur and Accolade.

Singh said the leadership team is now fully assembled and the company is hiring, though AI means headcount won’t grow the way it once did.

He didn’t disclose revenue but said the business is growing, especially internationally and with government customers, and that retention remains strong despite fears that AI would lead companies to abandon traditional software. More than 100 customers now pay Smartsheet at least $1 million a year, a record, he said.

He credited Smartsheet’s founders and past leaders with building a successful tool for project managers, calling former CEO Mark Mader and co-founder Brent Frei friends.

Singh said the bigger opportunity is to help businesses run better, and he sees no reason Smartsheet can’t become one of the most important software companies in the world.

“I’m 58 years old,” he said. “I’m not doing this because I need to make an extra buck. I’m doing this because I think there’s a very important company in here, and we just have to unearth it, and then we have to get to customers and make them see that new vision.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5472. 5 Things Western Entrepreneurs Should Know Before Doing Business in Hong Kong

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Four generations of family business in Hong Kong offer five practical lessons for Western entrepreneurs setting up in the city.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

More overseas companies are operating in Hong Kong than ever before. Government figures show a record 11,070 companies with parent companies outside the city in 2025, up 11% in a year, including 1,550 with U.S. parents. And Boston Consulting Group’s latest Global Wealth Report found that Hong Kong has overtaken Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth hub.

My family has been in business here for four generations, and I have watched many Western companies arrive. The ones that struggle are rarely let down by the numbers. More often, they arrive with the wrong assumptions about how business works here. These are the five things I would tell any Western entrepreneur before they start.

Hong Kong has an excellent legal system, and contracts here are taken seriously. But a contract is usually the last step, not the first. Most of the deals I have seen succeed began with an introduction from someone both sides trusted, followed by several meals and conversations before anyone discussed terms.

Western founders sometimes see this as slow. I see it as due diligence done in person. Trust takes a long time to build and surprisingly little time to lose, so it pays to invest in it early. If you can, ask someone respected locally to introduce you, and follow up in person rather than relying on email.

Many of Hong Kong’s best-known companies are still controlled by families, and the person across the meeting table is not always the person who decides. In some firms, the real decision is made quietly by a senior family member or a small inner circle before the formal meeting takes place.

In my own family’s business, we chose to bring in outside professionals to run the company rather than rely on family members. Many families here have done the same, but ownership and influence often stay with the family. Ask early how decisions are made and who needs to be comfortable with them. It can save you months.

It also helps to know which generation you are dealing with. Many younger family members were educated overseas, as I was, and are often open to new ideas and new partners. They will usually still want the senior generation’s blessing before they commit.

Hong Kong runs on common law, its currency is freely convertible, capital moves in and out freely, and English is an official language. That makes it easy for Western companies to set up here. It is also why mainland Chinese companies are arriving in growing numbers. The number of companies with mainland parents rose 18% last year to 3,090.

But doing business in Hong Kong is not the same as doing business in mainland China. The laws, regulations and ways of working are different. If the mainland or the wider Greater Bay Area is part of your plan, hire people who understand both systems and, ideally, speak Cantonese and Mandarin as well as English.

It is also worth speaking to InvestHK, the government’s investment promotion agency, before you arrive. It helped a record 560 companies set up or expand in the city in 2025, and its advice is free.

Hong Kong is not a cheap place to operate. Demand for offices is rising again, and CBRE reports that rents in Central have risen nearly 16% so far this year. In AmCham Hong Kong’s 2026 survey, 71% of members said the high cost of living was putting off foreign talent.

Rather than relying on expensive expatriate packages, hire and train good local people. I have spent 30 years funding education, and I have seen what talented young people can achieve when someone gives them an opportunity. The talent pool is also growing. The government’s talent schemes, including the Top Talent Pass, have approved more than 410,000 applications, according to figures given to the Legislative Council earlier this year. In my experience, companies that invest in their Hong Kong team tend to stay longer and do better.

Hong Kong rewards those who stay. I have seen the city written off during the Asian financial crisis, the SARS outbreak and the pandemic. Each time, the businesses that stayed and kept investing were well placed for the recovery.

Local partners notice who stays through the difficult periods, and they remember. If you ever need to scale back, explain why and keep in touch with your partners. In AmCham’s latest survey, 92% of members said they had no plans to move their headquarters out of the city. Come with a long-term plan and the patience to see it through.

Hong Kong is open for business, and the opportunities are real. But success here depends as much on the relationships you build, and how long you are willing to stay, as on your business plan. Get those right, and Hong Kong can be one of the most rewarding places in the world to build a company.

More overseas companies are operating in Hong Kong than ever before. Government figures show a record 11,070 companies with parent companies outside the city in 2025, up 11% in a year, including 1,550 with U.S. parents. And Boston Consulting Group’s latest Global Wealth Report found that Hong Kong has overtaken Switzerland as the world’s largest cross-border wealth hub.

My family has been in business here for four generations, and I have watched many Western companies arrive. The ones that struggle are rarely let down by the numbers. More often, they arrive with the wrong assumptions about how business works here. These are the five things I would tell any Western entrepreneur before they start.

Hong Kong has an excellent legal system, and contracts here are taken seriously. But a contract is usually the last step, not the first. Most of the deals I have seen succeed began with an introduction from someone both sides trusted, followed by several meals and conversations before anyone discussed terms.
