#5471. When a CFO, COO or CTO resigns: what 10 exit scenarios signal to investors

Free daily briefing on global business news.

When a CFO, COO or CTO resigns, the timing, Form 8-K wording and succession plan tell investors different things, and these 10 situations show how to read each

Three resignation letters can land on the same morning and mean three different things. A chief financial officer guards the numbers. A chief operating officer guards execution. A chief technology officer guards the product and the technology underneath it. When one of those seats goes empty, the question it raises for investors depends on which one it was.

That is why a CFO, COO or CTO resignation rarely reads as a single kind of event. A CFO who leaves weeks before an earnings release raises questions about the coming figures. A COO who exits after years as the presumed next chief executive raises questions about succession at the top. A CTO who departs halfway through a major platform overhaul raises questions about whether the program stays on schedule. The title on the press release points to the part of the business that now needs a closer look.

In the U.S., many of these departures become public fast. A public company must generally disclose the exit of its principal financial officer, principal operating officer or certain other senior officers. That disclosure goes on Form 8-K, under Item 5.02, within four business days. A CTO's exit falls under that rule only when the CTO holds one of the listed officer roles or is a named executive officer. The filing often states whether the departure involved a disagreement with the company. It also names a replacement or interim appointee if the board has chosen one.

The announcement itself carries less information than it appears to. Phrases such as "pursuing other opportunities" or "personal reasons" are standard language. On their own, they do not explain why someone left. The signal sits in the details around the announcement. Those details include timing relative to the reporting calendar, any accompanying filings about auditors or restated results, whether a successor is named and how long the transition runs.

The 10 situations below separate those details by role and by circumstance. Each one explains what a particular kind of executive departure tends to put in question and which documents to check. Several also show how a planned handover differs from an abrupt exit. None of them offers a formula for predicting a stock move. They offer a way to read a C-suite exit in context, with the filing open.

A CFO resignation draws closer scrutiny because the chief financial officer personally certifies the company's financial reports. When that person leaves, investors want to know whether the departure has anything to do with the numbers carrying their signature.

U.S. law ties the accuracy of the books to this executive. Under the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, the CFO and the CEO both sign certifications attached to a public company's quarterly and annual reports. Other C-suite officers, such as the chief operating officer or chief technology officer, do not carry that personal sign-off as part of the role.

The Section 302 certification covers a lot of ground. The signing officer states that they have reviewed the report. They state that it contains no untrue statement of a material fact and omits nothing needed to keep it from being misleading. They also state that the financial statements fairly present the company's financial condition and results in all material respects.

The certification extends to internal controls. The signers take responsibility for establishing and maintaining disclosure controls and internal control over financial reporting. They must also tell the company's auditors and the board's audit committee about significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in those controls. Any fraud involving management or other employees with a significant role in internal controls falls under the same disclosure.

Section 906 adds a separate certification with criminal penalties. An officer who knowingly certifies a periodic report that does not comply with the law faces fines and possible prison time. That exposure gives the finance chief's signature a legal weight that most other executive roles do not carry.

The CFO is also usually the executive who explains the numbers to the market. On earnings calls, the CFO typically walks analysts through results, margins, cash flow and guidance. A new finance chief means a new voice on those calls. Analysts lose the person whose explanations they have learned to interpret.

None of this makes every CFO departure a red flag. Finance chiefs leave for promotions, retirement and family reasons, as other executives do. The heavier scrutiny reflects the role, not a presumption about the person. What a given exit signals depends on its timing, the wording of the filing and who takes over the finance function.

A CFO resignation that lands shortly before an earnings release or an annual report deadline puts the spotlight on the numbers about to be published. The question it raises is whether the departing chief financial officer was prepared to stand behind those results.

The timing matters because of the CFO's role in the final stretch of a reporting cycle. The chief financial officer oversees the closing of the books and reviews the draft financial statements. The CFO also typically presents the results on the earnings call. For a 10-K or 10-Q, the CFO signs the certifications that accompany the filing. A finance chief who leaves before that work is finished hands the signature to someone else.

SEC deadlines define how tight that window is. Large accelerated filers must file a 10-K within 60 days of the end of the fiscal year. Accelerated filers get 75 days, and all other companies get 90. Quarterly 10-Q reports are due within 40 days for the two larger filer categories and 45 days for everyone else. An exit inside those windows leaves an interim officer little time to learn the accounts before certifying them.

The departure alone does not prove anything is wrong. Personal circumstances, a new job with a fixed start date or a board decision can each produce an awkward calendar. Even so, a planned finance transition is often scheduled to follow a completed reporting cycle. That makes a mid-cycle exit worth a closer look.

What follows the announcement carries more information than the announcement itself. Investors watch whether the earnings release arrives on its scheduled date. They also watch whether the company reaffirms, changes or withdraws its financial guidance. A results date that slips, or a call where management declines to discuss the outlook, adds to the uncertainty.

The filing is the clearest test. A company that cannot file its 10-K or 10-Q on time can submit Form 12b-25, a notification of late filing. That form allows up to 15 extra calendar days for an annual report and five for a quarterly report. A CFO exit followed by a 12b-25 tells investors the numbers were not ready on schedule. A CFO exit followed by an on-time filing, certified by an interim finance chief, suggests the close stayed on track.

A CFO who leaves around the same time a company changes auditors or restates its results raises a pointed question for investors. They want to know whether the departure is tied to the accounting itself. Answering that means reading every related filing, not just the resignation notice.

The overlap matters because of the chief financial officer's role. The CFO is one of the two executives who certify the periodic reports that a restatement goes back to correct. When those numbers are revised, the exit of an executive who vouched for them draws fresh attention to that certification.

U.S. disclosure rules split this situation across several parts of Form 8-K. Item 5.02 covers the officer's departure. Item 4.01 covers a change in the company's certifying accountant. Item 4.02 covers non-reliance on previously issued financial statements, which is the filing that accompanies a restatement. A company in this position may file two or three of these within a short span.

Each item carries its own clues. An Item 4.01 filing must say whether the auditor resigned, declined to stand for reelection or was dismissed. It must also disclose any disagreements with the former auditor over accounting or disclosure matters. The departing audit firm then provides a letter, filed as an exhibit, stating whether it agrees with the company's account.

An Item 4.02 filing shows who concluded that the old numbers could not be relied on. That conclusion can come from the board, its audit committee or authorized officers. It can also follow a notice from the outside auditor that the earlier statements should no longer be relied upon. The filing identifies which periods are affected and describes the facts behind the decision.

Read together, the filings establish the order of events. A CFO who leaves after a restatement is announced presents a different picture from one who leaves before the problem surfaces. An auditor that resigned on its own presents a different picture from one the company dismissed.

Pay is part of the picture too. Section 304 of Sarbanes-Oxley allows recovery of CEO and CFO bonuses and stock-sale profits after a restatement caused by misconduct. Under SEC Rule 10D-1, stock exchanges require listed companies to keep a policy for recovering incentive pay awarded on results that were later restated. That recovery applies whether or not anyone was at fault.

Not every restatement involves wrongdoing. Some correct technical errors in how a company applied accounting standards. The 8-K filings, along with any later disclosure of a material weakness in internal control over financial reporting, help investors tell the two apart.

A CFO who resigns to become a CEO, or to run finance at a larger company, usually leaves investors with a straightforward explanation. The departure has a visible cause that people outside the company can confirm.

That confirmation separates this case from a vague exit. A filing that says the executive is leaving to pursue other opportunities tells a shareholder very little. A named destination tells them where the person is going and why the move makes sense.

The new employer can supply a second record. If it is a U.S. public company, it will generally report the appointment of a new principal executive officer or principal financial officer on its own Form 8-K. Investors can then read both companies' filings side by side.

The career logic is easy to follow. A finance chief already works next to the CEO, runs the budget and answers analysts on earnings calls. Boards searching for a chief executive with command of the numbers may look to sitting CFOs. A move from a midsize company to a larger one fits a familiar path in corporate finance.

Bench strength shapes the impact on the company left behind. A company with a chief accounting officer, controller or treasurer ready to step up can absorb the loss more easily. A company that must run a long external search carries more risk in the meantime. Investors also look at whether the incoming finance chief has run a public-company finance function before.

Pay arrangements can add context. Executives who resign voluntarily usually forfeit unvested stock awards. Hiring companies sometimes offer replacement grants to cover that loss. When the hiring company files its 8-K, the filing generally describes any material compensation arrangement made with the new officer. An offer large enough to justify leaving unvested equity behind is consistent with a move driven by the new opportunity.

The destination itself carries information. A CEO seat or a clearly larger company reads as a step up. A sideways move to a similar-sized peer, or to a private company with no obvious promotion, invites more questions about what prompted the exit. Neither reading proves anything about the old company's books. Investors still weigh the next earnings release and filing alongside the announcement.

A COO resignation puts the spotlight on execution: the plants, supply chains, logistics and service operations that turn a company's strategy into delivered products and booked revenue. The core question for investors is whether that machinery keeps running smoothly once someone else is in charge of it.

The chief operating officer's job varies from company to company. Many companies have no COO at all. Where the role exists, it reflects a decision by the CEO to hand off day-to-day operations. At a manufacturer, the role often covers production, procurement and distribution. At a retailer, it may span stores, inventory and fulfillment. At a software or services business, it can mean customer support, sales operations and internal processes. Reading a COO departure starts with working out which of those functions actually reported to the person leaving.

That scope determines where the risk is likely to show up. A COO who led a large operational overhaul leaves behind work that is still in motion. Examples include a factory consolidation, a new distribution network or a multiyear cost-reduction program. The practical question is whether that program has a clear owner after the exit.

The company's response to the vacancy carries its own information. Some boards hire or promote a new COO. Others split the duties among division heads. Still others fold the responsibilities back under the CEO and leave the title empty. Each choice changes how much operational detail lands on the chief executive's desk. It also changes who answers for execution problems later.

The clearest read on execution usually comes later, in the operating results. Gross margin, inventory levels, delivery times, order backlog and management's guidance all reflect how well operations are running. Movement in those measures during the quarters after a COO leaves gives investors something concrete to weigh against the stated reason for the departure.

A COO exit does not by itself indicate trouble. Operating executives move to other companies, retire or step back for reasons unrelated to performance. The test is whether the operational numbers hold steady once the handover is complete.

When a chief operating officer widely seen as the next CEO resigns, the signal is mainly about succession, not operations. It tells investors the company's leadership plan has likely changed. It also reopens the question of who will eventually run the business.

The COO seat is a common proving ground for a future chief executive. The job covers operations and execution across the company. That gives a candidate broad exposure to the business before taking the top job. Yet the title has never guaranteed promotion. Some COOs go on to become CEO, and others never do.

Heir-apparent status comes in two forms. Sometimes a company signals it openly, through public comments about succession or a combined title such as president and chief operating officer. In other cases the label comes from investors and the business press rather than the board. A departure undercuts a stated plan more directly than it undercuts outside speculation.

The exit can fit one of several explanations. The COO may have concluded that the CEO was not stepping down soon. The board may have settled on a different candidate. Another company may have offered the chief executive role outright. The announcement rarely says which one applies.

Whatever the cause, the departure raises three broader questions. The first concerns the sitting CEO's timeline. If the expected successor walks away, investors may wonder whether the CEO intends to stay longer than anticipated. The second concerns the bench of internal talent. A board that loses its leading insider may promote another executive or open an external search. The third concerns governance. Repeated departures of likely successors can lead shareholders to ask how actively the board manages succession.

What the company does with the vacant role is also informative. It may appoint a new COO or split the duties among other executives. It may also leave the seat empty and have the CEO take over operations. Eliminating the position changes who could plausibly be next in line.

Many U.S. public companies describe the board's approach to CEO succession planning in their annual proxy statement. Comparing that language before and after the departure can show whether the plan has shifted. The executive's destination adds context as well. A COO who leaves to become CEO elsewhere fits a story of career ambition more than one of operational trouble.

A CTO resignation sends investors back to the product roadmap. The chief technology officer usually sets technology strategy and engineering direction. The central question is whether planned products and platform work will still arrive on schedule and in the same form.

The answer depends on what the job covered at that particular company. The CTO title has no fixed definition. At one company it means running the entire engineering organization, including hiring, budgets and delivery dates. At another, it describes a senior technologist who shapes long-range architecture. In that setup, a separate engineering or product executive manages the teams that build things.

That difference changes how much an exit matters. A CTO who owned delivery leaves a management gap that touches every release. A CTO whose role centered on vision and research leaves a gap in long-term direction. That gap may not show up in near-term results at all. Reading a departure starts with understanding the company's own structure. That structure is often visible on its leadership page and in its annual filings.

Disclosure varies too. Many CTOs do not hold a listed officer role and do not rank as a named executive officer. Their exits then fall outside the Item 5.02 requirement. Those departures may surface first through a press release, a social media post or an updated executive biography rather than a regulatory filing.

Founder status adds another layer. At younger technology companies, the CTO is frequently a co-founder who built much of the original system. That person may hold knowledge of the code and architecture that is not fully documented. A co-founder CTO leaving raises questions about that institutional knowledge in a way a hired executive's exit may not.

Investors then look for follow-through. The first useful signals usually come from the next earnings call or investor update. Management may restate product timelines, push back a launch or describe the roadmap in vaguer terms than before. Any of those shifts carries more information than the resignation announcement itself.

Who absorbs the role also matters. A company may promote an internal engineering leader, hire from outside or split the duties between a chief product officer and a head of engineering. An internal promotion points toward continuity in the existing technical plan. An outside hire can indicate that the board wants a different direction.

A final signal comes from the engineering bench. Senior engineers and technical leads sometimes follow a departing CTO, either to a new venture or to the same new employer. Later announcements and professional networking profiles can show whether people who reported to the CTO also left. That pattern helps show whether the exit stayed contained or reached deeper into the technical organization.

A CTO who leaves partway through a large AI build-out or cloud migration raises a specific question for investors: whether the program stays on schedule and on budget. The issue is less the departure itself than who now owns a multi-year project the company may already have described to shareholders.

Large technology programs often depend on the person who designed them. A cloud migration moves applications and data from company-run data centers to providers such as Amazon $AMZN Web Services, Microsoft $MSFT Azure or Google $GOOGL Cloud. The work frequently involves rewriting older applications, not just copying them over. The executive who chose the architecture and the order of the work often holds knowledge that is not fully written down.

Migrations also carry a cost overlap. Until legacy systems are switched off, a company typically pays to run old and new infrastructure at the same time. A delay stretches that overlap and pushes expected savings further out. Many companies also sign multi-year committed-spend agreements with cloud providers. Those contracts fix part of the cost whether or not the migration moves at the planned pace.

AI programs add a different set of exposures. Building or deploying AI models can require large purchases of specialized chips, data-center capacity and data infrastructure. Those outlays often show up in a company's capital expenditure guidance. When the executive steering that spending leaves, investors look at whether the company reaffirms or revises that guidance.

The first earnings call after the exit is usually the most direct place to look. Management may restate milestones for the program, name who now leads it or say nothing about timing. A reaffirmed timeline with a named owner reads differently from general language about continued investment.

Organizational structure shapes the reading as well. Some companies place AI work under a separate chief data officer or chief AI officer. Others run migrations through a dedicated program office. In those cases, the CTO's exit may touch the program less directly. Where the CTO personally led the effort, the continuity of the engineering leaders one level down becomes the main question.

The company's annual 10-K offers another reference point. Its risk factors section, Item 1A, often describes dependence on key personnel and the risks of major technology transitions. Comparing that language before and after the departure can show whether the company now treats the program as a larger risk.

A resignation announced alongside a named successor and a transition period usually points to a planned handover. An exit that takes effect immediately, with an interim appointee filling the seat, tells investors less about intent and leaves more open questions.

The difference lies in how the announcement is built, not in the job title. A planned succession tends to arrive as a single package. It names the departing executive, the replacement, the date the change takes effect and how long the outgoing officer will stay on to help. That structure suggests the board had time to prepare.

A transition period has practical value. An outgoing CFO can stay through a quarterly close. A departing COO can introduce a successor to suppliers and plant managers. A CTO can hand over an engineering roadmap before leaving. Each of those steps lowers the chance that working knowledge leaves the company on the executive's last day.

An effective-immediately announcement reads differently. The executive is gone on the day the news breaks, or close to it. The company often names an interim officer, sometimes someone already inside the business. That might be a controller, a deputy or the CEO taking on extra duties. An interim title signals that the board has not yet named a permanent choice.

That uncertainty is not the same as bad news. A sudden departure can follow a health issue, a family matter or an outside offer with a short deadline. The announcement alone rarely says which. What it does show is that the company did not have, or did not use, the lead time to arrange a smoother handoff.

After a sudden exit, the more useful signals tend to arrive over the following weeks and months. They include whether the company opens an external search and whether the interim appointee later drops the interim label. Later filings or earnings calls may also add detail about the change. A planned succession leaves fewer open questions to track. A sudden one shifts the weight onto what the company says next.

The Form 8-K is the first official record of a U.S. public company's executive departure. Its Item 5.02 section covers the timing, the stated reason, any disagreement language and the replacement. Read closely, it tells investors more than the press release headline.

Item 5.02 covers the departure of a company's principal executive officer, president, principal financial officer, principal accounting officer or principal operating officer. It also covers any named executive officer. A company generally has four business days to file after the triggering event. That deadline makes the filing date itself a data point. A filing that follows the news within the window is routine. A filing that arrives alongside other disclosures deserves a closer look at what else changed at the same time.

Not every senior exit produces an 8-K. When a departing executive does not hold one of the listed roles and is not a named executive officer, Item 5.02 does not require a filing. The company's most recent proxy statement lists its named executive officers, which shows whether a given departure falls under the rule.

The stated reason is the next layer. Phrases such as "to pursue other opportunities" or "for personal reasons" are standard language. They do not explain the cause on their own. They do not rule one out either. Specific details add meaning: a named new employer, a set retirement date or a defined advisory role through a transition period.

Many Item 5.02 filings also say whether the departure resulted from a disagreement with the company. A sentence stating there was no disagreement on matters relating to operations, policies or practices is common. Its absence does not prove a dispute, but it leaves the question open.

The replacement section completes the picture. If the company has named a successor or an interim appointee, it must disclose that person. A permanent appointment typically comes with the new officer's background and compensation arrangements. An interim title indicates that a search for a permanent hire may still be under way.

The exhibits can add one more layer. A separation agreement or press release attached to the 8-K may spell out severance, consulting arrangements or the departing executive's continued role during the handover.

#5470. Zillow CEO’s reality check on AI agents: ‘Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot’

by Todd Bishop on Nov 4, 2026 at 5:41 pmNovember 4, 2026 at 5:54 pm

People will let AI agents cancel subscriptions and book appointments, but most won’t want one to do their house hunting, predicts Zillow Group CEO Jeremy Wacksman.

Wacksman made the case Wednesday afternoon in prepared remarks on Zillow’s quarterly earnings call, addressing a big issue for the online real estate company: whether AI agents will shop on people’s behalf, bypassing sites such as Zillow.

“No one wants an AI agent to watch a movie or play a game for them, because the enjoyment is the point,” he said. “Dreaming and searching for a home is similar. It’s the fun part of the moving process that people want to do.”

Few decisions are as high-stakes as choosing a home, he said. “Finding a home isn’t a chore to hand off to a robot; it’s a milestone people want to live themselves.”

It’s a key issue for Zillow, which makes most of its money from the home-buying process, including fees from partner real estate agents and its mortgage lending business.

That depends on people browsing Zillow’s listings and connecting with those (human) agents and loan officers. An AI agent that does the searching could change those dynamics and potentially cut Zillow out of the process.

The issue has become more pressing with the rise of personal AI agents such as Meta’s Muse, which launched in September and can book travel and make purchases on people’s behalf, among other everyday tasks.

Amazon blocked Muse from shopping on its site less than two weeks after launch, saying it never agreed to let Muse shop there and that the agent doesn’t identify itself. Amazon is also suing Perplexity over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. A federal appeals court in August overturned an injunction Amazon had won in that case.

So far, Wacksman said, Zillow isn’t seeing meaningful traffic from AI platforms. The company has integrated with OpenAI and Google’s Gemini, and is now working with Anthropic. About 80% of its traffic comes directly to Zillow.

For the third quarter, Zillow’s revenue rose 7% to $724 million, short of its own forecast of $745 million to $760 million, as a sharp rise in mortgage rates slowed home sales.

The company posted a $158 million net loss for the quarter, mostly from agreeing to settle a shareholder lawsuit over Zillow Offers, its defunct home-flipping business.

#5469. Stock futures fall as Huang’s exit sends Nvidia reeling and oil prices rise

Samuel Boivin / NurPhoto via Getty Images

Nvidia $NVDA stock fell more than 10% after the company announced that CEO Jensen Huang resigned, weighing on U.S. stock futures on Thursday.

Nasdaq $NDAQ-100 futures were down 1.2%, S&P 500 futures slid 0.6%, and Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gave up 47 points, a 0.1% decline. Oil prices rose after President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social, "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed."

Shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom $AVGO rose about 2%. Other stocks tied to artificial intelligence fell with Nvidia. Oracle $ORCL stock lost 4%, and Nebius stock dropped 20% in premarket trading after the company issued third-quarter results and guidance.

West Texas Intermediate futures climbed over 1%, topping $87 a barrel. Brent crude futures added over 1% and moved past $94. Shares of Chevron $CVX and ExxonMobil $XOM rose about 1%, and Eli Lilly $LLY stock gained more than 1%.

Asian indexes fell as losses hit semiconductor makers and other artificial intelligence names. European stocks rose.

#5468. Amazon teams up with Uber on restaurant delivery, years after shutting down its own service

Amazon is bringing Uber Eats inside its own app, letting U.S. Prime members order restaurant delivery without a separate Uber account and skip the delivery fee on orders of $25 or more.

The deal replaces a Prime perk with Grubhub, which Amazon made an ongoing benefit in 2024 after a one-year trial. Amazon said in a statement to GeekWire that it has ended that agreement after identifying “an opportunity to deliver an even better restaurant delivery experience.”

The new Prime benefit covers hundreds of thousands of restaurants in nearly 10,000 U.S. cities and towns, from major metros to rural communities. Orders are placed with existing Amazon logins and payment methods, on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app.

Amazon says Prime members could save more than $175 a year through the delivery fee waiver and Prime-only promotions, which it notes is more than the $139 annual cost of Prime. Service fees still apply, the company confirmed. New users get $20 off their first two orders of $25 or more within 14 days, and Prime Visa cardholders earn 5% back on Uber Eats orders through Dec. 5.

Members who already pay for Uber One, which includes $0 delivery fees, keep those benefits. But Amazon said the two memberships operate independently, and the Prime perk applies only to Uber Eats orders placed through Amazon.

The deal marks Amazon’s latest approach to restaurant delivery. The company shut down its own Amazon Restaurants service in 2019, four years after launching it in Seattle and expanding to more than 20 U.S. cities. Uber had listed Amazon as an Uber Eats competitor in its IPO filing earlier that year.

The service let Prime members order meals through its website or the Prime Now app. Amazon cut jobs on the team in early 2018, closed the London service later that year, and also shut down Daily Dish, a workplace lunch delivery service it launched in 2016.

The Uber deal is part of Amazon’s broader push to add value to Prime. In February, the company made its Alexa+ AI assistant free for U.S. Prime members. Last year it ended a program that let members share free shipping with someone outside their household.

“We’re excited to connect our restaurant community with new Prime fans, while giving Prime members a seamless way to enjoy great food from restaurants through Uber Eats,” Andrew Macdonald, Uber’s president and COO, said in a statement.

Members can share the Uber Eats benefit with one adult in their household through Amazon Family.

#5466. Longtime investor Martin Tobias says no to 99% of startups — his new AI tool helps them find a yes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:01 amNovember 5, 2026 at 7:01 am

Martin Tobias was pitched by about 4,500 startups last year. He wrote 10 checks.

Now the pre-seed investor is offering the rest of them a consolation prize: an AI tool that tells founders which investors are most likely to say yes.

Tobias, a longtime figure in the Seattle tech scene, is now based in Spokane, Wash. He founded Loudeye, a digital media company that went public during the dot-com boom and later sold to Nokia, and went on to lead biofuel maker Imperium Renewables and group-buying startup Tippr.

He was a venture partner at Ignition Partners, an early backer of DocuSign, before starting Incisive Ventures in 2020. The firm closed a $10.5 million fund last year to back early-stage B2B software companies.

Investor Match started as an internal tool to help Incisive’s portfolio companies find seed and Series A investors. Tobias said he has 17,000 contacts but can only keep about 150 of them in his head, a limit known as Dunbar’s number.

To use the tool, founders upload a pitch deck, and Investor Match returns 20 investors ranked by fit, based on stage, check size, geography and what each firm has actually backed. It also drafts outreach emails, but it doesn’t send them.

Most founders send those emails cold, or pass the list to their existing investors and ask for warm introductions, Tobias said. Investors who have accounts on the platform can also respond to founders directly.

A free preview shows all 20 matches with fit scores, with the top three fully expanded. The full list costs $20, which Tobias said roughly covers the API costs of running it, about $1,000 a month.

Every founder Tobias turns down now gets pointed to the tool.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there,” he told GeekWire.

Incisive appears on the platform like any other investor. Some founders who were matched with the firm asked whether Tobias had tilted the algorithm toward himself. He said he hadn’t, and that he only wants pitches that actually fit.

“Just because I wasn’t the right investor for that company doesn’t mean that the right investor wasn’t out there.”

Other companies offer investor matching as part of broader fundraising platforms, including Metal and OpenVC, which Tobias said charge founders monthly subscriptions. He said OpenVC relies on simple keyword matching, while Investor Match uses AI to read each investor’s website, portfolio and blog posts, which takes “millions and millions of tokens.”

Some of those companies are trying to build venture-scale businesses off founders’ fundraising, Tobias said.

“I think that’s just f—ing evil,” he said. “I don’t think you should try to make money off people who quit their job and are putting everything into trying to raise their first one to $2 million.”

Founders have told Tobias they’ve raised more than $100 million from investors they found through the platform since it launched about six months ago, though he acknowledged he can’t verify that because the money doesn’t flow through Investor Match.

Investor Match is also an extension of his investing thesis. He said his fund looks for B2B software companies like DocuSign that “reduce friction at scale” by taking a business process and doing it better in software.

“That’s exactly what Investor Match is,” he said. “What’s the friction in the market that you’re dealing with? Investors finding founders, founders finding investors. OK, can software help with that? I think it can.”

#5465. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5464. Google and Samsung are opening preorders for AI smart glasses starting at $395

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Warby Parker and Gentle Monster models with Gemini built in are set to go on sale Dec. 10, with Gentle Monster frames at $449 and up

Alphabet $GOOGL's Google and Samsung Electronics opened preorders on Thursday for smart glasses with the Gemini AI assistant, with Warby Parker models starting at $395.

Samsung set a Dec. 10 release in the U.S. and South Korea. Warby Parker glasses start at $395 in the U.S., and Gentle Monster glasses range from $449 to $489, depending on the model. Both collections will launch in the U.S., and the Gentle Monster collection will also launch in South Korea.

The lineup has 30 designs across six Gentle Monster frame styles and three Warby Parker styles, Samsung said. Samsung engineered the hardware, and Google developed the product with it.

The glasses weigh around 41 grams (about 1.4 ounces) and have a battery rated for up to nine hours, Google said. The charging case can recharge the frames up to seven times. The glasses have a 12-megapixel camera and open-ear speakers, and they work with Pixel phones, Samsung phones and iPhones.

Users can say “Hey Gemini” or tap the frames to get help. Google said Gemini can add items to a grocery list, check a user’s Google Calendar when they look at an event poster, and handle calls and messages hands-free. Google Maps provides turn-by-turn directions, and Google Translate offers real-time speech translation in more than 70 languages.

Google said camera visuals from Gemini never go into Gemini History, and they are also kept out of AI model training and ad targeting. The glasses are designed to redact bystanders' faces before Gemini processes images. An indicator light turns on whenever the user captures a picture or clip, and the glasses are built to halt recording should anyone block or disable that light. Samsung said the glasses are designed for users aged 18 and over, with age verification required for activation.

Preorders are live online and in stores at Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, Google said. Customers can sign up for a guided demo at more than 360 Warby Parker locations, and hands-on demos will be available at select Google Store locations.

Google will not sell the glasses directly at launch, according to Bloomberg. The glasses run Google's Android XR operating system, and Meta $META Platforms leads the smart-glasses category.

"As glasses become more capable, our focus is on creating helpful experiences that make both wearers and bystanders feel protected," Shahram Izadi, Google's vice president and general manager of its XR unit, wrote in a separate post on Thursday, according to Bloomberg.

#5463. Uncommon Thinkers: Curiosity led Mary Brunkow to an immune breakthrough — and a Nobel Prize

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 5, 2026 at 7:54 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:03 am

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Mary Brunkow had considered becoming a veterinarian or doctor — she knew she wanted to do good in the world and help people. Then, as an undergraduate at the University of Washington, she stepped into a research lab for the first time.

Inside, a professor she admired and his team were using fruit flies to study genetics.

“You walked in this door and it was like entering this new world,” Brunkow said, recalling the collaborative, passionate environment. “I just loved it. There was the smell of ether in the air. There was this real love of the science.”

After graduating and going on to earn a doctorate, Brunkow built a career in research. She joined Seattle-area startup Darwin Molecular and oversaw a team studying mutant mice afflicted by severe autoimmune disease. The scientists painstakingly identified the responsible gene, which led to valuable insights into the immune system’s T cells.

Brunkow worked on other projects at Darwin, too. But after an acquisition and a merger, the company’s local R&D operation shut down. Brunkow moved on. She ultimately landed at the Institute for Systems Biology (ISB), her immune-system research well in the past.

Then, in October 2025, came an unexpected call: She would share the Nobel Prize in Medicine with former Darwin colleague Fred Ramsdell and Osaka University’s Shimon Sakaguchi for discoveries explaining how the immune system avoids attacking the body’s own tissues.

Now a distinguished investigator at ISB, Brunkow was stunned by the honor. But Jim Heath, president of the institute, sees it as well deserved.

“Mary brings an exceptional combination of scientific rigor, intellectual curiosity, and humility to her work,” he said. “She’s driven by fundamental questions about biology and isn’t afraid to challenge conventional thinking in pursuit of answers.”

Beyond her scientific prowess, Heath also praised Brunkow’s efforts to create a workplace as welcoming and vibrant as the one that captivated her as a college undergrad.

“She’s a generous colleague who values collaboration and helps create an environment where other scientists can do their best work. She’s deeply committed to creating opportunities for students who will become tomorrow’s scientists,” Heath said. “Those qualities are every bit as important as the discoveries themselves.”

When Brunkow joined Darwin in 1994, the biotech — whose backers included Microsoft co-founders Bill Gates and Paul Allen — was riding a wave of advances from the Human Genome Project, an effort to sequence humanity’s DNA playbook. Darwin scientists sought genes linked to disease that might point the way toward new treatments.

“It wasn’t a one-drug company. It wasn’t hyper-focused on something very specific. It was trying to figure out how we can affect change in patients,” Ramsdell said at Life Science Washington’s annual conference in April.

One project focused on “scurfy” mice, which carried an inherited mutation that caused devastating autoimmune disease. Researchers suspected the mutation disrupted a crucial regulator of the immune system. Darwin wasn’t set up for mouse research, so Brunkow commandeered a janitor’s closet and began carefully breeding the mice to narrow down the area containing the mutant gene.

The work was far more laborious and slow compared to today’s technology, but it was groundbreaking for that period. It delighted Brunkow.

“It was a really exciting time,” Brunkow said. “It took a lot of problem solving and troubleshooting to get to the answer.”

The scientists narrowed their search to 20 genes on the X chromosome and began painstakingly sequencing them. In the final gene, they found a tiny error — two extra DNA letters inserted into the sequence that rendered the protein useless.

Working with Ramsdell and other collaborators, the researchers identified the mouse gene and showed that mutations in its human counterpart, FOXP3, cause a rare autoimmune disorder called IPEX.

“It was nice to pull the story together. So we published a couple of nice papers. We filed patent inventions. We went to conferences and talked about it,” Brunkow said. “And then in 2004, the company closed down.”

Brunkow stayed friends with Ramsdell and followed developments in the field, but her own interests took her elsewhere. She was drawn less to one particular disease than to the challenge of finding a tiny genetic change that could have an enormous biological effect — and potentially point toward a treatment.

Meanwhile, other researchers were building on the discoveries.

Later research established the gene’s essential role in regulatory T cells, or Tregs — cells that restrain immune responses and protect the body from attacking itself.

“I didn’t actually understand the extent to which our publications kind of blew open a whole new area in immunology,” Brunkow said.

That work is now reaching patients. In June, the FDA approved Tregzi, a treatment incorporating regulatory T cells that helps prevent a serious complication of donor stem cell transplants in adults with blood cancers.

At ISB, Brunkow has embraced a broader view of biology. The organization takes a holistic approach to medical research, bringing together scientists in areas including cancer, infectious diseases and chronic illnesses.

For her, it is a natural progression from studying individual genes to investigating the complex networks in which they operate. The ultimate goal is personalized medicine: understanding what pushes someone from health toward disease, detecting those changes early and finding ways to intervene.

The Nobel recognition has given Brunkow a chance to broaden her impact beyond research — a platform to advocate for issues she cares about. That includes sustained research funding, support for women and other underrepresented groups in science, and stronger STEM education. She also wants to encourage scientists to support one another and work well together — the qualities she encountered in that UW fruit fly lab.

“You’ve got to figure out how to play well with others,” Brunkow said. “It makes science more fun. It makes science move faster.”

#5461. No sweat: High-tech T-shirt brand Neat survives ‘Shark Tank’ and lands $400K deal with Lori Greiner

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:45 amNovember 5, 2026 at 9:45 am

If Jim Huffman and Tyler Stelter were sweating during their pitch on ABC’s “Shark Tank,” their T-shirts didn’t show it. It probably helped them land a deal.

Huffman is CEO and Stelter is COO of Seattle-based Neat, which makes shirts designed to hide sweat. They survived a grilling from the Sharks on the popular reality TV series and secured an investment from Lori Greiner on Wednesday night’s episode.

Greiner agreed to invest $400,000 for a 15% stake in the company, plus 75 cents per order until she earns back her investment. Huffman said the deal is still being finalized.

“I love the product. I’m gonna be a huge customer,” Greiner, an inventor and longtime QVC personality, said on the show. “I already have 10,000 ideas of videos we’re gonna do.”

“It felt like a business knife fight,” Huffman told GeekWire on Thursday. The most intense part, he said, was negotiating with several Sharks at once while doing revenue-share math in his head.

Neat sells T-shirts and other tops lined with a patented “Sweat Maze,” a pattern of water-repelling and water-attracting zones that pulls moisture inward and spreads it across the inside of the shirt so it dries before it shows through.

The technology came out of research funded by the National Science Foundation and was originally developed for military personnel, firefighters and first responders.

“Shark Tank,” now in its 18th season on ABC, features entrepreneurs pitching their businesses to a panel of wealthy investors, known as Sharks, in hopes of landing an investment in exchange for a stake in their company. The show is based on “Dragons’ Den,” a Japanese format, and has won five Emmy Awards.

Joining Greiner on Neat’s panel were Kendra Scott, founder of the jewelry brand that bears her name; Kind snack bar founder Daniel Lubetzky; investor Kevin O’Leary; and Rashaun Williams, a venture capitalist and chief investment officer of Harbinger Sports Partners.

Huffman applied for the show on a whim, filling out an online form late one night. About 10,000 companies apply each season and roughly 70 make it on air, he said producers told him.

Huffman and Stelter filmed their pitch in June at Tyler Perry Studios in Atlanta. Taping there in the summer made it “the ultimate test” for the shirt, said Huffman, who added that he runs hot when presenting, even without studio lights.

Huffman and Stelter came into the tank asking for $400,000 for 5% of Neat, valuing the company at $8 million. O’Leary was so put off by the valuation that he said a lightning bolt should “come through the ceiling and fry you both.” He then dropped out.

O’Leary and Williams saw Neat as a niche product, Huffman said. But Scott and Lubetzky both made offers, and Lubetzky’s interest caught the Neat team off guard. “We weren’t ready for that!” Huffman said.

When O’Leary argued that the shirts only appealed to men, Scott countered that women sweat, too. “Have you heard of a hot flash, darling? Because it’s a real thing,” she said.

Scott offered $400,000 for 20%, saying the product “has got licensing power, but your valuation is nuts.” Lubetzky offered the same amount for 25% before pulling out. Greiner then came in at 15% plus the per-order royalty, and the Neat team took her deal.

“We’ve never built an eight- or nine-figure brand, and Lori has, so bringing in someone with that experience and knowledge is extremely exciting,” Huffman said.

Huffman and Stelter began working on the brand in 2024. Huffman also runs GrowthHit, a Seattle-based growth marketing agency he founded in 2016.

Huffman came across Neat through a GrowthHit client, a sports performance brand whose team had developed the technology. Having grown up in Oklahoma and lived in Texas and New York, Huffman said he knew the pain of hot days when you can “never wear heather gray.” When the client sent him a shirt, his reaction was, “Oh my gosh, this is amazing!”

GrowthHit had been looking for a brand of its own after earlier attempts to launch products didn’t pan out, Huffman said. The agency took over Neat, with the original team continuing to handle product development while GrowthHit ran branding and marketing.

Neat’s net sales grew more than 300% in 2025, to about $700,000, and the company is on track for $1.5 million to $2 million in sales this year, Huffman said.

Huffman credits the growth to basic growth-marketing moves. Neat positioned itself as something other than a regular cotton tee, pushed bundles over single shirts, upgraded its product photos and raised prices.

Neat’s newest shirt, the Sweat Defender Crew, sells for $59.99, with discounts for bundles. Huffman told the Sharks that each shirt costs about $11.70 to make.

The company scaled through Instagram and Facebook ads, going from about $20 a day in ad spend to roughly $2,000 a day.

Its best-known ad pops a water balloon inside a shirt to show the outside staying dry. “We need to be able to demonstrate the product in five seconds, or you’re toast,” Huffman said.

Neat is profitable and hasn’t raised venture funding, Huffman said. He said the company is on track for a 15% profit margin this year.

The company has four employees, two in Seattle and two in Portland. Its shirts are made in Vietnam and sold directly to consumers. They’re not on Amazon or in stores yet, but Huffman said “Shark Tank” could open new sales channels.

Traffic to Neat’s site jumped about 20-fold from the East Coast and Central time zones as soon as the segment aired, Huffman said. The company did more sales during the nine-minute segment than it does on a strong holiday, with a second wave when the show aired on the West Coast.

The most popular color since the show aired is the sage green Huffman and Stelter wore in the tank, which is also the color Neat has the least of in stock.

“Our main priorities right now are making sure the site doesn’t crash and that customer service can keep up,” Huffman said.

#5460. How 4 finance executives rose, and how many S&P 500 CFOs became CEOs

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The CFO to CEO path, traced through careers at Oracle, TikTok, Hertz and Deutsche Bank, plus data on how many S&P 500 CFOs who switched jobs became CEOs

Russell Reynolds Associates found that 33% of S&P 500 chief financial officers who changed jobs in 2022 moved into chief executive roles. In 2021, that share was 8.8%. Those two figures frame this slideshow: the move from CFO to CEO, and the executives whose careers run alongside it.

The finance job itself has widened. The role has moved well beyond number crunching. Today's CFO analyzes data to spot trends, weighs risks and plans for growth. Finance chiefs also often drive digital transformation, the effort to rebuild how a company runs around newer technology.

The careers in this selection trace that move in different ways. Safra Catz has been an Oracle $ORCL executive since April 1999. She served as co-president and CFO starting in 2011 and later became the company's sole CEO. Shou Zi Chew was CFO at Xiaomi and then at ByteDance before taking over as TikTok's chief executive. Stephen M. Scheer started at Goldman Sachs $GS in 1993, held a CFO role from 2018 and became CEO of Hertz in February 2022.

Not every path here ends in the top job. James von Moltke became Deutsche Bank's CFO in 2017. He has also served as the bank's president since March 2022 while keeping the finance role. At TikTok, the stretch between Kevin Mayer's exit after a few months as CEO and Chew's appointment was covered by Vanessa Pappas. She was the company's General Manager, not its CFO, and served as interim global head.

The slides that follow trace these careers one at a time. They then step back to the wider pattern. That includes the share of S&P 500 finance chiefs moving into chief executive roles and the analytical and technology work that now sits with the CFO. It also covers the banking backgrounds several of these executives share. Goldman Sachs appears in the early careers of both Chew and Scheer. Von Moltke started at Credit Suisse First Boston in London in 1992 and spent eight years at Citigroup $C. Catz's route ran instead through a long tenure inside Oracle.

Safra Catz reached the top of Oracle $ORCL by moving up through the company's own ranks. She joined as an executive in April 1999 and later served as co-president and chief financial officer. She then shared the chief executive role with Mark Hurd before becoming Oracle's sole CEO.

Her climb took place inside a single company. Catz was not an outside hire brought in to run Oracle.

A board seat came early. Oracle added Catz to its board of directors in 2001, about two years after she started as an executive there. She had a place in the company's governance before she held the president title.

In 2004, she was named president. Her board appointment had come three years earlier.

The finance role followed in 2011, when Catz became co-president and CFO. In that position, she reported to Larry Ellison, Oracle's cofounder. The post put her in charge of the company's finances while she kept a share of the president's title.

The order of those appointments sets her career apart from a straight finance track. Seven years separated her appointment as president from her move into the finance job. She did not rise through finance first and then move into general management. The CFO post came after she had already reached a senior leadership title.

The route to chief executive opened when Ellison stepped down as CEO. Catz did not take the post alone at first. She became co-CEO alongside Mark Hurd, and the two split the top job.

She later became Oracle's sole CEO. That ended the period in which the top job was divided between two executives.

Her profile extends beyond Oracle. Fortune has listed her among the most powerful women in business. She has also sat on Disney $DIS's board since 2018. That seat gives her a governance role at a second large U.S. company.

Shou Zi Chew became TikTok's CEO after serving as chief financial officer at two technology companies, Xiaomi and ByteDance. He took over the role after Kevin Mayer quit as TikTok's chief executive.

Chew began his career in banking. He spent two years as a banker at Goldman Sachs $GS in London.

He then moved to the investing side. Chew worked at venture firms, including DST Global.

During that stretch he led investments in JD.com and Xiaomi. Those deals put him on the investor side of both companies before he held a job inside either one.

One of those investments became his next employer. Chew was named Xiaomi's CFO in 2015. The appointment moved him from backing the smartphone maker to running its finances.

His second finance chief role came at ByteDance, TikTok's parent company. Chew became ByteDance's CFO in March 2021.

That post placed him inside the company that owns TikTok. When he later became TikTok's chief executive, he moved from the parent company's finance office to the head of its subsidiary.

The opening came when Mayer left the CEO post after a few months in the role. Vanessa Pappas, TikTok's General Manager, served as interim global head until Chew took over.

Each stage of Chew's career connects to the one before it. A banking start led to venture investing. An investment in Xiaomi led to a finance job there. A finance job at ByteDance led to the top job at TikTok.

He held the CFO title at two different companies before he ran one.

Vanessa Pappas, TikTok's General Manager, served as the company's interim global head after Kevin Mayer quit as CEO. She held that position until Shou Zi Chew took over the top job. She is the only interim leader among the executives profiled here.

Mayer's stint as chief executive was brief. He left after only a few months. Pappas then led the company during the gap before a permanent CEO was named.

An interim chief's job is to keep the company running through a leadership transition. At TikTok, that role went to an executive who already worked at the company.

Pappas did not come to the job through finance. Her title at TikTok was General Manager, not chief financial officer. Every other executive profiled in this selection held a CFO title at some point. That makes her the exception in a list built around finance leaders. Her case shows that a temporary top post does not have to go to the finance chief.

Pappas is Australian. She graduated from the University of Queensland in Brisbane. Before joining TikTok, she worked at Next New Networks and at YouTube. Both companies are online video businesses. That background sits in the same field as TikTok, an app built around short videos.

She also commented on the app's commercial direction. In an interview with CNBC, Pappas said she saw ways Walmart $WMT could work together with the e-commerce features newly added to the TikTok app. Walmart is a U.S. retail chain.

The permanent job went to Chew, whose career had run through finance roles. His appointment ended the interim period that Pappas had overseen.

The TikTok handover ran from Mayer to Pappas to Chew. The temporary leader in that sequence came from outside the finance function. The finance executive arrived afterward and took the CEO title.

Stephen M. Scheer became CEO of Hertz in February 2022 after a career spent in finance. He also holds a seat on the Hertz board. That places him on the company's governing body as well as at the head of its management.

His career started in 1993 in the Financial Institutions Group at Goldman Sachs $GS. At an investment bank, a financial institutions group advises banks, insurers, asset managers and other financial companies on mergers, acquisitions and capital raising. That work centers on the balance sheets and regulation of lenders and other financial firms.

Scheer moved into a chief financial officer role in 2018. He held that post in 2019, the year Goldman Sachs and Apple $AAPL launched Apple Card. The card took a Wall Street bank into consumer credit cards in partnership with a consumer technology company.

The Hertz appointment put a longtime finance executive in charge of a car rental company. A rental business of that kind buys large numbers of vehicles, finances them, rents them out and later sells them. Fleet funding and used-car values sit close to the core of its economics.

Outside Hertz, Scheer sits on the boards of the Jewish Museum and the New York Stem Cell Foundation. The Jewish Museum is an art and culture museum on Fifth Avenue in Manhattan. The New York Stem Cell Foundation is a nonprofit that funds and conducts stem cell research.

He is also a member of the Business Roundtable, the Council on Foreign Relations and the U.S. Travel and Tourism Advisory Board. The Business Roundtable is an association of chief executives of major U.S. companies. The Council on Foreign Relations is a New York-based membership organization and think tank focused on foreign policy. The travel advisory board counsels the U.S. secretary of commerce on policy affecting travel and tourism. That industry is the market Hertz serves.

James von Moltke has been Deutsche Bank's chief financial officer since 2017, and since March 2022 he has also served as the bank's president. He kept the finance job when he took the second title. He now holds both posts at once.

That sets his case apart from the others in this selection. Von Moltke is not Deutsche Bank's CEO. His career shows a finance chief whose remit widened inside one company. It does not show a move from the CFO seat into the chief executive's chair.

His banking career spans more than 30 years. It began in 1992 at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. He later spent eight years at Citigroup $C. He became Deutsche Bank's finance chief in 2017. That put 25 years of banking between his first job and his arrival in the bank's CFO role. Deutsche Bank is the third bank named in that record.

The president title came about five years into his tenure as CFO. A Deutsche Bank release describing changes to the responsibilities of its management board stated that von Moltke was to remain chief financial officer.

His responsibilities grew again in 2023. Since that year he has overseen Asset Management. That adds a business division to a portfolio that already combined the CFO and president roles.

Read in sequence, the changes follow one line. Von Moltke became CFO in 2017, added the president's title in March 2022 and took on Asset Management in 2023. Each change happened at the same bank. None of them involved the chief executive's job.

His titles are president and CFO. That places him outside the CFO to CEO path followed by Safra Catz at Oracle $ORCL, Shou Zi Chew at TikTok and Stephen M. Scheer at Hertz. Catz, Chew and Scheer each reached the chief executive's office. Von Moltke widened his remit without leaving the finance post.

In 2022, 33% of S&P 500 chief financial officers who changed jobs became chief executives, according to Russell Reynolds Associates. In 2021, the share was 8.8%.

That is a rise of 24.2 percentage points in one year. The 2022 share was about 3.75 times the 2021 level.

Put in plainer terms, roughly one in three job-changing finance chiefs landed the top post in 2022. A year earlier, fewer than one in 10 did.

The figure covers a defined group. It counts S&P 500 CFOs who moved to a new position during the year, not every finance chief in the index. A CFO who stayed in the same role through 2022 is outside the calculation.

Both numbers are shares, not head counts. The data does not state how many CFOs changed jobs in either year. A percentage can rise because more finance chiefs became CEOs, because fewer changed jobs overall, or both. The figures alone cannot separate those effects.

The measure records one step in a career. It shows whether a departing finance chief's next job was the top executive post. The two percentages do not say whether those CEO roles were permanent or interim. They also say nothing about how the new chief executives performed after taking over.

This limits what the figures can support about stand-in leaders. The data cannot show how often a company names its own CFO as an interim CEO. It also does not record whether a new CEO post came at the same company or at a different one. Safra Catz followed the same-company route at Oracle $ORCL, where she was CFO before becoming CEO.

The data spans two years, 2021 and 2022. It describes a one-year jump among job-changing CFOs at the large U.S. public companies in the S&P 500, not a longer trend. The figures carry no breakdown by sector and no stated cause for the jump.

The modern CFO's job reaches beyond bookkeeping. Rydoo describes finance chiefs who study company data to find trends, assess risks and map out growth, not only produce the numbers.

Number crunching remains part of the work. In Rydoo's account, it is no longer the whole of it.

Each of the three tasks Rydoo names covers a different part of the job. Spotting trends means reading data for patterns that matter to the business. Weighing risk means judging what could go wrong and how much exposure a company can carry. Planning growth means deciding where the business should put its money and effort next.

Rydoo sets out this wider scope in its CFO Corner piece on finance leaders who moved into chief executive roles.

Finance chiefs often drive digital transformation inside their companies, according to Rydoo's CFO Corner. The publication lists that work among the responsibilities that now sit with the CFO.

Rydoo presents digital transformation as one sign of how far the finance job has broadened.

The publication makes the point in its coverage of finance leaders who went on to become chief executives.

Shou Zi Chew, Stephen M. Scheer and James von Moltke all began their careers at large investment banks before reaching finance leadership. Chew and Scheer started at Goldman Sachs $GS. Von Moltke started at Credit Suisse First Boston.

Scheer's first job, in 1993, was in the Financial Institutions Group at Goldman Sachs. Von Moltke began a year earlier, in 1992, at Credit Suisse First Boston in London. He went on to spend eight years at Citigroup $C. In total, he has more than 30 years in banking.

The two reached the finance chief's office on nearly matching timelines. Von Moltke became Deutsche Bank's CFO in 2017. Scheer held a CFO post from 2018. In both cases, 25 years separated the first banking job from the CFO title.

Chew's banking stint was much shorter. He spent two years as a Goldman Sachs banker in London. He then moved into venture investing at firms including DST Global. There he led investments in JD.com and Xiaomi. In 2015 he became CFO of Xiaomi, a company he had backed as an investor. His route to finance leadership ran through deal-making rather than a long run inside a bank.

The banking start did not lead to a single outcome. Chew moved on to the CFO post at ByteDance in March 2021. He later took over as TikTok's CEO after Kevin Mayer quit. Scheer became CEO of Hertz in February 2022. Von Moltke has stayed in finance at Deutsche Bank. He added the president's title in March 2022 and oversight of Asset Management in 2023 while keeping the CFO role. He does not hold the CEO post.

Catz's route is measured in years at one company. She has been an Oracle $ORCL executive since April 1999. She became co-president and CFO in 2011, 12 years later. After Larry Ellison stepped down as CEO, she shared the top job with Mark Hurd. She later held it alone.

Across these four careers, two routes to the CFO office appear. One starts at a bank and then moves through other firms. The other runs through long tenure inside a single company, with the finance role serving as one step toward the chief executive's office.

#5459. Tencent's founder is willing to move half its workforce into AI-native businesses

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Tencent's public relations director said the 50% figure is an example of organizational change, not a layoff target

Tencent founder Pony Ma told employees he is willing to redeploy half of the company's personnel to AI-native businesses, according to Bloomberg.

Ma spoke at Tencent's 28th anniversary meeting on Wednesday, according to TokenPost. He described the company's main operations as an army, with its new AI work playing the part of a navy. "The army must leverage AI to maximize its efficiency, while we redeploy 50% of our personnel to the navy to support AI-native businesses," he said, according to Bloomberg.

Bloomberg said the speech seemed aimed at getting the entire workforce to adopt AI instead of announcing a major restructuring. Ma said one portion of Tencent, comprising half the company, would work on making current businesses run more efficiently, and the remaining portion would look for new ways to grow.

Tencent's public relations director said the 50% number was an example of organizational change rather than a goal for job cuts, according to TokenPost. Tencent has not publicly outlined any move to cut half of its staff, TokenPost said. Social media posts in China claimed that the company would cut half of its staff.

Ma also pushed for a less hierarchical setup with fewer layers of middle managers, according to Bloomberg. He said the push is meant to reshape the way teams operate and speed up decisions using the current workforce, setting it apart from previous cost-cutting and efficiency campaigns, according to TokenPost. He asked managers to limit drawn-out discussions with staff when handing out new assignments, TokenPost said.

It is not yet known how Tencent intends to restructure, according to Bloomberg. The company's last companywide reorganization came in 2018. Tencent had 115,927 employees as of June, up from 111,221 a year earlier.

Tencent's AI spending has climbed. Capital expenditures for AI projects and computing rose 176% to 52.8 billion yuan ($7.9 billion) in the quarter ended in June, as the company works to close ground on ByteDance and Alibaba.

Tencent stock has fallen about a third so far this year, which puts the company's valuation near $470 billion. Ma described Tencent as a "leaky ship" at a shareholder gathering in May, according to Bloomberg, after the company's Yuanbao chatbot failed to overtake ByteDance's Doubao and its work on large language models fell behind.

Tencent is scheduled to release its third-quarter results on Nov. 18. A Tencent spokesperson did not respond to Bloomberg's request for comment.
