#5458. Shield AI to buy Bill Gates-backed radar maker Echodyne in $5.3B deal, doubling down on Seattle area

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 5, 2026 at 9:47 amNovember 5, 2026 at 10:41 am

Shield AI, the defense tech company planning to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet south of Seattle, agreed to acquire Kirkland, Wash.-based Echodyne, which makes compact radar systems that detect and track drones, in a transaction valued at up to $5.3 billion.

It’s a major exit for one of the Seattle region’s best-known deep-tech startups. Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona.

Echodyne, ranked No. 9 on the GeekWire 200, has raised about $200 million in total, and PitchBook put its valuation at $485 million after its last priced round in 2022.

The deal is believed to be the second-largest acquisition of a private venture-backed company in Washington state history, behind Okta’s $6.5 billion acquisition of Auth0 in 2021, Madrona’s Tim Porter wrote in a blog post. It’s among the top exits in the history of the Seattle-based venture firm, Porter said, noting that Echodyne is profitable.

To help pay for the acquisition, San Diego-based Shield said it’s raising $2.5 billion, including $1 billion in new funding at a $28.8 billion valuation. That’s more than double the $12.7 billion valuation it reached in March.

What Echodyne does: Echodyne’s radar is built into hundreds of counter-drone and security systems used in more than 40 countries, according to the companies. It’s used in remote weapon stations, high-energy lasers and microwave weapons, and it helps point interceptors at incoming drones.

Stadiums and airports use the same technology to spot drones that aren’t supposed to be there. Shield, best known for its Hivemind autonomy software and V-BAT drone, has served only government end users so far, CEO Gary Steele told Bloomberg.

Steele called Echodyne the company’s first step into hardware with civilian as well as military uses. “Think about public safety — whether it’s the Super Bowl or FIFA, just literally every single thing is going to need protection from drones,” he said.

Impact on jobs: Echodyne has about 400 employees, up from 260 when it opened a $40 million manufacturing facility in Woodinville, Wash., in July. No layoffs are planned, and Echodyne employees won’t be required to relocate, a Shield spokesperson said.

The combined company will have about 2,700 employees. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will remain in that role, reporting directly to Steele, and will stay in charge of its products and manufacturing as well as its relationships with customers and partners.

Madrona invested $5.5 million in Echodyne’s initial $15 million round, at a $24 million pre-money valuation, and Porter joined the board. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders, according to the venture firm.

Echodyne makes all of its radar systems in the Seattle region, and Shield will continue to double down on that growth along with its investment in X-BAT manufacturing, Porter said via email.

“Seattle as a defense tech hub is real,” he said.

Shield said in September that it expects to employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle region by the early 2030s as X-BAT production ramps up at its site in Des Moines, Wash. The company projects the program will support about 8,000 jobs in the region in that time, including at suppliers.

The deal is Shield’s fifth acquisition and its largest. The others were Heron Systems and Martin UAV in 2021, Sentient Vision Systems in 2024 and Aechelon Technology in June.

The acquisition is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approvals. Shield will pay $4.8 billion at closing, with up to $500 million more if Echodyne hits performance targets, and the $2.5 billion financing won’t go through if the deal falls apart, according to the companies.

Dartmouth and Onyx roots: Frankenberg has “a unique knack for getting brilliant people to believe in a vision, even when there’s plenty of skepticism around them,” said Brent Frei, the Smartsheet co-founder, who met Frankenberg as a freshman at Dartmouth and later roomed with him.

“We were a little bit like the Odd Couple; he was the consummate gentleman from North Carolina: well-mannered, organized, focused and very smart,” Frei said. “By contrast, I was the other character.”

Frei founded Onyx Software in 1994 and built it largely with a group of Dartmouth friends, including Frankenberg. Mark Mader, another of the group, later built Smartsheet with Frei, and Rob Eleveld went on to sell Ekata to Mastercard for more than $800 million.

“Our running joke is that we keep building 10-to-12-year overnight successes,” Frei said.

Matt McIlwain, a Madrona managing director who also goes back to Dartmouth with Frankenberg, called the Onyx “family tree” a “great example of how the innovation ecosystem and flywheel gets built over decades in a community like Seattle.”

#5457. Telegram Doesn’t Need to Convert Crypto Users: 1M Wallets in 48 Hours Reveal Its Massive Distribution Advantage

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Telegram is gaining crypto users without having to convince them to download another app. More than 1 million self-custodial wallets appeared on the messaging platform within 48 hours. Founder Pavel Durov says the growth reflects a simple feature: wallets activate automatically when users receive Grams. The milestone shows Telegram’s biggest advantage in crypto: distribution.

Unlike traditional crypto wallets, Telegram’s native wallet operates inside an application millions already use daily. Crypto traders, project founders, airdrop hunters, and blockchain communities have long relied on Telegram. That existing audience gives its wallet a distribution advantage that standalone crypto applications must spend years building.

The latest growth also raises an interesting question about blockchain adoption. Does crypto really need another wave of new users, or does it need easier access for people already participating? Telegram could provide exactly that bridge, provided wallet registrations translate into meaningful economic activity.

Durov reported more than 1million new self-custodial wallets over 48 hours in an X post. The dashboard accompanying his announcement showed more than 1 million registrations across the period.

1M+ self-custodial Gram wallets activated on Telegram in just 48 hours. $GRAM is up 10% in 24h, the #1 gainer in the CMC top 100. pic.twitter.com/VGVTT5AZQk

According to Durov, users do not need to manually create a wallet before receiving crypto. Their wallets activate when someone sends them Grams.

This creates a potentially powerful viral distribution mechanism. One user sends tokens to another, introducing the recipient to an on-chain wallet. The recipient can then hold or transfer assets without leaving Telegram.

This approach removes several familiar barriers to crypto adoption. New users do not necessarily need to understand seed phrases, download separate applications, or navigate an exchange. Telegram already provides the social environment where these transactions can begin.

The platform also has more than one billion monthly users, giving its crypto ambitions an enormous potential audience. Even a small conversion rate could produce substantial wallet growth.

The latest wallet milestone is not the only sign of expanding activity across The Open Network (TON), the blockchain powering Telegram’s wallet. TON averaged 4.06 million daily transactions during October. The network also added approximately 2.73 million wallets throughout the month, its strongest monthly addition since October 2024.

Stablecoin activity offers another indication of growing utility. TON averaged 37,693 daily stablecoin users in October, representing a 23.44% increase from September.

The stablecoin figures are particularly interesting because they point toward activity beyond token speculation. Payments and transfers could give Telegram crypto a more practical role in everyday digital interactions.

TON’s stablecoin supply stood at $585 million today. Its decentralized finance total value locked, however, remained comparatively modest at approximately $44 million.

Payments, stablecoin transfers, digital collectibles, and Telegram’s mini-app ecosystem could provide reasons to return. These services could gradually make blockchain transactions feel like another ordinary messaging feature.

#5456. As AI Gets Cheaper, the Real Business Opportunity Is Shifting. Here’s Where the Value Is Moving.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

As models become cheaper and more interchangeable, more value may move to the companies that own the customer relationship, workflow and distribution.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For the past few years, the AI industry has operated on a fairly simple assumption: Better models would create more valuable companies. The enormous investment going into chips, data centers and foundational models has largely been built around that idea.

China is starting to test the assumption.

In October, Reuters reported that China’s STAR50 technology index had fallen 40% in less than four months, wiping out around $480 billion in market value. AI-related stocks had grown to represent 42% of Chinese market capitalization and 57% of trading turnover across mainland China and Hong Kong.

Some of this is simply what happens when valuations run ahead of financial performance. But I think there is a more interesting change happening underneath the market correction. AI is continuing to become more capable while the cost of accessing that capability is falling and competition between model providers is increasing.

For businesses using AI, that is very good news. For every company investing billions to build the underlying technology, the economics may be more complicated.

The AI industry could create enormous economic value without the companies building foundational models capturing most of it.

The pace of model development is still extraordinary, but the gap between the strongest models is getting smaller.

The 2026 Stanford AI Index found that Anthropic, xAI, Google and OpenAI were all within 25 points of each other on the Arena leaderboard in March. Chinese models are also closing the gap, with Stanford describing the performance difference between leading U.S. and Chinese models as having “effectively closed.”

That matters because when several providers can complete the same task well, the buying decision starts to change. Businesses begin looking beyond which model is technically the best. Cost matters. Reliability matters. Speed matters. The ability to use a model inside an existing workflow matters.

I have seen this change in how we approach AI internally. When we started building more AI agents and automations, it was easy to focus heavily on the model. We would look at which model produced the best output and build around it.

As the technology has improved, the question has become much more practical: What is the cheapest reliable way to complete this particular task?

The best model for analyzing a complex problem may be unnecessary for extracting information from a document. A cheaper model may work perfectly well for a repetitive classification task. Some workflows can even use several models, depending on what needs to happen at each step.

Once models become components rather than the product itself, the economics of AI start to look different.

There is a tendency to assume that the companies responsible for the biggest technological advances will also capture most of the financial value those advances create. Technology markets do not always work that way.

Consider what happens when the cost of completing an AI task falls significantly. A customer service team can process more conversations. A developer can run more coding agents. A marketing team can analyse more campaigns and build more experiments. A small business can automate administrative work that previously required another employee or an external service.

The economic value of all those activities can increase even while the amount paid to the model provider for each task decreases.

This is why aggressive competition between model providers is so important. As capabilities converge and prices fall, some of the value created by AI moves downstream to the companies applying it.

For a business owner, cheaper models can mean better margins or the ability to automate a process that was previously too expensive. For a software company, it can make an AI feature viable for thousands of smaller customers rather than only large businesses.

The technology improves while the cost of using it falls. That can be great for the AI economy without necessarily being great for every company building AI infrastructure.

This also changes where founders should look for defensibility.

A model can have a significant technical lead and lose part of that lead within a few months. Building a long-term company around access to one particular model therefore looks increasingly difficult.

Customer relationships are harder to replicate. So are distribution, proprietary context and a deep understanding of how work is actually performed. This is especially relevant in business software.

Most customers are not trying to buy artificial intelligence. They are trying to get something done. They want to respond to a customer, prepare a proposal, reconcile an expense, schedule employees, create a campaign or understand why revenue changed. The model is only one part of delivering that outcome.

This is similar to a shift I have seen as we have become more AI-native as a company. The useful part is rarely the model in isolation. The difficult work is connecting AI to the right data, giving it enough context, building the workflow around it and deciding where a person still needs to intervene.

That business context becomes increasingly valuable as the underlying intelligence becomes easier to access. A company that already understands a customer’s workflow can potentially apply each improvement in AI much faster than a new entrant that first has to understand the customer.

I think that is where some of the more durable advantages in the application layer will come from.

There is another issue that founders building AI products need to understand early: Usage now has a cost.

Traditional SaaS created an attractive economic model because the marginal cost of another customer using a feature was usually very small. Whether somebody opened a dashboard five times or 50 times did not dramatically change the infrastructure economics.

Generating documents, analyzing conversations, reasoning across data or running autonomous workflows consumes compute each time the task is performed. This means a customer using an AI product heavily can also become significantly more expensive to serve.

It changes what good growth looks like. A team can celebrate that customers generated one million AI actions this month, but that number has little meaning on its own. If every action costs more than the value it creates, greater adoption simply increases the problem.

When I look at an AI workflow now, I am increasingly interested in cost per successful outcome.

How much does it cost to complete the task? How often does the AI succeed without intervention? How much human work remains? Does the task create revenue, save meaningful time or improve the customer experience?

Those are much more useful questions than how many prompts or tokens were consumed.

This also puts pressure on the subscription model that has dominated software for the past two decades. SaaS largely trained customers to pay for access. Choose a plan, pay a monthly fee and use the software.

AI introduces a meaningful variable cost into parts of the product. That does not mean every software company needs to abandon subscriptions. But it does mean businesses need a clearer understanding of the relationship between usage, customer value and cost. For some products, a traditional subscription may still work perfectly well. Others may move towards credits, usage allowances or a combination of subscription and consumption pricing.

What matters is that pricing and infrastructure economics cannot be separated.

If heavier usage makes a product less profitable, the pricing model eventually has to reflect that. If inference costs continue to fall, the opposite can happen: Previously expensive capabilities can be included more broadly, making the product more useful without damaging margins.

This is one reason falling model prices could have a much bigger effect on software than many people expect.

The correction in China does not make me less optimistic about AI. If anything, it reinforces why I think the opportunity for companies applying AI is becoming larger.

More competition between foundational models should produce better models, lower prices and more choices for businesses building on top of them. Stanford’s data already shows the performance gap narrowing, which means competition increasingly moves towards cost, reliability and usefulness in specific domains.

Founders should design around that direction of travel. Avoid making a single model the entire competitive advantage. Understand the workflows where the business has genuine expertise. Measure the cost of completing tasks rather than simply celebrating AI usage. Build systems that can take advantage of cheaper or better models when they become available.

Most importantly, focus on what happens after the model produces an answer.

The biggest business opportunities may not sit inside the model at all. They may sit in the customer relationship, the proprietary context, the workflow and the distribution required to turn intelligence into something useful.

That is why China’s correction is worth watching even for founders who have no interest in Chinese technology stocks. The important signal is not that AI is losing value. It is that creating value with AI and capturing that value are two different things.

As intelligence becomes cheaper and more widely available, that distinction will become increasingly important for anyone building a business around it.

For the past few years, the AI industry has operated on a fairly simple assumption: Better models would create more valuable companies. The enormous investment going into chips, data centers and foundational models has largely been built around that idea.

China is starting to test the assumption.

In October, Reuters reported that China’s STAR50 technology index had fallen 40% in less than four months, wiping out around $480 billion in market value. AI-related stocks had grown to represent 42% of Chinese market capitalization and 57% of trading turnover across mainland China and Hong Kong.

In a free Entrepreneur virtual event, Davis-Ross broke down what actually drives revenue online and what’s just noise. Here are five key takeaways from the session, from the metrics worth tracking to where to focus when your time and budget are limited.

Followers are easy to count, which is exactly why they became the default measure of success. But a follower who never engages, clicks or buys adds nothing to your bottom line.

If you’ve ever felt discouraged by slow follower growth, this section reframes what progress really looks like.

This may be the most encouraging idea in the session for early-stage founders. A tight community that knows, likes and trusts you can generate more revenue than an audience many times its size.

Not every business owner can post daily on five platforms. Davis-Ross addresses where to put your limited time and budget first, the common hurdles creators face, and the strategy and persistence it takes to push through them.

She also covers what it takes to scale a creator-led business once the foundation is in place. The session closes with an audience Q&A on platform choice and growth, where viewers asked the questions many entrepreneurs are wrestling with right now.

If your social strategy still revolves around follower milestones, this conversation is worth 40 minutes of your time. Davis-Ross draws on work with more than 100 creators to show what converts, what doesn’t, and where to focus first.

Seattle startup OneCourt is bringing its haptic devices for blind and low-vision sports fans to hockey, with the NHL and Ticketmaster making the tablets available free at the league’s marquee events this season and at all home games for four teams.

The device turns real-time game data into vibrations that users follow with their fingertips. For hockey, OneCourt draws on the NHL’s EDGE puck and player tracking data.

The hockey launch builds on OneCourt’s work in other leagues, starting with the NBA’s Portland Trail Blazers. Since 2025, Ticketmaster has offered the tablets at every home game for nine NBA teams, and it backed an NFL pilot during the 2025 season with four clubs, including the Seattle Seahawks, along with Super Bowl LX.

Mace started OneCourt as a University of Washington student studying industrial and product design. His co-founders are three fellow UW grads: COO Antyush Bollini, CTO Andrew Buckingham and CIO Nick Durand.

Time named OneCourt’s tablet to its Best Inventions of 2026 list last month, in the accessibility category. It was one of several Seattle-area innovations on the list.

#5452. Jensen Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO after affairs and spy scandal

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The move capped a remarkable fall from power for an executive who had been one of the faces of the generative artificial intelligence boom

Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO of Nvidia $NVDA, the company said Thursday, capping a remarkable fall from power for an executive who had been one of the faces of the generative artificial intelligence boom. CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO, the company said, after revelations of multiple extramarital affairs by Huang, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang also left the board, effective immediately, Nvidia said.

Nvidia’s board appointed Harvey C. Jones, a former CEO and executive chairman of Synopsys $SNPS, as its first-ever chair. The board is starting a search for a permanent CEO and will consider internal and external candidates. Kress will keep her CFO role while she serves as interim CEO.

"The Board has full confidence in Colette and the leadership team, and we expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption," Jones said in a statement. Kress said in a statement that she is committed to building on the foundation Huang created over 33 years as Nvidia's founder and CEO.

Nvidia stock was down about 7% in Thursday morning trading. It began a sharp fall in after-hours trading Wednesday evening after reports that the board was meeting to consider ousting Huang.

The resignation follows reports of two extramarital affairs. Huang, 63, admitted to infidelity in a note sent to employees on Sunday. That relationship was with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer. U.S. intelligence officials suspect she is an agent of Beijing’s spy agencies. (Jensen Huang and Alice Huang are not related.)

The second affair was with Kimberly Powell, according to The Wall Street Journal and other outlets. Powell, who runs Nvidia's healthcare business, has not commented publicly.

Jensen Huang rejected claims that his actions put U.S. security or the chipmaker's confidential information at risk once the reports about Alice Huang surfaced. The Justice Department is heading several separate probes that touch on Alice Huang, according to The Journal. Megaspeed and Nvidia have denied wrongdoing in a U.S. probe of suspected chip smuggling into China. And China's Foreign Ministry has called the espionage allegation unsubstantiated.

Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation on Sunday, overseen by a committee of independent directors. The company said Tuesday that the directors retained Joon H. Kim, a former acting U.S. attorney, and the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct it. The board said it had no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Three House Republican committee chairs have asked Jensen Huang to appear for a private session with lawmakers on Nov. 18.

The company is set to report third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.

#5451. Agility Robotics co-founder on its Nasdaq debut, lessons from Amazon, and the future of work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 5, 2026 at 6:51 pmNovember 5, 2026 at 6:51 pm

Agility Robotics of Salem, Ore., made its Nasdaq debut Thursday as the first publicly traded U.S. company devoted solely to humanoid robots — offering an ambitious vision for how the technology will change work, and a cautious view of how long it will take.

“Maybe we’ll never have faster-than-light travel. Maybe we’ll never have transporters from Star Trek,” said Jonathan Hurst, the company’s co-founder and chief robot officer. “But we absolutely will have machines that can do all of the physical work that a person can do.”

However, he cautioned, “It’s not going to be next year or five years from now. It’s really a grand challenge.”

Agility went public through a merger with Churchill Capital Corp XI, a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, led by financier Michael Klein. The deal valued Agility at $2.5 billion before the new investment and brought in about $465 million in gross proceeds. Its shares trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker AGLT.

After initially dipping below its opening price, the stock closed Thursday at $11.51, up 2.2%, bucking the trend on a day when the Nasdaq fell 5.5%, its worst day in 18 months.

Agility’s robot: The company’s main character is Digit, a two-legged robot with two arms mounted near the top of its torso that let it lift bins high and recover from falls. It moves totes and containers in warehouses and factories.

Digit 5, the latest version, was unveiled in September. Standing 5-foot-11 and weighing 284 pounds, it’s covered in sensors, with cameras and antennas in its head and safety-rated sensors in protective housings around its body. Agility says it can lift 50 pounds, reach 7.2 feet high and work more than 20 hours in a 24-hour day.

But the big advance is that Digit 5 was designed to work alongside people without a barrier. Earlier versions had to be fenced off from workers, which limited where customers could use them.

Agility learned how much that mattered at Amazon, an early investor in the company, which tested prior versions of Digit for moving and stacking bins in its warehouses.

Digit did useful work in tests there, Hurst said, but when Agility asked about scaling up, Amazon said it couldn’t deploy the robots. It showed Agility what it had taken to get its own wheeled robot through three to four years of safety certification, and said it didn’t know how a balancing robot would ever get there.

“The safety case to do this is unbelievably hard,” Hurst said. “Nobody has ever deployed a dynamically stable balancing machine, and it brings new risks.”

Getting a robot out from behind the barrier took years of engineering and standards work. Agility has been co-authoring ISO safety standards for the category and making its case to insurance companies and warehouse operators who want proof in numbers before putting a balancing machine next to a person.

Digit 5 uses AI and multiple sensors to watch for nearby people. Depending on the situation, it steers around them, stops or sits down. Visual and audio cues signal what it’s about to do, and a safety controller triggers its responses when someone gets too close.

Hurst credits the lessons from Amazon, along with ones from GXO, Toyota and Schaeffler, with shaping the design of Digit 5.

“Amazon was a huge, huge part of getting us to that point,” he said.

Amazon made an initial deposit in 2024 toward a $1.05 million purchase of five robots, according to Agility’s filings. Agility recorded about $1.04 million in net sales from Amazon in 2025, 58% of its total for the year. Hurst said he couldn’t speak to whether Amazon is a customer now.

With the safety improvements and other advancements, Hurst called Digit 5 “the scaling moment” for Agility. “That is the unlock,” he said.

One customer, which Agility has not named, has committed to a $300 million, three-year contract for 1,000 Digit 5 robots, according to its filings. The robots would be rented rather than sold, the commitment is subject to milestones and specifications, and the customer gets warrants that vest as the robots are deployed.

Agility has built about 10 Digit 5 robots, Hurst said, with the first prototypes just coming off the line. Its factory in Salem was built to eventually produce as many as 10,000 robots a year.

Financial picture: Agility’s business is still small, with revenue of $1.78 million last year and about $174,000 in the first six months of this year. It lost $362 million in the first half, up from $71.8 million a year earlier. Stock-based compensation, an accounting charge for employee equity awards, rose by about $252 million over the same period.

Agility had $14.7 million in cash at the end of June, before the deal closed, and management said in its interim financial statements that there was substantial doubt about the company’s ability to keep operating.

Hurst called the public markets his biggest unknown.

“I’m completely confident in our market path, our technological path,” he said. If public shareholders agree, he said, Agility will be able to “continue on this mission successfully and raise money when we need to.” If they doubt the company, “that’s going to make our life a lot harder.”

What Agility has that most rivals don’t is robots doing commercial work. As of May, its Digit 4 model had logged more than 65,000 hours across nine committed customer deployments, according to its filings. Digit 4 robots have moved more than 100,000 totes since June 2024 at a Georgia facility run by the logistics company GXO.

Investors have put far higher values on rivals still working largely in pilots, including Figure AI at a reported $39 billion, more than 15 times Agility’s valuation in the merger.

“Digit is doing real work in customer operations today, taking on repetitive, physically demanding tasks,” said Peggy Johnson, Agility’s CEO, in a statement. Going public, she said, gives the company more resources to put Digit into more workplaces.

Johnson became CEO in March 2024, when Hurst moved from CTO to chief robot officer. She previously ran Magic Leap, and before that spent six years as a Microsoft executive, leading business development and dealmaking under CEO Satya Nadella.

In an interview with GeekWire earlier in the week, Hurst took the long view on the stock listing, calling it a milestone on a much longer path. Treating a listing day as the achievement, he said, is a finance person’s frame: “I just don’t live in that world.”

From CMU to OSU: Hurst has been on that path for almost three decades.

He built his first walking robot in 1997, as a freshman at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh. He stayed at Carnegie Mellon for a Ph.D. in robotics, finishing in 2008, when fewer than 100 people in the world had earned one, he said.

That year he joined Oregon State University in Corvallis, planning from the start to eventually spin a company out of his research. In his Oregon State lab, Hurst’s team built ATRIAS, a two-legged robot that didn’t look like any animal because it was based on a mathematical model of walking and running. It was the first machine to reproduce the dynamics of human walking.

He started Agility in 2015 with Damion Shelton, a Carnegie Mellon classmate who was CEO until 2024, and Mikhail Jones, one of his Oregon State students, out of his lab there.

Being in Oregon helped from the start, Hurst said. Agility was almost alone in trying to build humanoid robots, and the engineers who moved to Oregon to join it were committed to that mission. The company had almost no turnover, unlike the Silicon Valley pattern of people jumping to a new job every six months.

But as it passed 400 employees, it needed experienced engineering managers, and Oregon had no robotics industry large enough to have produced them. Agility had been hiring those people in California and flying them north, so it opened an office there. Today Agility has offices in Pittsburgh and Fremont, Calif., in addition to Oregon.

Impact on jobs: For the time being, Agility pitches Digit as a way to fill jobs that are difficult to staff. Johnson told TechCrunch this week that the company has focused on “manual, very repetitive jobs, that it’s hard to find humans to do.”

Hurst calls the first commercial uses of the technology “step one” toward what he describes as the dream: “robots as part of everyday human life, doing the things people would rather not do.”

Asked what happens to the people whose work the robots replace, Hurst pointed to farming as an example of automation improving people’s lives.

“Early in American history, 90% of Americans worked in agriculture, and today 2% do,” he said. “And the only reason that’s true is because of automation.”

#5450. Let there be LEDs: Tech upgrade helps James Turrell’s Skyspace shine again at UW art museum

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:01 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:42 am

For most of the past dozen years, a James Turrell artwork on the University of Washington campus in Seattle — built to glow at sunrise and sunset — has been running on daylight alone.

That changes Nov. 14, when UW’s Henry Art Gallery relights “Light Reign,” its Turrell Skyspace, after a restoration that replaced aging lights with hundreds of new fixtures and a control system synced to the sun.

Originally installed in 2003 near the Henry’s entrance along 15th Avenue N.E., “Light Reign” is one of dozens of skyspaces by Turrell, the 83-year-old artist known for turning light itself into his medium.

Inside the artwork’s oval chamber, LEDs bathe the walls in slowly shifting color, and when the weather cooperates, a retractable lid opens to an oculus that frames the sky. From outside, the glass-paneled shell lights up with its own program — a 21st-century mood ring just steps from a bronze George Washington who has been gazing west toward the Olympics since 1909.

The relighting comes as the Henry, Washington’s first public art museum, heads into its 100th year. The museum opened on campus in February 1927, and officials are hinting that bigger changes are on the way for the centennial.

Trouble with “Light Reign” started around 2015, said Sage Sommer, the Henry’s director of exhibitions and collections. The original lights, by then more than a decade old, were reaching the end of their lifespan, and over time the museum lost the ability to run them.

Through those years, the Skyspace stayed open. Visitors could still sit inside, meditate and watch clouds and birds pass over the oculus, just without the color.

After years of planning, the Henry settled on a full lighting overhaul that also folds in ideas Turrell has used in his newer skyspaces. The exterior already ran on LEDs, but a very early generation of them, while the interior and oculus were lit by neon tubes made by Western Neon.

The museum didn’t work with Turrell directly. Instead it worked with lighting designer Ryan Pike, whose company, RHMP, works only on Turrell installations, from upgrades of existing pieces to new projects. Pike has worked on Turrell artworks since 2013.

For Pike, the toughest part was the exterior. “It’s just over 700 lights, in nine DMX universes, so each fixture can output independently of the rest,” he said in an email. DMX is the standard protocol for controlling stage and architectural lighting. Splitting the facade across multiple universes lets every fixture be programmed on its own.

Sommer said the Skyspace isn’t strictly time-based media, a museum term for art that relies on equipment and unfolds over time. But it raises the same questions. Sometimes the fix is simple, like converting a VHS tape to a digital file. Other times the hardware is integral to the work. Some artists insist a piece be shown only on a CRT TV, and some come back with a remastered version and want only that one shown.

“We work really closely with the artists to make sure that it is as they envision,” she said.

The Henry isn’t the only museum to face the problem. In 2023, Minneapolis’ Walker Art Center restored its own Turrell skyspace, “Sky Pesher,” after it became impossible to find the cold cathode tubes — a 1920s-era technology — that powered its sunrise and sunset lighting program.

Working with Turrell and his studio, the Walker switched to LEDs, which allowed more control and a much wider range of color. What had been “shades of tinted white” is now multicolored, Joe King, the Walker’s director of collections and exhibition management, said in an interview published by the museum.

The Henry’s new system uses roughly 840 LED fixtures, about 710 outside and 130 inside, Sommer said. The exterior program kicks in a half-hour before dawn and dusk. The morning show is brief, about 36 minutes, while the evening one currently runs about four hours after sunset.

“The very cool thing about this space, because we are so far north, is just how connected to sunrise and sunset it is, and how drastically different it is throughout the year,” Sommer said.

The roof has its own engineering pedigree. The Skyspace’s hydraulic lid, which lifts and slides out of the way, was designed by submarine manufacturers in Everett. It stays shut in the rain.

The museum closed the Skyspace in late July and used the downtime for physical restoration, too: repainting the interior, refinishing the teak benches, waxing floors, replacing worn locks, refitting doors that had swollen and cleaning out the gutters. Everything had to be rewired, and the project took longer than expected.

“Light Reign” is the most visible piece in the Henry’s collection of about 30,000 objects, including more than 18,000 textiles and 7,000 works on paper. Only a sliver is ever on view, so the Henry is putting its collection database online. The project was funded by UW’s Student Technology Fee. Anyone can book an appointment at its study center to see a piece up close.

Technology is also the focus of the Henry’s centennial exhibition, opening in late February. Swagato Chakravorty, associate curator, said he was surprised that no major museum had mounted a large, ambitious show on contemporary art and technology in decades, even as Seattle was transformed around it. His show looks at technology “from below,” focusing on the people and communities most directly affected rather than a “great man” story.

The exhibition is loosely organized around three threads. One is bioethics, including a work the Henry commissioned in 2002 with UW geneticist Mary-Claire King, which is being revived 25 years later. Another pairs Indigenous knowledge with tools like 3D printing and algorithms. The third is technology’s material toll, from data centers to water use.

Chakravorty said he deliberately avoids taking a side on whether technology is good or bad for art.

“Writing is a technology. Cave painting was a technology,” he said. As for AI: “It’s not going to kill art.”

The public unveiling of the refurbished “Light Reign” runs 3:30 to 6 p.m. Nov. 14, with remarks from Henry Executive Director Kris Lewis and the exterior illumination starting at 4 p.m. Admission is free, though the Henry encourages RSVPs, and interior viewing is limited to 25 people at a time for about 10 minutes each.

#5449. Lori Huang, not Jensen, is president of the Huangs’ $9 billion foundation—and co-trustee of the trusts holding most of their Nvidia stake

Jensen Huang’s future at Nvidia hangs in the balance as the board is reportedly preparing to oust the CEO, people familiar with the matter told The Wall Street Journal. The move follows two extramarital affairs by Huang, one of them with a suspected Chinese spy and another one reportedly with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, according to The New York Times.

Huang admitted in a company memo made public on Nov. 8 to extramarital actions: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Lori has not commented publicly on the memo.

Huang’s position has raised questions about Nvidia’s future, including who would take the reins in his absence, given that he’s the face of the $4 trillion chipmaking giant. But in the family’s philanthropy, his wife, Lori Huang, holds the top title.

Lori is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, according to its most recent tax filing reviewed by Fortune. Jensen is listed as the foundation’s secretary and CFO, and Lori has held the president title on every filing available dating back to 2014.

Her role also extends to most of the Huangs’ Nvidia shares. As of March 23, Lori and Jensen were co-trustees of three family trusts holding nearly 669 million Nvidia shares, according to Nvidia’s latest proxy statement reviewed by Fortune. That’s most of the 870.6 million shares (worth roughly $151 billion as of late Nov. 11) the proxy reports as beneficially owned by Jensen, a figure that also includes the foundation’s stock.

The proxy also says that as board members of the foundation since 2007, the couple may be deemed to share voting and investment power over its 58.7 million Nvidia shares, though neither has a financial interest in them.

Nvidia’s board said Nov. 8 it was investigating reports Jensen had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, but said it “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The independent directors later hired former acting U.S. Attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to run the probe. China’s foreign ministry has called the spying allegations groundless.

Lori, born Lori Mills, met Jensen when the two were paired as lab partners in an electrical fundamentals class at Oregon State University, where she graduated in 1985. He was 17 and she was 19. They married in 1985, and a few years later she left the workforce to raise their two children. Both children, Madison and Spencer, now work at Nvidia. Jensen said in an interview with Singapore-based media outlet CNA that “every moment of Nvidia, she was there.”

The foundation’s growth has tracked the Huangs’ gifts of Nvidia stock and the company’s rise. Its net assets climbed from about $819 million at the end of 2020 to more than $9.1 billion at the end of 2024, and about $8.6 billion of its holdings that year were in stocks, according to its tax filings. In 2024 alone, it gained about $5 billion in paper gains. Nvidia’s proxy shows the foundation held 58.7 million Nvidia shares as of March.

In June and September 2024, Jensen and Lori, as co-trustees of their living trust, gave the foundation a combined 1.3 million Nvidia shares, according to Jensen’s Form 4 filings and the foundation’s tax return. The foundation valued those gifts at about $160 million. In September, the trust also gave 688,000 shares to an unnamed donor-advised fund.

The foundation reported paying no salaries in 2024. Its only listed officers, Lori and Jensen, each report working one hour a week, unpaid, and its paid outside help consisted of an investment manager and an accounting firm.

In 2024, the foundation paid out about $126.3 million in grants. More than $82 million went to Schwab Charitable Fund, which sponsors donor-advised funds, and the filing notes the foundation gave to a donor-advised fund over which it or an insider had advisory privileges. Other 2024 recipients included Oregon State, which received about $30.5 million, and Crisis Text Line, which received about $10.8 million.

The filing also shows the foundation was required to distribute roughly $344.6 million in 2025 under federal payout rules. Its 2025 return, which would show whether it met that requirement, hasn’t been made public. Some public announcements from 2025 show the foundation matched $22.5 million in donations to the California College of the Arts, and in November, the Huangs announced a multi-year commitment of $5 million a year to San Francisco Opera.

This year, the foundation bought about $108.3 million worth of computing capacity from CoreWeave to donate to universities and nonprofit research institutes, a filing Reuters reviewed shows. Also in 2026, Vanderbilt University announced a $75 million matching gift from the Huangs for its art, architecture, and design San Francisco campus.

Nvidia and the foundation did not respond to Fortune’s requests for comment.

Sydney Lake is an associate editor at Fortune, where she writes and edits news for the publication's global news desk.

#5448. Amazon’s AI shopping agent moves into text messages, taking orders and tracking prices

by Todd Bishop on Nov 6, 2026 at 8:07 amNovember 6, 2026 at 9:35 am

Amazon is rolling out a new feature to let customers shop by text message — sending requests to its Alexa for Shopping AI agent, which will search for products, compare options and place orders on their behalf.

The idea is to make shopping work more like messaging a personal assistant. Amazon says the agent works in the background after it gets a request or a photo, and texts back when the task is done.

It’s part throwback and part hot new thing, reflecting a broader shift in how tech companies are offering AI agents for everyday use. OpenAI added texting to Dot, its personal AI agent, last month, and DoorDash rolled out text ordering in September.

The expansion of Amazon’s AI shopping assistant comes amid a larger fight over who controls online shopping when agents do the buying. Amazon has moved to block outside agents from Meta, Perplexity, Google and OpenAI from shopping its site while building its own.

The text thread is also a new place for Amazon to sell. The company says order updates, delivery notifications and deals will eventually land in the same conversation.

Digiday reports that sponsored products can appear among the options the agent texts back, free to advertisers for now, while purchases the agent completes on its own stay ad-free. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising sales in 2025.

The text feature started rolling out Friday to a small group of U.S. customers by invitation, and millions more will get access in the coming weeks, the company says.

Customers who opt in get a contact called “Alexa Shopping” and can send it requests that range from a note that they’re out of dog food to a photo of a recipe they want turned into a grocery order, according to Amazon’s examples.

The agent searches, texts back with options and completes the purchase with the customer’s approval. Customers can also turn on auto-buy to have it purchase an item automatically when the price hits their target. It can also watch for price drops, reorder past purchases and check on packages, and Amazon says a conversation started by text will carry over to the Amazon app, the website and Alexa devices.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, merging its Rufus shopping chatbot with Alexa+, the generative AI version of its voice assistant.

#5447. Which business moats will still matter in the age of AI?

Michael Joseph, CFA, is a portfolio manager and deputy chief investment officer at Meristead Wealth (formerly Stansberry Asset Management) and writes about markets, investing and the economy. As of June 30, 2026, Meristead portfolio strategies held positions in Planet Fitness, Meta Platforms and Amazon, which are mentioned in this piece.

For many investors, a company’s economic moat is one of the most important things to understand. A strong moat can protect market share, support pricing power and help a business earn attractive returns for years, even as competitors try to take those profits away.

The best moats usually come from something genuinely hard to replicate: a unique product, valuable intellectual property, scarce assets, scale or some other lasting competitive advantage.

Some businesses may be protected, at least in part, by the fact that their customers are human.

People are busy. We forget things. We don’t always read the fine print. We put off switching banks or insurance companies because it sounds like a hassle. We keep paying for subscriptions we barely use. And when shopping for something becomes too complicated, we often settle for good enough.

I think of these as behavioral moats. And the rise of personal AI agents could put some of them at risk.

We got an early look at that concern in September, when Meta’s Muse AI agent caught investors’ attention. Shares of companies that could be vulnerable to declining consumer inertia sold off. Charles Schwab fell more than 6%, insurer Allstate dropped 5.5%, Planet Fitness fell as much as 11%, and travel companies including Expedia and Booking Holdings also came under pressure. (Bloomberg)

The reaction may prove overdone. Agentic AI is still young, and there are major questions around security, trust and how much authority consumers will actually hand over to software.

But the underlying question is worth considering now:

Would a company’s advantage still exist if every customer had a tireless personal assistant constantly looking for a better deal?

Financial services may be one of the clearest examples.

Consumers routinely leave money in accounts paying less interest than they could earn elsewhere. That isn’t necessarily because they believe their bank offers the best deal. Moving accounts can mean comparing alternatives, filling out forms, changing direct deposits and reconnecting automatic payments.

An AI agent does not. In theory, it could regularly compare savings rates, credit card rewards or brokerage products and tell its owner when there is a better alternative. Eventually, agents could handle more of the switching process themselves.

That possibility has already gotten the attention of financial companies. Schwab CEO Rick Wurster recently said the company is blocking unauthorized outside AI agents attempting to access customer accounts or move money. Schwab is instead building controlled ways for outside AI systems to connect to its platform, while limiting what they can do. Other major banks are taking similar precautions. (Bloomberg)

There are legitimate security reasons for that. Giving software free access to your life savings is very different from asking it to order paper towels.

Still, the situation illustrates the broader issue. Friction can protect a business, whether that friction exists for good reasons or not. As agents become better at safely handling tedious financial tasks, some of that protection could weaken.

Sometimes consumers don’t stick with a company because switching is hard. They stick because comparing the alternatives is hard.

Insurance is a good example. Comparing two policies means looking beyond the headline premium to deductibles, coverage limits, exclusions and other details. Telecom plans can involve different data limits, bundles, promotional prices and fees.

A person may eventually decide the potential savings aren’t worth the effort.

Software doesn’t get frustrated after the sixth page of fine print.

This is another area where businesses are already preparing for change. Kin Insurance recently said it would welcome AI shopping agents rather than block them and has since built tools designed to make it easier for agents to obtain home insurance quotes. Insurance marketplace Insurify has also launched an AI Agent Gateway that allows agents to gather and compare real-time quotes while preserving details such as deductibles, limits and disclosures. (Kin / PR Newswire)

That may offer a preview of how companies adapt.

If AI makes comparison easier, businesses can try to fight the change—or make themselves easier for agents to shop. In some industries, being the company that gives an agent the clearest information and easiest path to a transaction could eventually become an advantage of its own.

Subscriptions may be the easiest behavioral moat to understand.

Many of us have looked at a credit card statement and found something we forgot we were still paying for. Sometimes it is a streaming service. Sometimes it is an app. Sometimes it is the gym membership that seemed like a great idea in January.

An AI agent could make that kind of inattention much less common. It could regularly scan recurring charges, compare them with usage and ask whether you still want to keep paying.

That concern helped send Planet Fitness shares sharply lower following the launch of Muse, as investors considered what easier cancellation might mean for businesses that rely on recurring memberships. (StreetInsider)

There may be some customers who keep Netflix because canceling is one more thing they haven’t gotten around to doing. Agentic AI could put pressure on that part of the business.

But Netflix also has something much harder for an agent to eliminate: content people actually want to watch. If a consumer wants a show that is only available on Netflix, an AI agent cannot shop around and recreate it somewhere else.

That is the difference between a behavioral moat and a real one.

Even when prices are relatively clear and switching is easy, comparison takes time.

Most people do not check every travel site each morning to see whether another hotel has dropped its price. We don’t constantly search every retailer to make sure something we bought last week is still the best deal. At some point, we stop looking and buy.

Travel companies are already building around this idea. Priceline’s Penny can compare destinations, prices and availability and move from a broad travel request toward an actual booking within one conversation. (Priceline)

But perhaps the most interesting response is happening in retail, where Walmart and Amazon are taking very different approaches.

Walmart recently introduced an Agent Gateway designed to allow outside AI agents to connect directly with its systems, search products and make purchases for customers. Shoppers will be able to control what their agents can buy and set limits on their activity. (Walmart)

Amazon, meanwhile, has blocked Muse from shopping on its platform, citing concerns including security and unauthorized access. Amazon is also developing its own AI shopping tools rather than simply opening its ecosystem to outside agents. (Axios)

Both approaches may prove reasonable. This technology is new, and companies have legitimate reasons to be careful about letting outside software interact with customer accounts.

But the contrast between the world’s two largest retailers shows how important the issue could become.

Today, a consumer might go directly to Amazon or Walmart to shop for a television. Tomorrow, that person might simply tell an agent, “Find me the best 55-inch television under $700.”

If the agent does the searching, comparing and buying, the retailer may no longer own the first interaction with the customer. That could eventually change the value of advertising, loyalty programs and simply being the default place where consumers begin their search.

Companies including Mastercard are already building infrastructure around this possibility, helping merchants make products available to AI agents while maintaining control over pricing, fulfillment and transactions. (Mastercard)

None of this means traditional business moats are disappearing.

If anything, agentic AI may make it easier to tell which ones were real.

A patented product or valuable piece of intellectual property cannot simply be compared away. Neither can truly scarce physical assets. A competitor cannot instantly create another well-located piece of infrastructure, another ski mountain or another casino license in a market where those licenses are limited.

The same can apply to real-world experiences. AI may find a cheaper vacation, but it cannot recreate the exact cruise, resort or experience a customer wants.

Those businesses still have to compete. But their advantage comes from offering something difficult to duplicate, rather than relying primarily on consumers being too busy or frustrated to find an alternative.

That distinction could become increasingly important as AI agents get better.

For decades, some companies have benefited not just because they offered the best product, but because consumers were imperfect shoppers. We didn’t have enough time, information or patience to constantly make the optimal choice.

AI may not eliminate those imperfections overnight. Consumers still need to trust agents with their money and personal information, and companies will continue putting limits around what outside software can do.

But if agents begin taking more of the work out of shopping, switching and canceling, one question may become increasingly important for businesses across the economy:

How much of your moat comes from being genuinely better—and how much comes from customers not bothering to leave?

#5445. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5444. The cracks in venture are beginning to show, just as Anthropic gets ready to IPO

On the eve of a historic IPO for Silicon Valley’s investor community, the fragilities of venture are as clear as they’ve ever been to me.

I’ve been thinking about this irony for days: Anthropic is set to go public as soon as next week (everything I’m hearing says “Jensen Huang’s affair be damned, all systems go”), and while this is primed to be a banner moment for VC, venture seems to be structurally over its skis.

Consider recent data from PitchBook: Hitting a $5 billion valuation takes 80% less time, but 74% more capital, according to the company’s latest U.S. Valuations report.

“Higher valuations raise the bar to achieve profitable exits, and AI is expensive to run,” said Emily Zheng, PitchBook senior research analyst, via email. “Cracks are beginning to show in venture, including large amounts of AI-related debt and a likely slowdown in data center expansion given the recent election.”

The reality is this: Valuations are soaring higher and more readily, but exits are still tough. Zheng is clear that the IPO window—unless a company is in a very select group like SpaceX or Anthropic—remains shut.

“The IPO window has not reopened,” she said via email. “Most listings this year have been in health care, with the high-growth tech names LPs need for distributions largely absent. Removing mega IPOs from 2026’s totals reveals that exit value remains at the same constrained level that has defined every year since the pandemic.”

M&A remains a viable option, but in many deals, Zheng said, “valuation compression remains the dominant theme, as Q3 revealed with Bending Spoons’ acquisitions of Airtable and Miro at significant discounts.” (Airtable, for example, was acquired for $1.28 billion in cash, a vertiginous drop from its 2021 $11.7 billion peak valuation.) Rising rates and broader economic uncertainty are primed to render these pressures worse.

Historical data also suggests the current venture vintage could be in trouble, according to PitchBook’s recent U.S. VC Fundraising and Returns data: Past funds haven’t necessarily performed well during periods characterized by high interest rates (new Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh already hiked rates once in 2026, and another hike’s on the table for December). There’s no way to prove causality, but the stressors of high rates, high valuations, and sluggish exits definitionally create pressure.

“The current market is a strange mix of high prices, low liquidity, and a relatively uncertain outlook,” said Zheng via email. “ The outlook for current vintages will likely not look as great as their current markups.”

And as the day of Anthropic’s seemingly imminent IPO approaches, it’s worth remembering that post-IPO performance has been dicey for the few major IPOs we’ve seen: CoreWeave and Circle, up about 52% and 116% respectively since their listing days, are the exception. Figma’s down about 42% in its life as a public company, while Cerebras is down roughly 45%. Nevertheless, what happens next with Anthropic will be the harbinger of where venture and startups go from here.

“Strong performance would validate AI’s enormous private valuations, spurring dealmaking and exit activity as real distributions are injected back into LP portfolios,” said Zheng via email. “Weak performance would bring into question whether AI companies are wildly overvalued.”

That is, of course, the multi-trillion-dollar question.

#5443. How to be unemployed: Glenn Kelman on life after Redfin

by Glenn Kelman on Nov 6, 2026 at 12:47 pmNovember 6, 2026 at 12:52 pm

After 20 years at Redfin, and 10 months of unemployment, I’ve co-founded a new company. My business partner and I will announce our plans after we’ve built our product, but in the meantime GeekWire asked me to explain what I learned in the transition between Redfin and this new venture.

Many of us are in transition because society is in transition, with AI hollowing out big companies and making it easier to start new companies.

In the past, my own transitions had been harrowing, because I ran out of money or lost my sense of purpose. Leaving Redfin, I thought “here we go again.” I felt self-conscious being in the grocery store at 11 a.m. on a weekday. I was ashamed when I couldn’t come up with an idea for a company. But I made it to the other side.

To do that, I had to convince myself that I was an intrepid explorer, even if what I was exploring wasn’t Mount Everest, but instead what I could be. I wanted to feel brave about encounters I otherwise would’ve found embarrassing. Over the last year, I met people about becoming a high school teacher, a Whistler bagel shopkeeper, a candidate for the state legislature, the founder of a tree-planting nonprofit, the CEO of a pre-IPO company and a project leader for Sound Transit.

The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.

At the beginning of my exploration, a CEO recruiter told me the startup scene in Seattle was “dead” and that, for all of Seattle’s talent, more companies were forming in New York and even LA. I Googled “high-growth Seattle startups” and the list included one company that went bankrupt in 2023, and Redfin, which was acquired in 2025.

Another friend told me that she was on a Discord channel with a bunch of CTOs who were miserable trying to do “AI transformations” at businesses with legacy codebases. At least for me, the logical response to all this has been to start an AI-native company in Seattle.

“The way to prepare yourself to do one thing for a long time is first to consider everything else.”

It took me months to feel ready to do that. In January, a friend told me I wasn’t allowed to make any big decisions until September. Another said I had to wait until the frenzy of my last job had subsided. “You’ll know it has happened,” he said, “because food will start tasting better” (it never happened).

At a conference, a fashion entrepreneur who’d built and abandoned vast residences in Jackson Hole and Costa Rica, and got divorced twice in the past three years, gave me a bracelet that said “we are enough.”

Since I’d often been thinking I hadn’t done enough in the morning to deserve lunch, it was a relief to feel that I didn’t have to be creative or productive in order to justify my existence. But relieving that pressure also made it easier to be creative and productive.

On a call walking through Volunteer Park, I told a friend that the bracelet reminded me I could be happy and never start a company again. She said, “YOU JUST NEED A CO-FOUNDER.”

She told me to share flawed ideas with people who could make them better. I set up meetings with potential co-founders, and we shared our ideas before they were ready, because our meetings had become deadlines. Then we used AI to turn our ideas into products, so we could see what was good and bad about each idea. Starting a company started to feel like a natural progression, instead of Athena sprouting out of Zeus’s head.

When I confessed to a friend that everything we were working on still seemed so small, she said, “What about breakfast burritos?” She outlined her vision for a shop serving breakfast burritos all day, with a line out the door. Then she started talking about inventing a nursing home “that makes everyone happy.” Rather than running a McKinsey market-sizing analysis, she just thought about what she wanted to exist in the world.

That’s something almost anyone can do. In her living room, I suddenly felt that humanity would always have an instinct — this is a bizarre word, but it’s what popped into my head — to fructify. I remember walking home from her house with my wife and hearing the thick sound of insects humming in the night as proof of life’s rich pageant. This is what I mean by surrounding yourself with good vibes.

The last step in my process maybe should’ve come first, choosing where I wanted to make a difference. I thought about all the companies that I honestly would’ve been proud to start, and they were all in the same industry. I had no experience in that industry, but a friend said I could offset that if I were willing to give it everything I have, which is what I’m now doing. I met amazing, generous investors who gave me a good idea, and a business partner who helped me think it through.

Through all of this, I depended on my wife more than any husband ever should. She works herself to the bone treating people with cancer, but she took my calls in the middle of her workday, when I would talk in detail about what to cook for dinner and then — one more thing! — what’s the meaning of my life?

Once, she was getting into our Chevy Bolt for her morning commute while I was rounding the corner with the dog, and I saw her brighten in the way many people did back when I was Redfin’s CEO.

I found myself full of anticipation. She reached into the car, as if to grab a small gift, and heaved something at me from across the street, saying it “needs reprogramming.” Before I realized it was a garage clicker, I thought she had said I was the one who needed reprogramming. “Maybe that’s true,” I said to myself, trudging past the browned lawn, and the dirty dishes, and into a world of possibilities.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
