#5442. How Megaspeed built a network in Singapore and Malaysia to move $7.5 billion of Nvidia chips to Chinese companies

The chip-smuggling controversy swirling around Nvidia centers on one company: Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing provider that, according to several media reports, is suspected of funneling advanced AI processors to Chinese companies.

While details of what Megaspeed is alleged to have done remain murky, experts say the case shows how Chinese firms rely on Southeast Asia to skirt U.S. trade controls.

“Chinese firms can access data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—and their computing capacity—without having to import restricted semiconductors,” Ja Ian Chong, a political science expert from the National University of Singapore (NUS), tells Fortune. “But the ease of shipping [chips] through Singapore and Malaysia also makes them attractive for firms and people who wish to circumvent U.S. controls.”

Washington restricts the export of Nvidia’s top-end Blackwell and Rubin chips to China, out of fear Beijing could use them to supercharge its AI ambitions.

According to The Information, Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, used her personal relationship with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to move at least $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips through Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary, Speedmatrix.

Singapore says it is investigating Megaspeed for “suspected breaches of our domestic laws,” but it separately rejected reports that its authorities were investigating Alice Huang over the espionage allegations. U.S. officials had also been investigating Megaspeed for potential export-control violations.

Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing; Nvidia has previously claimed that it found no evidence of illicit chip transfers.

Nvidia’s board said in a Nov. 8 statement that it was initiating an independent investigation into whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, though it added it had no reason to believe “either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” The board said it “prioritizes U.S. national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of NVIDIA and its shareholders.”

Following reports that Huang conducted a second affair, this time with an Nvidia executive, the chipmaker’s board is now considering removing Huang as CEO, the Wall Street Journal reports.

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based neocloud that supplies AI computing power. Originally incorporated in 2015 as 7Road International, a Chinese gaming firm with ties to state-backed investors, the company changed its name to Megaspeed in early 2023, the same year that Alice Huang joined the company.

Another Singapore-registered firm, Swiftdata, acquired Megaspeed in November 2023. Alice Huang stepped down as Megaspeed’s managing director, while Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong—who owns Swiftdata—became its sole director. (Tan owns another Singapore-registered company, Monster Investment.)

In 2024, Tan established Speedmatrix, a Malaysia-based subsidiary of Megaspeed, which was reportedly used to receive shipments of Nvidia chips. According to the New York Times, between June 2024 and June 2025, Speedmatrix received over 200 shipments of restricted Nvidia technology.

These chips—which are subject to U.S. restrictions on sales to China—were eventually used to power data centers built by Shanghai Century Litong, a Chinese firm in which Alice’s younger sister, Huang Yu, is a founding shareholder, according to The Information. The firm, which builds data centers in the Chinese cities of Shanghai and Shenzhen, then provides high-performance AI computing capacity to Chinese tech giants including Alibaba and Tencent.

“AI chip distributors and resellers often spend too little effort vetting customers, usually relying on paperwork the customer provides,” notes Erich Grunewald, a senior researcher at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy (IAPS), a U.S. nonpartisan think tank.

Malaysia has been one of Southeast Asia’s biggest beneficiaries of the AI boom, drawing $94 billion in data center investments between 2021 and mid-2026, including from global tech hyperscalers like Google, AWS and Microsoft. “Malaysia has ample land and relatively cheap electricity and water, at least for now,” Chong notes. “The fact that it sits next to key submarine cables also makes it attractive as a spot for data centers.”

Singapore, on the other hand, is favored by multinationals for its open economy, stable political environment and business-friendly policies. Many AI firms, including U.S. firms Anthropic and OpenAI, have chosen to house their APAC headquarters there.

Companies like Megaspeed typically offer two routes to restricted silicon. The first is renting out chips already housed in data centers in Singapore and Malaysia—which, under current rules, is legal. The second is buying chips through front companies and shipping them to China, potentially in violation of U.S. export controls.

(Megaspeed reportedly did both: it set up data center operations in Sedenak Tech Park in the Malaysian state of Johor, and according to the reports, also shuttled chips to Shanghai Century Litong’s facilities in China.)

Under current U.S. export rules, it is legal to give Chinese companies access to AI processors housed outside of China—though previous deals have invited regulatory scrutiny. On Nov. 3, The Financial Times reported that Oracle had canceled a $7 billion deal to grant Tencent access to 100,000 AI chips in data centers across Southeast Asia after U.S. officials raised concerns. The FT also reported that Nvidia is telling cloud computing clients they must sell at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese companies.

The U.S. House of Representatives passed a law—the Remote Access Security Act—that would close the loophole allowing Chinese companies to use AI processors housed in other countries; the bill is now before the U.S. Senate.

Both Singapore and Malaysia have cracked down on chip smuggling. In addition to its investigation of Megaspeed, the Singaporean government last year charged three individuals with fraud after they diverted AI servers bound for Singapore to Malaysia instead.

In October, Malaysian customs officials seized $12.1 million worth of advanced AI chips at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. Initial investigations found the 30 servers—falsely declared as electronic components—were being transferred from one Asian country to another, though officials declined to say which.

Megaspeed, however, has denied the allegations. “There has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company,” it wrote in a statement last December. “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.”

Chong says the escalating AI arms race between the U.S. and China means both Beijing and Washington will subject third parties like Singapore and Malaysia to deeper scrutiny to keep their own technology from leaking.

“Both Singapore and Malaysia will want to continue to benefit from trust by Beijing and Washington for as long as they can,” concludes Chong. “But they may face greater suspicion, scrutiny, restrictions and even punishment from one or both major powers going forward, and perceptions that they are unreliable or duplicitous partners will only increase such pressure.”

Angelica Ang is a Singapore-based journalist who covers the Asia-Pacific region.

#5441. XRP Price Prediction: Brad Garlinghouse Faces $1.05 Test as Whales Buy $72M

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP whales accumulated $72 million over four days, but its price remains dangerously close to critical support. Meanwhile, spot XRP ETFs recorded $10.4 million in net outflows, their largest single-day withdrawal since March.

XRP is hovering around $1.05, a level that could determine its next major move. With selling pressure mounting, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse faces another test of confidence in the token.

Garlinghouse has spent years positioning Ripple as a major player in institutional payments. Its ambitions extend across cross-border transfers, financial infrastructure, and institutional adoption.

However, XRP holders still need those developments to translate into stronger token demand. Ripple’s business expansion and XRP’s market performance are two different things. That gap has widened as investors reconsider their exposure to established crypto. Institutional partnerships can strengthen Ripple’s business without automatically triggering additional XRP purchases.

The latest whale accumulation offers some encouragement. Large holders adding $72 million worth of XRP suggests certain investors see value near current levels. But ETF withdrawals tell a different story. The $10.4 million outflow shows institutional demand remains inconsistent, even as whales accumulate.

Bitcoin’s investment narrative is gradually expanding beyond digital gold. Developers are increasingly exploring ways to bring faster transactions, decentralized finance, and additional applications into its ecosystem.

That shift could create opportunities for infrastructure projects targeting Bitcoin’s limitations. Bitcoin Layer 2 networks aim to make the underlying ecosystem more useful without replacing Bitcoin itself.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project pursuing this direction. Its approach combines Bitcoin-focused infrastructure with Solana Virtual Machine execution, targeting faster transactions and broader application development.

The project has raised $33.2 million at its current presale stage. Its current token price stands at a low $0.0136, with staking rewards reaching 35% APY. But its presale is scheduled to conclude on November 26, putting a deadline on the current entry opportunity.

XRP represents an established payments-focused crypto, while Bitcoin Hyper targets an emerging infrastructure opportunity.

For investors seeking exposure to earlier-stage projects, the potential appeal lies in entering before an ecosystem reaches maturity. Established cryptocurrencies offer greater market recognition, but emerging infrastructure projects can attract attention through their expansion potential.

Bitcoin Hyper’s pitch centers on making Bitcoin more functional. That proposition could appeal to investors who believe Bitcoin’s next growth chapter will involve more than simply holding BTC.

The immediate XRP price outlook remains heavily dependent on the $1.05 support level. Losing this floor could expose XRP to another wave of selling. The next downside target sits around $0.99. A move below psychological support could further weaken confidence among short-term traders.

However, XRP’s Relative Strength Index has fallen to approximately 24. That places the indicator deep inside oversold territory, suggesting selling pressure has become unusually intense.

Oversold conditions can create opportunities for a relief rally, particularly when large holders continue accumulating. But buyers still need to demonstrate enough strength to reclaim lost resistance levels.

A recovery toward $1.30 would provide an initial bullish target. Stronger momentum could subsequently bring the $1.50 area back into focus.

For now, the XRP price faces two competing forces. Whale accumulation and oversold conditions offer reasons for optimism, while ETF outflows and fragile support keep downside risks alive. Defending $1.05 could give bulls another opportunity to rebuild momentum. Losing it would put $0.99 firmly on the radar.

#5439. Current price of oil as of November 11, 2026

At 7:30 a.m. Eastern Time on November 11, 2026, the price of oil sits at $95.72 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s an increase of $2.74 since yesterday morning and roughly $30 more than at this time last year.

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted.

It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating.

Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas.

Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

Joseph is a staff writer on Fortune's personal finance commerce team. He's covered personal finance since 2016, previously serving as a reporter and editor at sites like Business Insider and The Points Guy. He has also contributed to major outlets such as AP News, CNN, Newsweek, and many more.

#5438. This 28-Year-Old Started a Caffeinated Side Hustle. It Made $125K in Year 1 — So She Quit Corporate to Work on It Full-Time.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Rosie Goldwasser wanted to create a product delivering calm, focused energy without the crash.

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Rosie Goldwasser, 28, of Santa Monica, California. Goldwasser was working full-time as a customer experience strategist at PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers) when she started her side hustle: More Than Matcha, a premium matcha and lifestyle brand.

The business hit $125,000 in revenue without spending a single dollar on advertising in its first year and doubled revenue in its second. Goldwasser left her corporate role in March 2026 to focus on More Than Match full-time. The brand is on track for between $400,000 and $500,000 in revenue this year. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

When did you start your side hustle, and where did you find the inspiration for it? I started building More Than Matcha in 2023 and officially launched in March 2024. The idea actually came from a personal frustration. For years, I was either too tired to function or too wired, jittery and anxious from coffee to sleep. There was no in-between until I discovered matcha. It was love at first sip. It gave me a calm, focused energy that actually lasted.

But finding high-quality matcha was challenging. Cafés charged $10 for drinks that consistently left me disappointed. At-home options lacked quality, consistency and a brand I could genuinely connect with.

Having spent four years in marketing and six years in customer experience consulting, I’ve always been fascinated by what makes consumers fall in love with brands and how to create experiences that exceed their expectations. As a daily matcha consumer myself, I saw a gap I couldn’t ignore.

What were some of the first steps you took to get your side hustle off the ground? How much money did it take to launch? I was never going to launch a matcha brand unless I found a matcha powder so good that I felt I’d be doing the world a disservice by not bringing it to market.

So I spent months researching, sourcing, sampling and learning everything I could about what makes exceptional matcha, from growing regions and cultivars to harvesting methods and sustainable farming practices. I finally discovered the four-cultivar blend we use. To this day, it’s the best matcha I’ve ever tasted. I’ve since had the opportunity to visit our supplier in Japan, meet some of the farmers behind our matcha and see firsthand the care that goes into producing it.

After finding the right product, I invested $25,000 of my own savings into building the matcha brand, without any outside funding. Over the next several months, I brought every detail to life: branding, packaging, website development, product photography — and all the little things that go into creating a brand from scratch.

Are there any free or paid resources that have been especially helpful for you in starting and running this business? For the first year of More Than Matcha, I packed and shipped every single order myself, spending nights and weekends fulfilling orders. I’d recruit friends and family to help pack during busy periods, turning my 700 square-foot apartment into a makeshift fulfillment center.

At first, doing everything myself felt like the smartest way to save money. But eventually, I realized I was spending so much time keeping the business running that I had almost no time left to actually grow it.

Making the decision to outsource fulfillment was a turning point. Yes, it was an added expense, but it gave me back something far more valuable: my time. Suddenly, I could focus on product development, marketing, partnerships and all the things that would actually move the business forward.

If you could go back in your business journey and change one process or approach, what would it be, and how do you wish you’d done it differently? I would have been much more disciplined about focusing on our hero product before expanding into other categories. When we first launched More Than Matcha, we introduced our matcha powder alongside four different hats. I loved the idea of building a lifestyle brand and imagined people wearing our merchandise everywhere.

But the problem was that nobody knew who we were yet. We spent so much time and money sampling, designing and producing merchandise before we had built a community of people who actually wanted to represent our brand.

If I could do it again, I would put that money and energy into making our core product even more successful, building customer loyalty and understanding what our audience wanted next.

When it comes to this specific business, what is something you’ve found particularly challenging and/or surprising that people who get into this type of work should be prepared for, but likely aren’t?Especially in the CPG space, you’re constantly making decisions that could change the trajectory of your business. From the products you develop and the manufacturers you trust, to your branding, pricing, hiring, retail partners and which sales channels to pursue. And when you’re a bootstrapped, solo founder, there’s no team of executives to turn to for the final call.

I’ve learned to start the decision-making process long before I actually need to make the decision. I’ll start interviewing candidates months before I’m ready to hire and begin conversations with manufacturers long before I need to make the switch. I’ll ask other founders about challenges they’ve faced before I’ve even encountered those challenges myself.

In a business where one decision can impact your product, customers and cash flow for months to come, that preparation can make all the difference.

Can you recall a specific instance when something went very wrong — how did you fix it? Just a few weeks ago, we were gearing up to launch our new matcha travel collection. After months of development, I had approved the final sample of our single-serve matcha sticks and moved forward with producing 25,000 units.

But the manufacturer kept delaying production. It wasn’t until the night before launch that the first four boxes finally arrived. I had a gut feeling something was wrong, so I drove to our fulfillment center to inspect them myself. Unfortunately, I was right.

The product was nothing like what I had approved. Matcha powder was leaking out of both ends of the sticks, covering the other products in the boxes. They were completely unsellable.

We had spent weeks teasing the collection, built an entire marketing campaign, redesigned our website and generated so much excitement. And just like that, on launch day, I had to cancel everything.

Rather than trying to hide what happened, I picked up my phone, filmed a video in one take and told our community exactly what went wrong. The response was beyond anything I could have imagined. Instead of being disappointed, our customers rallied around us. The comments and DMs poured in, thanking me for being transparent and refusing to compromise on quality.

We’re now working with a new manufacturer to bring these sticks to market the right way, and somehow our community is even more excited for their eventual launch.

How long did it take you to see consistent monthly revenue? How much did the side hustle earn? It took about four months to start seeing consistent monthly revenue. In our first year, we generated $125,000 in revenue without spending a single dollar on advertising. In our second year, we more than doubled that revenue, continuing to grow organically and reinvest what we earned back into the business.

What does growth and revenue look like now? 2026 has been a major reinvestment year for More Than Matcha. Rather than focusing solely on short-term revenue growth, we made the intentional decision to invest in the long-term future of the brand.

We completely rebranded, upgraded everything from our packaging to our website and spent much of the year developing our new matcha travel collection, our biggest product launch yet, now scheduled for early 2027.

Even with so much of our time and resources focused on building for the future, we’re still on track to generate between $400,000 and $500,000 in revenue this year, all while remaining completely bootstrapped.

What is your best piece of specific, actionable business advice? Done is better than perfect. When I first started More Than Matcha, I didn’t have a three-year, five-year or 10-year business plan. My goal was simply to get my idea out into the world to see if others believed in it too.

Looking back, I actually think that was one of the best things I could have done. Had I tried to map out everything I wanted this business to become before I even launched, I might have gotten so overwhelmed that I never would have started in the first place. Instead, I focused on getting a product I was proud of into customers’ hands, letting them validate the idea, and learning, iterating and adjusting along the way. About a year into the business, after seeing how customers responded and what opportunities were opening up, my long-term vision became so much clearer.

So figure out the smallest version of your idea that you’re genuinely proud to put into the world and launch it. Don’t wait until you have the perfect website, the perfect packaging or a five-year roadmap. Let real customers help you figure out what comes next.

This Side Hustle Spotlight Q&A features Rosie Goldwasser, 28, of Santa Monica, California. Goldwasser was working full-time as a customer experience strategist at PwC (PricewaterhouseCoopers) when she started her side hustle: More Than Matcha, a premium matcha and lifestyle brand.

The business hit $125,000 in revenue without spending a single dollar on advertising in its first year and doubled revenue in its second. Goldwasser left her corporate role in March 2026 to focus on More Than Match full-time. The brand is on track for between $400,000 and $500,000 in revenue this year. Responses have been edited for length and clarity.

There was no in-between until I discovered matcha. It was love at first sip. It gave me a calm, focused energy that actually lasted.

#5437. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5436. CFOs face a tough choice on AI spending as borrowing costs rise, expert warns

Good morning. Companies may need to rethink how much they spend on AI as financing costs rise and economic uncertainty grows. But pulling back too aggressively could leave them at a competitive disadvantage, finance expert Mark Williams told a group of CFOs gathered in New York City on Tuesday evening.

I had a fireside chat with Williams, a master lecturer at Boston University’s Questrom School of Business and a former bank examiner for the Federal Reserve Bank, during a Fortune Modern CFO dinner, sponsored by Deloitte.

“I think it’s going to be reduced,” he said of AI spending, arguing that a more difficult financing environment will bring greater scrutiny to investment decisions.

His cautionary concerns were part of a broader discussion about the post-midterm economic outlook, inflation, interest rates and risks across the AI investment ecosystem. Williams urged executives to prepare for higher capital costs without allowing uncertainty to paralyze investment.

“If we do nothing, then we’re going to lose our competitive edge,” he said.

For CFOs, that means being more disciplined about how they fund AI initiatives and evaluate their returns. Williams recommended having explicit measures of success or failure along with connecting project spending to financial results and considering shorter-term financing rather than automatically borrowing for the long term.

Post-midterm election, regulatory uncertainty adds another aspect to consider. Greater uncertainty can lower growth assumptions and reduce a project’s net present value, making fewer investments financially attractive, Williams explained.

The pressure won’t be evenly distributed across the AI industry. He described a divide between highly rated technology companies and lower-rated AI borrowers, with weaker credits facing greater financing pressure.

Companies with stronger balance sheets may be better positioned to continue investing, while more leveraged businesses could find themselves forced to reconsider their plans, he said.

That preparation should extend beyond investment budgets. Williams suggested finance leaders “stress-rest” accounts receivable and consider whether customers would be able to pay if economic conditions weakened.

He tied those risks to his broader inflation outlook. Persistent price pressures could keep borrowing costs elevated, raising the hurdle for new investments and challenging companies’ ability to generate sufficient returns.

“I think you should assume the cost of capital is going up,” he said when I asked what CFOs should do before year-end.

That preparation should extend beyond investment budgets. Williams suggested finance leaders analyze accounts receivable and consider whether customers would be able to pay if economic conditions weakened. He also questioned whether consumer spending would continue supporting the economy through the holiday season.

But his message is not to retreat from AI. Instead, he predicts finance chiefs will be more discerning about where they place their bets.

“Hold your chief risk officers close,” Williams said. “I think they’re going to be very useful for you in the next couple of months.”

Dev Ahuja was appointed CFO of QXO (NYSE: QXO), a building products distributor, effective in January. He will succeed Ihsan Essaid, who will become vice chairman, an executive role, at the same time. Ahuja brings more than two decades of experience. He joins from aluminum producer Novelis, where he has served as CFO since 2016. Previously, he held CFO roles at Novartis for Alcon North America, Alcon Japan and the company’s South Korean business. Essaid, who has served as QXO’s CFO since July 2024, will oversee mergers and acquisitions and capital-raising activities, reporting to chairman and CEO Brad Jacobs.

Adrian Wood was appointed CFO of BHP Group Limited, a global resources company, effective Feb. 17. He will succeed Vandita Pant, who will step down following the release of BHP’s half-year results on Feb. 16 and remain with the company through March 29. Wood currently serves as VP of projects, minerals Australia. He joined BHP in 2015 and previously served as VP of finance, minerals Australia, and group investor relations officer. He brings more than 25 years of experience, including at UBS and Macquarie Group.

Stanford’s 2026 AI100 report finds that AI has become a mainstream force reshaping science, industry, and society faster than expected, while governance and public oversight struggle to keep pace.

AI is accelerating scientific discovery and disrupting fields once considered resistant to automation, including creative work, software development, and mathematics. Yet the unprecedented investment boom in AI infrastructure has brought environmental pressures and concerns about a financial bubble, with broad economic gains and corporate returns still uncertain.

The central message is that AI’s trajectory should be shaped through meaningful public participation and coordinated, enforceable governance, not solely technological competition and market forces.

"It is up to the board to ensure a company’s owners benefit from the genius of founders but are protected by the madness."

—Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld and Steven Tian write in a Fortune opinion piece titled "Nvidia board’s idolatry of Jensen Huang could open the door to shareholder lawsuits in Delaware Chancery Court."

Sheryl Estrada is a senior writer at Fortune, where she covers the corporate finance industry, Wall Street, and corporate leadership. She also authors CFO Daily.

#5434. Cisco’s people chief: ‘We can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead’

Cisco is preparing its 85,000 employees to learn new skills, experiment with AI, and rethink how they work.

That takes more than teaching people how to use the technology. It takes time to learn, freedom to experiment, and leaders who are willing to change alongside them.

Cisco has invested in AI tools, role-specific training, coaching, mentoring, and new career development opportunities.

That focus on its people has helped earn it the No. 2 spot on the 2026 Fortune World’s Best Workplaces™ list.

Cisco is also seeing record business performance. It closed its 2026 fiscal year with record revenue and a record quarter, including record revenue per employee.

“Our focus is building learning agility: the ability to learn, unlearn, experiment, and apply new capabilities as work evolves,” says Francine Katsoudas, Cisco’s executive vice president and chief people, policy & purpose officer. “We want our people to be able to influence what changes, rather than simply react to it.”

Katsoudas says human judgment is one of the most important capabilities employees will need, “and the critical thinking, curiosity, and creativity that make it possible.”

“As AI takes on more work, we need people to challenge assumptions and make thoughtful decisions,” she says.

Research from the AI Workforce Consortium found growing demand for human capabilities, including ethical reasoning and systems thinking, in cybersecurity-related jobs.

At Cisco, employees are developing human skills alongside technical ones through coaching, mentoring, and opportunities to experiment with AI.

That requires something employees rarely have enough of: time.

Cisco’s Time to Grow initiative gives every employee four dedicated hours each month to learn.

“We’ve all experienced how easily learning can fall to the bottom of the priority list when business demands take over, but the skills our people will need tomorrow require investment today,” Katsoudas says.

Leaders have to make time for learning, too.

“When leaders openly invest in their own development, they help establish a culture where personal growth is expected and supported at every level.”

At Cisco, some executives are taking that a step further: They’re learning from employees.

Cisco’s AI Mentorship Program, or CAMP, pairs employee AI “super users” with senior leaders. Employees are the mentors; executives are the mentees.

“Understanding AI at a strategic level is very different from seeing how people actually use it in their work,” Katsoudas says.

Executives aren’t just learning about AI. Every participant in the first cohort said CAMP created space for candid conversations, shared learning, and experimentation.

“Our first CAMP cohort reinforced that AI fluency is less about mastering technology and more about building trust.”

That trust matters when employees are being asked to try new things.

“We can’t ask people to innovate if they’re afraid to take risks or try something that might not work,” Katsoudas says.

Eighty-nine percent of Cisco employees say management recognizes honest mistakes as part of doing business, compared with 38% at a typical global technology company. That makes Cisco employees 134% more likely to report that experience.

And 87% of Cisco employees are learning AI through experimentation, Katsoudas says.

For Katsoudas, what happens when an experiment doesn’t work is just as important.

“When things go wrong, do we create opportunities to learn and improve together? If we want to innovate faster, we have to accept that some experiments won’t work and learn from them.”

Eighty-eight percent of Cisco employees say people who try new and better ways of doing things are celebrated, compared with 65% at a typical global technology company. The same percentage say people quickly adapt to change, compared with 68%.

For Cisco, getting more from AI starts with leadership.

“The biggest lesson is that we can’t transform our workforce without fundamentally rethinking how we lead,” Katsoudas says.

How leaders use AI matters, too. Cisco employees are twice as likely to use AI when their direct leader does.

But role modeling is only part of the job. Employees also need to understand where the company is going and the role they have in getting there.

“In periods of significant change, people need clarity about where they’re headed, confidence that they have a meaningful role in getting us there, and trust in the decisions being made,” Katsoudas says.

Cisco also had its strongest year for employee productivity in 30 years, Katsoudas says.

Nine in 10 Cisco employees say people are willing to put in extra effort, compared with about two-thirds at a typical global technology company, according to Great Place To Work data.

Katsoudas says Cisco is seeing higher productivity and engagement among employees who consistently use AI.

“That’s encouraging because we’re seeing benefits that extend beyond efficiency,” she says.

Cisco also wants employees to spend more time on customers, relationships, and solving complex problems.

For Katsoudas, the companies that ultimately get AI right will be as intentional about investing in people as they are in technology.

“AI is changing what technology can do, but we need to be equally ambitious about what people can become.”

Roula Amire is the senior content director at Great Place To Work. Follow her on LinkedIn and sign up for the Great Place To Work LinkedIn newsletter to get the latest research on what drives business success.

#5433. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 10:44 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

#5432. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5431. The ‘boring job’ that millennials abandoned is one of the hottest seasonal jobs on the market—and could lead Gen Z to $200K salaries with training

It’s been called one of the dullest jobs in America. Boomers are leaving it in droves, millennials decided they’d rather do almost anything else, and AI was supposed to kill it off. Yet accounting has made it onto the holiday hiring list again for a second year in a row.

According to Monster’s Seasonal Hiring Index 2026, tax associates and tax experts were among the 13 job titles with the most seasonal activity across its platform—and it’s so hot, it appears twice on their list.

Last year, tax accountants topped Monster’s seasonal rankings.

The industry faces a huge talent shortage. In 2024, the U.S. was short of 340,000 accountants—and the problem is only getting worse. The average company now has 17 open accounting and finance roles they’re trying to fill, up from just five last year.

And so seasonal accounting cover could be a foot in the door to a six-figure career beyond the holidays.

“Seasonal work is more than a short-term paycheck; it’s often the start of a longer career journey,” last year’s report said, while adding that many companies use seasonal roles to test the waters for permanent ones.

To get in, tax accountants typically need at least a bachelor’s degree. Those with a CPA (certified public accountant) qualification can unlock higher wages of around $200,000.

Plenty of young people could use the work. Millions of Gen Zers are NEETs, meaning not in employment, education, or training. And with entry-level roles disappearing thanks to AI, young job hunters are three times less likely than previous generations to have a job lined up when they leave school. For many, even a temporary paycheck over the holidays would be a welcome start.

But Gen Zers who have just started thinking about nabbing a job over the festive period may already be too late.

In fact, Monster found that seasonal hiring jumped 44% from August to September last year and peaked in October. Then it fell by about 24% by November—and that drop showed up in both years Monster analyzed.

Tax and accounting postings were especially concentrated in September and October, well before the weather turns frosty and people are thinking about their Christmas plans.

And to make matters even harder, finding the few seasonal jobs left right now could be like finding a needle in a haystack. Many of them are hiding in plain sight.

Less than 3% of seasonal postings in 2025 used words like “seasonal,” “holiday,” or “temporary” in their title. So stop searching for “holiday jobs” and instead search by the actual job title, such as “tax associate.”

Monster also advises late starters to broaden their search to more titles and industries, and to use December to get ahead of the next hiring wave, because tax season, summer camps, and hospitality jobs often recruit months in advance.

Accounting aside, most seasonal jobs trending right now are retail, which probably isn’t surprising since stores need all hands on deck to get through the Christmas shopping rush.

Nine of the 13 jobs on Monster’s list are in retail or involve handling and delivering packages, so whether shoppers head to the shops or click “buy now,” a seasonal worker is probably behind it.

“Retail remains an important part of the seasonal market,” the report noted, before adding that the data shows seasonal opportunities across delivery, warehouse and logistics, tax and accounting, and hospitality.

“If working a cash register doesn’t appeal to you, consider fulfillment or warehouse work,” the report added. “The wider you cast your search, the more likely you are to find a seasonal position that fits your skills and schedule.

Orianna Rosa Royle is the Success associate editor at Fortune, overseeing careers, leadership, and company culture coverage. She was previously the senior reporter at Management Today, Britain's longest-running publication for CEOs.

#5430. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

#5429. Andrew Cuomo: Wall Street is ready. Congress needs to catch up

History shows that technological innovations have brought great advances to our nation’s financial system, but only after disruption, opposition and regulatory reform.

For over a century, Wall Street ran on paper, phones and people racing across hectic exchange floors. The “Canyon” was ruled by institutional giants whose power extended through the halls of government.

In the late 1960s, new technology challenged the status quo, with computers offering electronic pricing and trading. In 1969, a company called Instinet pioneered electronic stock trading. This major disruption threatened the Wall Street establishment and was met with skepticism, hostility and warnings about the perils of electronic systems. But while vested interests were opposed, the broader market was beginning to see the benefits.

In 1971, Nasdaq was formed to use an electronic platform to distribute quotes, but most trades were still executed over the telephone through existing brokerage firms. Following the national debacle of the 1987 market crash, when Wall Street was under tremendous public pressure, participation in an electronic execution system became mandatory for market makers. In the mid-1990s, emerging electronic trading networks, including Island and Archipelago, joined Instinet in posing a viable challenge to traditional trading.

In 1996, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt, a seasoned and courageous official, adopted landmark regulations increasing transparency and facilitating competition from electronic communication networks (ECNs). The SEC then adopted electronic trading regulations creating a more comprehensive regulatory framework for alternative trading systems (ATS).

Once unleashed, the benefits of electronic trading became undeniable, and the Wall Street establishment had a choice: either accept and incorporate the new technology or be replaced by it.

They are survivors. Today, electronic trading is simply trading, and the rest is history.

Now blockchain technology presents the same kind of moment, offering a new foundation for issuing securities, recording ownership and trading. Like electronic trading before it, blockchain has arrived, challenging the status quo, prompting vocal critics and forcing regulators to examine changing circumstances.

Blockchain technology is built on cryptography. Cryptography uses mathematics to protect information, verify authenticity and secure transactions. Blockchain uses these techniques to create verifiable, tamper-resistant records of transactions. Early applications of blockchain became widely known through cryptocurrencies and digital tokens, which could be exchanged for traditional currencies. But the underlying technology has applications far beyond cryptocurrency trading, including the issuance, transfer and recording of ownership of traditional financial assets.

In 2011, as governor of New York, my technology advisers and financial professionals introduced me to cryptography and blockchain as technological innovations that could streamline our financial system and help New York maintain its position as the global financial capital.

Our interest was piqued by the potential of cryptography and blockchain technology rather than simply by companies trading digital tokens. New York was the first state to license these companies. That underlying technology is what presents the great opportunity today.

Electronic trading ultimately earned its place because it delivered faster, better execution, greater transparency and lower friction. Blockchain presents the potential for the next step forward, offering faster settlement, a more direct connection between issuers and investors, greater transparency and, importantly, the possibility of a 24/7 global marketplace that could attract additional investment to American securities markets.

The days of nine-to-five hours and “closed for the weekend” signs are long gone for almost every economic enterprise, except Wall Street!

The SEC recently established an innovation exemption to facilitate the trading of certain U.S. stocks using blockchain technology. Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, and OKX, a leading financial technology and blockchain company, have formed a joint venture, OKXICE, which has submitted notice of its intent to operate a securities venue under that framework.

While there are regulatory hurdles, the SEC exemption is a groundbreaking first step toward using blockchain technology to trade actual securities, with the potential for around-the-clock access and faster settlement.

Adoption of new technology is disrupting businesses around the world. In finance, some intermediary functions may become less necessary or be fundamentally redesigned.

And 24/7 trading means investors can react in real time to information and developments in the public arena.

We already know blockchain technology can be successfully utilized in financial markets. Europe and other jurisdictions have already established frameworks to authorize its use. And we have seen explosive consumer growth in digital platforms offering 24/7 trading.

We also know that much of the financial establishment is changing its position. Initial opposition has increasingly given way to competition to adopt this new technology.

Once again, like electronic trading, companies face a choice: incorporate the new technology or risk being overtaken by competitors that do.

The next step in this evolution is for government regulators to adjust to the new reality. Congress’s failure to advance the CLARITY Act in September was a lost opportunity to establish a durable regulatory framework for digital assets.

With the midterms behind us, this should be a moment to put politics aside and focus on the economic stakes. The administration and incoming Congress must find consensus on developing a system that adopts this proven technology, protects consumers, ensures ethical behavior by our government officials and opens our markets for a new generation of growth.

America has always turned breakthrough ideas into lasting advances. Wall Street’s next electronic revolution is underway.

Congress should make sure America leads rather than follows.

The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

Andrew M. Cuomo is the former governor of New York and previously served as the state’s attorney general and as U.S. secretary of Housing and Urban Development. He co-chairs OKXICE, a joint venture between Intercontinental Exchange, the parent company of the New York Stock Exchange, and OKX, focused on developing infrastructure for tokenized and digitally native financial products, and serves on the board of OKX. OKXICE, OKX and Intercontinental Exchange are all named in this piece.

#5428. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
